Additionally, the omission of all conversation starters — which the final rule adopted as a required component to encourage investor engagement — violated the instructions set forth in Section II.A.4.

Second, the fee and conflict of interest disclosures were materially deficient. The Form CRS instructions under Section II.B.3 (Summary of Fees, Costs, Conflicts, and Standard of Conduct) require firms to describe principal fees and costs, including transaction-based fees for broker-dealer services, and to explain the conflicts of interest that arise from different compensation models. Ridgeline's vague description of advisory fees with no mention of transaction-based brokerage compensation denied retail investors the ability to understand the fundamental economic incentives at play — precisely the comparative information the SEC intended to elicit.

Third, the disciplinary history disclosure was misleading. Section II.B.4 (Disciplinary History) requires firms to affirmatively disclose whether the firm or its financial professionals have reportable legal or disciplinary history and direct investors to Investor.gov/CRS for details. By stating that its professionals 'maintain high ethical standards' while two professionals had material reportable events — a $185,000 arbitration award and a state regulatory suspension — Ridgeline made an affirmatively misleading statement rather than the required 'yes' disclosure. This omission could independently implicate the antifraud provisions of Section 206 of the Advisers Act.

Fourth, the failure to deliver the Form CRS to 310 new retail clients at or before the time of initial recommendation or the entering into of an advisory agreement violated the delivery requirements under Rule 204-5(b) and Rule 17a-14. See Section II.C.3 (Delivery Requirements). Retroactive mailing months later does not cure the violation, as the purpose of timely delivery is to inform investors before they make decisions about the relationship. The failure to self-report compounds the concern but is not itself a Form CRS violation.

Ridgeline's conduct reflects systemic non-compliance across content, format, and delivery obligations.
applicable_standard: Rule 204-5 under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (17 CFR 275.204-5); Rule 17a-14 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (17 CFR 240.17a-14); Form CRS (Form ADV Part 3 / Form CRS under Exchange Act); SEC Release Nos. 34-86032 and IA-5247; Investment Advisers Act §206 (15 U.S.C. §80b-6)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Ridgeline's Form CRS was deficient in format, omitted required fee and conflict disclosures, made affirmatively misleading disciplinary history statements, and was not timely delivered to over 300 new retail clients before initial recommendations were made.

fact_pattern:
Granite Peak Securities, Inc. (CRD #189432), a mid-sized broker-dealer headquartered in Rochester, New York, maintained a product shelf that included inverse and leveraged exchange-traded products (NT-ETPs), such as the ProShares UltraPro Short QQQ (SQQQ) and the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares (SOXL). Between March 2024 and January 2025, registered representative Kevin Moriarty (CRD #6418823) recommended NT-ETP positions to 47 retail customers through the firm's standard brokerage accounts. Among these customers was Margaret Dalton, age 72, a retired school administrator with a $340,000 portfolio, a moderate risk tolerance, an income-oriented investment objective, and a stated need for liquidity to cover assisted-living expenses anticipated within 18 months. Moriarty recommended that Dalton purchase $51,000 in SOXL and hold the position as a long-term growth allocation. Dalton held SOXL for 94 trading days, during which volatility decay eroded the position's value by approximately $18,340. Across all 47 customers, Moriarty's NT-ETP recommendations resulted in aggregate realized and unrealized losses of $127,615, with average holding periods ranging from 38 to 112 trading days.

Granite Peak's written supervisory procedures required registered representatives to complete an online NT-ETP training module and sign a one-page attestation confirming familiarity with the risks of holding leveraged and inverse products beyond a single trading session. The firm's WSPs assigned a supervising principal to review each NT-ETP transaction at the point of sale, but the review checklist consisted solely of confirming (a) that the representative had signed the attestation and (b) that the customer's account was approved for options or speculative trading. The WSPs contained no guidance on evaluating intended holding periods, no automated alerts for positions held beyond five trading days, and no reference to Regulation Best Interest or the obligation to assess whether a recommendation was in the customer's best interest under Rule 15l-1. The supervising principal, Diana Cho, approved all 47 transactions using the two-item checklist without further inquiry into suitability or best-interest considerations.

In February 2025, FINRA's Department of Enforcement opened an examination after a customer complaint from Dalton. The examination revealed that 31 of the 47 customers were aged 65 or older, that none were informed of the risks of holding NT-ETPs beyond a single session in any personalized manner, and that Granite Peak had not updated its compliance manual to incorporate Reg BI obligations with respect to complex products since the rule's June 30, 2020 compliance date.
question: Did Granite Peak Securities violate Regulation Best Interest and its supervisory obligations under FINRA Rules by failing to establish a reasonably designed system for overseeing NT-ETP recommendations, and what is the likely regulatory outcome?
answer:
Granite Peak Securities violated Regulation Best Interest (Rule 15l-1 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934) and FINRA Rules 3110 (Supervision) and 2111 (Suitability, to the extent pre-Reg BI conduct is implicated). The violation is clear on multiple independent grounds.

First, under Reg BI's Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)), a broker-dealer and its associated persons must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the risks, rewards, and costs of a recommended security and to have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the retail customer's best interest at the time it is made, considering the customer's investment profile. NT-ETPs are designed to deliver leveraged or inverse daily returns; holding them beyond a single trading session exposes customers to compounding and volatility decay that can diverge dramatically from the underlying index's return. Moriarty's recommendation that Margaret Dalton—a 72-year-old retiree with moderate risk tolerance, income needs, and an 18-month liquidity horizon—purchase and hold SOXL (a 3x leveraged semiconductor ETF) for 94 days was facially inconsistent with her investment profile. The $18,340 loss is a direct, foreseeable consequence of the holding-period mismatch. This analysis extends to the broader cohort of 47 customers, 31 of whom were seniors.

Second, Reg BI's Compliance Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iv)) requires firms to establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with the rule. Granite Peak's WSPs failed entirely to address Reg BI as applied to NT-ETPs: they contained no holding-period guidance, no best-interest analytical framework, and no automated surveillance for extended positions. The supervising principal's review was limited to a mechanical two-item checklist—attestation signature and account approval—which is analogous to the deficiency found in the Pinnacle Investments AWC cited in FINRA's July 2025 disciplinary report. Such a perfunctory review is per se insufficient under FINRA Rule 3110(a), which mandates a supervisory system reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and regulations.

Third, the firm's failure to update its compliance manual to incorporate Reg BI obligations five years after the rule's compliance date demonstrates a systemic disregard for regulatory requirements, which aggravates the violation.

Granite Peak has no viable defense. The attestation program, standing alone, does not satisfy the Care or Compliance Obligations because it does not ensure that representatives actually understand product-specific risks or apply that understanding to individualized recommendations. The likely regulatory outcome is an AWC imposing a censure, a fine in the range of $100,000–$200,000, restitution of realized losses (approximately $127,615 plus interest), and undertakings requiring wholesale revision of the firm's NT-ETP supervisory framework.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest, Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii) (Care Obligation) and Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iv) (Compliance Obligation) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); SEC Release No. 34-86031 (Reg BI Adopting Release)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The firm's supervisory system for NT-ETP recommendations was limited to verifying representative attestations and account approvals, with no mechanism to evaluate holding periods or assess whether recommendations were in the customer's best interest under Reg BI.

fact_pattern:
Greystone Wealth Partners LLC ('Greystone') is a broker-dealer registered with the SEC and a FINRA member firm based in Greenwich, Connecticut. In March 2023, Greystone began servicing the Harrington Family Office ('HFO'), a company organized to manage the investment portfolio of the extended Harrington family, whose combined investable assets exceed $450 million. HFO was established in 2018 and meets the definition of a 'family office' under Investment Advisers Act Rule 202(a)(11)(G)-1: it has no clients other than family clients, is wholly owned by family clients, is exclusively controlled by Margaret Harrington (the family matriarch) and her two sons, and does not hold itself out to the public as an investment adviser.

Grounded in the December 23, 2020 SIFMA no-action letter, Greystone's compliance department classified HFO as an 'Institutional Family Office' and determined that Reg BI's 'retail customer' obligations would not apply. However, Greystone's classification analysis was incomplete. While HFO technically met the family office definition, Greystone did not verify whether HFO satisfied the additional conditions set forth in the SIFMA request letter for qualifying as an 'Institutional Family Office.' Specifically, HFO's investment decisions were not made by a chief investment officer or investment committee with institutional-level sophistication; instead, day-to-day investment decisions were delegated to Margaret Harrington's 26-year-old grandson, Tyler Harrington, who had only two years of experience as a junior equity analyst and no professional certifications.

Relying on the institutional classification, Greystone's registered representative, Daniel Kessler, recommended that HFO allocate $35 million into a series of illiquid structured credit products with 7-year lockup periods, embedded leverage of 3:1, and annual management fees of 2.75%. Kessler did not conduct a Reg BI care obligation analysis, did not evaluate the recommendation against HFO's investment profile, and did not disclose material conflicts of interest—including that Greystone received a $525,000 placement fee from the structured product sponsor. Greystone also did not deliver a Form CRS to HFO, reasoning that the institutional classification exempted them from that requirement as well. In September 2023, the structured credit products suffered a 40% decline in value, and Tyler Harrington, on behalf of HFO, filed a complaint with FINRA.
question: Did Greystone Wealth Partners properly rely on the December 2020 SIFMA no-action letter to classify the Harrington Family Office as an Institutional Family Office exempt from Reg BI and Form CRS requirements?
answer:
No. Greystone's reliance on the SIFMA no-action letter was improper, and its failure to apply Reg BI and Form CRS requirements to HFO constitutes a compliance failure.

The December 23, 2020 no-action letter from the SEC Division of Trading and Markets' Chief Counsel, Emily Westerberg Russell, provided that the Staff would not recommend enforcement action against broker-dealers that do not treat family offices qualifying as 'Institutional Family Offices' as 'retail customers' under Reg BI (Rule 15l-1 under the Exchange Act) or as 'retail investors' for Form CRS purposes. However, the letter explicitly states that the Staff's position is 'based strictly on the facts and circumstances discussed in [the SIFMA] Request, and any different facts or circumstances might require a different response.'

This is critical because the no-action relief was conditioned on the specific representations and conditions outlined in SIFMA's request letter. An 'Institutional Family Office' classification requires more than merely satisfying the family office definition under Advisers Act Rule 202(a)(11)(G)-1. The SIFMA letter contemplated that qualifying Institutional Family Offices would possess institutional-level sophistication in their investment decision-making—analogous to the sophistication standards applied to qualified purchasers or institutional accounts under FINRA Rule 4512(c). Greystone failed to verify whether HFO met these conditions. The fact that Tyler Harrington—a 26-year-old with only two years of junior-level experience and no professional designations—was making investment decisions for a $450 million portfolio undermines any claim of institutional sophistication.

Because HFO does not qualify as an Institutional Family Office under the specific conditions of the no-action letter, it remains a 'retail customer' under Reg BI Rule 15l-1(b)(1), which defines a retail customer as a natural person or the legal representative of such person who receives a recommendation of any securities transaction or investment strategy involving securities from a broker-dealer. Greystone therefore was obligated to comply with all four component obligations of Reg BI: Disclosure (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i)), Care (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)), Conflict of Interest (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iii)), and Compliance (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iv)).

Kessler's failure to evaluate the suitability of a $35 million illiquid structured credit allocation with 3:1 leverage for HFO's profile violates the Care Obligation. The non-disclosure of the $525,000 placement fee violates the Disclosure and Conflict of Interest Obligations. The failure to deliver Form CRS violates Rule 17a-14. Moreover, the no-action letter's footnote 5 reminds firms that under Exchange Act Section 29(a), Reg BI protections cannot be waived—reinforcing that improper classification cannot serve as a shield. Greystone bears significant enforcement risk.
applicable_standard: Reg BI Rule 15l-1(a)(1)-(2) (Exchange Act); Reg BI Care Obligation Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii); Reg BI Disclosure Obligation Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i); Reg BI Conflict of Interest Obligation Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iii); Form CRS Rule 17a-14; Investment Advisers Act Rule 202(a)(11)(G)-1; Exchange Act Section 29(a); SIFMA No-Action Letter (Dec. 23, 2020)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Greystone failed to verify that the Harrington Family Office met the specific conditions for 'Institutional Family Office' classification under the SIFMA no-action letter—particularly the requirement of institutional-level investment sophistication—rendering its exemption from Reg BI and Form CRS inapplicable.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Webb is a registered representative with Ridgeline Securities, LLC, a mid-sized broker-dealer based in Charlotte, North Carolina. On August 15, 2020—after the June 30, 2020 Reg BI compliance date—Marcus received a call from Patricia Dominguez, a 68-year-old retired schoolteacher with a $410,000 rollover IRA and approximately $85,000 in a taxable brokerage account at Ridgeline. Patricia's investment profile, documented during her most recent account update in January 2020, listed her risk tolerance as 'moderate-conservative,' her time horizon as '10-15 years,' her annual income from pension and Social Security as $52,000, and her liquid net worth (exclusive of her primary residence) as $510,000. She told Marcus she wanted 'steady income with some growth to keep up with inflation.'

Marcus recommended that Patricia invest $200,000 of her IRA into the Ridgeline Structured Income Note Series 7, a proprietary structured product with a seven-year maturity, a 5.25% coupon tied to the S&P 500 remaining above a 70% knock-in barrier, and an early redemption penalty equivalent to 4% of principal. Ridgeline earned a 3.1% placement fee on these notes, compared to 0.75% on third-party bond funds that Marcus could also have recommended. Ridgeline's compliance department had recently updated its conflict-of-interest policies in response to Reg BI but had not yet implemented a process to evaluate whether the heightened compensation on proprietary structured notes created a material conflict requiring mitigation under the Conflict of Interest Obligation. The firm's product committee had approved the note for sale to customers with 'moderate' or higher risk tolerances but performed no comparative cost-benefit analysis against reasonably available alternatives.

Marcus did not discuss any alternative income-producing investments with Patricia, nor did he disclose the magnitude of the compensation differential between the proprietary note and comparable third-party products. He provided the standard Form CRS but did not furnish any supplemental written disclosure regarding the specific conflicts associated with this transaction. The trade was executed on August 20, 2020. Patricia's IRA was now approximately 49% concentrated in a single illiquid structured product. Three months later, when Patricia needed $30,000 for unexpected medical expenses, she discovered that early redemption would cost her $8,000 in penalties, and she filed a complaint with FINRA.
question: Did Marcus Webb and Ridgeline Securities comply with Regulation Best Interest in connection with the recommendation of the proprietary structured note to Patricia Dominguez?
answer:
No. Marcus Webb and Ridgeline Securities failed to comply with Regulation Best Interest (Rule 15l-1 under the Exchange Act) on multiple grounds. Because this recommendation was made to a retail customer after June 30, 2020, it is squarely subject to Reg BI rather than FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), consistent with FINRA's proposed amendments in SR-FINRA-2020-007, which added Supplementary Material .08 to Rule 2111 stating that the suitability rule does not apply to recommendations subject to Reg BI.

Reg BI imposes four component obligations: Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance. Marcus and Ridgeline fell short on at least three.

First, regarding the Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B)), the broker-dealer must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the potential risks, rewards, and costs of the recommendation, have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the customer's best interest, and consider reasonably available alternatives. Marcus recommended concentrating nearly half of Patricia's IRA—her primary retirement asset—in a single illiquid structured product with a seven-year lockup and a knock-in barrier tied to equity index performance, for a client who is 68 years old, moderate-conservative in risk tolerance, and dependent on retirement income. He failed to consider or present any reasonably available alternatives, such as diversified bond funds or Treasury ladders, which would have offered income with significantly greater liquidity and lower cost. The 4% early redemption penalty was materially inconsistent with Patricia's potential liquidity needs.

Second, regarding the Conflict of Interest Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(C)), Ridgeline was required to establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to identify and mitigate conflicts of interest, including those arising from compensation structures that incentivize recommendations of proprietary products. The 3.1% placement fee—more than four times the compensation on comparable alternatives—is a textbook material conflict. Ridgeline's compliance department acknowledged the need to update its procedures but had not yet implemented a process to evaluate or mitigate this specific compensation-driven conflict, rendering its policies deficient.

Third, regarding the Disclosure Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(A)), while Form CRS was provided, it is a general document. The SEC's Release No. 86031 makes clear that material facts relating to conflicts associated with a specific recommendation must be disclosed prior to or at the time of the recommendation. Marcus failed to disclose the compensation differential or the specific conflicts associated with recommending the proprietary note.

Ridgeline cannot defend on the basis that the product was approved by its product committee, because the approval process itself was inadequate—no comparative cost analysis was performed. The pivotal failures here are the absence of a reasonable alternatives analysis, the unmitigated compensation conflict, and the inadequate disclosure, all of which collectively demonstrate a recommendation that did not meet the best interest standard.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest, Rule 15l-1 (17 CFR 240.15l-1), including the Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B)), Conflict of Interest Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(C)), and Disclosure Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(A)); SEC Release No. 34-86031 (84 FR 33318); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) as amended by SR-FINRA-2020-007 (Release No. 34-88422), Supplementary Material .08
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Marcus failed to consider reasonably available alternatives or mitigate the material compensation conflict created by a proprietary product placement fee more than four times higher than that of comparable third-party products, while concentrating nearly half of a retired client's IRA in a single illiquid structured note.

fact_pattern:
Ridgeline Capital Partners, LLC ('Ridgeline') is a dually registered broker-dealer and investment adviser with 47 registered representatives operating across six branch offices in the southeastern United States. In March 2025, Ridgeline entered into a selling agreement with Pinnacle Insurance Group to distribute Pinnacle's new registered index-linked annuity (RILA) product, the 'Pinnacle Shield Plus 10,' which offers a 10% downside buffer with participation rates tied to the S&P 500 and a six-year surrender period with declining surrender charges starting at 8.5%.

Ridgeline's Chief Compliance Officer, Dana Whitfield, conducted a brief due diligence review of Pinnacle but did not evaluate Pinnacle's financial stability ratings, claims-paying history, or the specific fee layers embedded in the RILA product—including a 1.25% annual spread fee and a 0.40% rider charge for an optional death benefit that was automatically included in all customer recommendations. Ridgeline also failed to update its written supervisory procedures (WSPs) to address the unique characteristics of RILAs as a distinct product category, instead relying on its existing variable annuity procedures. No product-specific training was provided to registered representatives before they began recommending the Pinnacle Shield Plus 10.

Between April and August 2025, registered representative Marcus Delano recommended the Pinnacle Shield Plus 10 to 23 retail customers, including 68-year-old recently retired schoolteacher Gloria Fuentes. Ms. Fuentes had $340,000 in a traditional IRA rollover, a moderate risk tolerance, an annual income need of $28,000 from her portfolio beginning in two years, and had explicitly stated on her new account form that she needed access to her funds within three to five years for potential healthcare expenses. Delano recommended that Ms. Fuentes invest $280,000—approximately 82% of her liquid retirement assets—into the Pinnacle Shield Plus 10 without discussing the six-year surrender period, the surrender charges, or the embedded rider costs. Delano's rationale, documented in a single sentence in the firm's CRM system, stated only: 'Client wants downside protection and growth potential—RILA suitable.' Ridgeline's supervisory principal, Kevin Marsh, approved the transaction the same day without requesting additional documentation or questioning the concentration level or the liquidity mismatch.
question: Did Ridgeline Capital Partners and its registered representative Marcus Delano satisfy their obligations under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) and applicable FINRA supervisory rules in connection with the recommendation of the Pinnacle Shield Plus 10 RILA to Gloria Fuentes?
answer:
No. Ridgeline and Delano failed to satisfy multiple component obligations of Regulation Best Interest (SEC Rule 15l-1) and violated FINRA supervisory requirements. The analysis proceeds through each Reg BI component obligation and applicable FINRA rules.

First, regarding the Care Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(B), a broker-dealer must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the recommended security, then have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the retail customer's best interest based on the customer's investment profile. Ms. Fuentes's profile—68 years old, recently retired, moderate risk tolerance, near-term income needs of $28,000 annually starting within two years, and stated need for liquidity within three to five years for healthcare—is fundamentally incompatible with an 82% allocation to a product carrying a six-year surrender period with 8.5% initial surrender charges. The concentration of $280,000 out of $340,000 in a single illiquid product creates a severe liquidity mismatch. Delano's one-sentence rationale is facially insufficient to demonstrate reasonable diligence regarding costs, risks, and alternatives. This fails both the customer-specific and reasonable-basis suitability prongs embedded in the Care Obligation.

Second, regarding the Disclosure Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i), Delano failed to disclose material facts about the RILA, including the surrender period, surrender charges, embedded spread fee of 1.25%, and the 0.40% automatic rider charge. These are material cost and liquidity facts that a reasonable investor would consider important.

Third, the Compliance Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iv) requires firms to establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI. Ridgeline's failure to create RILA-specific WSPs, instead relying on variable annuity procedures that do not address the distinct risk-return profile of index-linked annuities (which feature buffer structures and spread fees), constitutes a deficiency. The 2025 FINRA Annual Regulatory Oversight Report specifically highlights RILAs as a new topic area, signaling heightened regulatory expectations for product-specific supervisory frameworks.

Fourth, under FINRA Rules 3110(a) and (b), Ridgeline was required to establish and maintain a supervisory system and WSPs reasonably designed to supervise each type of business in which it engages. Supervisory principal Kevin Marsh's same-day approval without reviewing the concentration, liquidity mismatch, or adequacy of documentation reflects a failure of supervisory review. Additionally, under the third-party risk landscape discussion new for 2025 in the Report, Ridgeline's inadequate due diligence on Pinnacle—omitting financial stability analysis and product fee evaluation—represents a failure to manage third-party product risk.

Ridgeline cannot defend on the basis that the RILA offered downside protection, as the buffer feature does not cure the fundamental liquidity and concentration mismatch. The pivotal facts are the six-year lock-up against a three-to-five-year liquidity need and the overwhelming concentration of retirement assets in a single illiquid product.
applicable_standard: SEC Regulation Best Interest Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i)-(iv) (Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance Obligations); FINRA Rule 3110(a) and (b) (Supervision and Written Supervisory Procedures); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability, as incorporated into Reg BI analysis); SEC Release No. 34-86031 (Reg BI Adopting Release, June 2019)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The recommendation placed 82% of a 68-year-old retiree's liquid retirement assets into a product with a six-year surrender period despite her documented need for liquidity within three to five years, demonstrating a fundamental failure of the Reg BI Care Obligation.

fact_pattern:
AlgoWealth Advisors, LLC ('AlgoWealth') is a registered investment adviser based in Austin, Texas, that launched its robo-advisory platform in March 2021. The platform provides discretionary asset management services to retail clients through a mobile application and website, with no option for direct human interaction with investment advisory personnel. As of December 2023, AlgoWealth manages approximately $1.2 billion in assets for roughly 47,000 client accounts, with an average account size of $25,500. The firm charges 0.25% annually on assets under management.

AlgoWealth's onboarding process requires new clients to complete a five-question intake questionnaire. The questions ask for: (1) the client's age, (2) approximate annual income (selected from four brackets: under $50K, $50K–$100K, $100K–$250K, over $250K), (3) a self-assessed risk tolerance on a scale of 1–5, (4) a general investment goal selected from three options ('Grow my wealth,' 'Save for retirement,' or 'Preserve my capital'), and (5) an estimated investment time horizon chosen from three ranges (under 5 years, 5–15 years, over 15 years). The questionnaire does not ask about the client's total net worth, existing investment holdings outside AlgoWealth, liquidity needs, tax situation, debt obligations, or any specific financial circumstances such as upcoming major expenses or dependents.

In September 2023, Margaret Cho, a 62-year-old recently widowed schoolteacher in San Diego earning $68,000 annually, opened an account with AlgoWealth and deposited $410,000—the entirety of her late husband's life insurance payout. She selected 'Save for retirement' as her goal, indicated a risk tolerance of 3 out of 5, and chose the '5–15 years' time horizon. Based solely on these inputs, AlgoWealth's algorithm placed her in a 'Moderate Growth' portfolio consisting of 70% equity ETFs (including 15% in emerging markets and 10% in small-cap growth) and 30% fixed-income ETFs. The algorithm did not account for the fact that this $410,000 represented substantially all of Ms. Cho's liquid assets, that she had no other retirement savings beyond a modest CalSTRS pension, or that she would need to begin drawing on these funds within three years when she planned to retire at age 65.

By February 2024, Ms. Cho's portfolio had declined approximately 14% to $352,600 due to a significant emerging markets selloff and rising interest rates impacting small-cap equities. When she attempted to contact AlgoWealth about her losses, she could only reach a chatbot that directed her to FAQ pages. AlgoWealth's compliance program had no procedures for escalating client concerns to human compliance personnel, nor did it include any periodic review mechanism to assess whether the algorithm's recommendations remained suitable for clients whose circumstances may have changed. The firm's Form ADV Part 2A brochure disclosed the algorithmic nature of the service and stated that 'investment recommendations are based on information provided by the client,' but did not explain the limitations of its questionnaire or the risks of relying on limited client data.
question: Did AlgoWealth Advisors, LLC violate its fiduciary obligations under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 by relying on an inadequate client questionnaire and failing to implement a compliance program reasonably designed to address the risks of providing automated investment advice?
answer:
Yes, AlgoWealth violated its fiduciary obligations under the Advisers Act in multiple, overlapping respects. The analysis proceeds along the three areas identified in IM Guidance Update 2017-02.

First, regarding the duty to obtain sufficient client information (Advisers Act §206(1) and (2) fiduciary duty; IM Guidance 2017-02, Section 2): The Staff guidance specifically states that robo-advisers have an obligation to obtain information from clients sufficient to support a duty to provide suitable advice. The guidance emphasizes that robo-advisers should consider whether their questionnaires elicit sufficient information to meet the suitability obligation and whether the questions are designed to address potential inconsistencies in client responses. AlgoWealth's five-question intake was critically deficient. It failed to gather information about Ms. Cho's total net worth, existing retirement savings, liquidity needs, debt obligations, tax situation, or the fact that the deposited funds represented substantially all of her liquid wealth. Without this information, the algorithm could not meaningfully assess suitability. Placing a 62-year-old client who is three years from retirement, with no material savings beyond this single deposit, into a 70% equity portfolio with significant emerging markets and small-cap exposure is facially unsuitable when viewed against the totality of her circumstances.

Second, regarding disclosure obligations (Advisers Act §206(1), (2), and (4); Form ADV Part 2A; IM Guidance 2017-02, Section 1): The guidance instructs robo-advisers to provide meaningful disclosure about the limitations of their services, including the scope and limitations of the advisory services, the risks of relying on limited client data, and the degree of human oversight. AlgoWealth's Form ADV disclosure was boilerplate and failed to clearly explain that the questionnaire captured only a narrow slice of relevant financial data, that no human review supplemented the algorithm's output, and that clients with complex financial situations—such as those investing the entirety of their liquid assets—faced heightened risk from algorithmic recommendations based on incomplete information.

Third, regarding the compliance program (Advisers Act §206(4); Rule 206(4)-7; IM Guidance 2017-02, Section 3): The guidance specifically states that robo-advisers should adopt and implement compliance programs reasonably designed to address concerns particular to providing automated advice, including periodic review of the algorithm's performance and suitability determinations, and mechanisms for clients to escalate issues to human personnel. AlgoWealth had no escalation procedure—Ms. Cho could reach only a chatbot—and no periodic suitability review mechanism. This represents a clear failure to adopt policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations, as required by Rule 206(4)-7.

AlgoWealth might argue that its disclosure placed the burden on the client to provide accurate and complete information. However, the fiduciary duty under §206 is non-delegable; an adviser cannot disclaim its obligation to gather adequate information by shifting the burden to an unsophisticated retail client. The firm's inadequate questionnaire made it structurally impossible for clients to provide the information the algorithm would have needed to generate suitable recommendations.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§206(1), 206(2), 206(4); Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Programs); Form ADV Part 2A disclosure obligations; SEC IM Guidance Update No. 2017-02 (Robo-Advisers), Sections 1–3; Rule 3a-4 under the Investment Company Act of 1940
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: AlgoWealth's five-question intake questionnaire was materially insufficient to gather the client information necessary to support the robo-adviser's fiduciary duty to provide suitable investment advice, and no compliance mechanism existed to identify or remediate this deficiency.

fact_pattern:
Pinnacle Wealth Advisors, LLC ('Pinnacle') is an SEC-registered investment adviser headquartered in Denver, Colorado, managing approximately $4.2 billion in client assets across its turnkey asset management platform ('TAMP'). Pinnacle offers clients access to model portfolios constructed by its in-house investment committee and allows clients to select from four approved custodians to hold their assets. One of those custodians, Pinnacle Trust Company ('PTC'), is a wholly owned subsidiary of Pinnacle's parent holding company, Pinnacle Financial Group, Inc.

From March 2017 through December 2022, all Pinnacle clients who selected PTC as their custodian were automatically enrolled in PTC's 'CashGuard FDIC Sweep Program,' which swept uninvested cash balances into interest-bearing deposit accounts at a network of twelve partner banks. Pinnacle's investment policy required all platform clients to maintain a minimum 2.5% cash allocation to cover advisory fees, rebalancing costs, and other operational expenses. For the approximately 14,800 client accounts custodied at PTC during this period — representing roughly $1.8 billion in assets — the average cash balance was approximately $12,400 per account. PTC charged a program fee on CashGuard assets that was deducted from the gross interest earned on the bank deposits before any interest was credited to client accounts. Critically, the CashGuard program fee was determined jointly by senior executives at both Pinnacle and PTC pursuant to an internal revenue-sharing agreement approved by the parent company's CFO, Margaret Chen. Between 2017 and 2022, PTC collected approximately $28.6 million in CashGuard fees, of which roughly $11.4 million was remitted upstream to Pinnacle Financial Group.

During this same period, Pinnacle's Form ADV Part 2A brochure stated only that 'PTC may earn revenue from its cash sweep program, and clients should be aware that cash balances may earn less interest than could be obtained through other arrangements.' The brochure did not disclose that Pinnacle itself played a role in setting the CashGuard fee, that Pinnacle's parent entity received a portion of CashGuard revenues, or that the affiliated relationship created a financial incentive for Pinnacle to recommend PTC over unaffiliated custodians. Pinnacle's Chief Compliance Officer, David Torrance, had flagged the inadequacy of the disclosure language in an internal memo dated June 2019, but the firm's general counsel determined that the existing language was 'sufficient under industry standards' and no changes were made until January 2023, after the SEC's Division of Examinations issued a deficiency letter.

Additionally, from January 2017 through September 2020, two of Pinnacle's three unaffiliated custodians — National Brokerage Services and Allied Custody Corp — paid Pinnacle quarterly 'platform integration fees' totaling approximately $3.9 million, calculated as 5 basis points on assets held in no-transaction-fee mutual fund share classes on the Pinnacle platform. Pinnacle's ADV disclosed the existence of these payments but did not disclose that lower-cost institutional share classes of the same funds were available that would not have triggered integration fee payments to Pinnacle, and which would have reduced client expense ratios by an average of 18 basis points annually.
question: Did Pinnacle Wealth Advisors breach its fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 by failing to provide full and fair disclosure of the conflicts of interest arising from the CashGuard sweep program and the custodial platform integration fee arrangements?
answer:
Yes, Pinnacle Wealth Advisors breached its fiduciary duty and violated Sections 206(2) and 206(4) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, as well as Rule 206(4)-7 thereunder. The analysis proceeds on multiple grounds.

First, regarding the CashGuard sweep program: Under Section 206(2), an investment adviser owes a fiduciary duty to its clients that includes an obligation to provide 'full and fair disclosure of all material facts' and to 'eliminate, or at least expose, all conflicts of interest which might incline an investment adviser — consciously or unconsciously — to render advice which was not disinterested.' SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963). Pinnacle's role in jointly setting the CashGuard fee with its affiliate PTC — and the upstream revenue-sharing arrangement with Pinnacle Financial Group — constituted material conflicts of interest. The fact that Pinnacle could influence the fee level directly affected how much interest clients received on their mandatory cash balances and simultaneously determined revenue flowing to Pinnacle's corporate parent. The ADV disclosure that PTC 'may earn revenue' was materially misleading because it omitted Pinnacle's own active involvement in determining the fee and the economic benefits accruing to Pinnacle's parent entity. This mirrors the SEC's findings in In the Matter of AssetMark, Inc. (IA Release No. 6434), where AssetMark's failure to disclose its role alongside its affiliated custodian in setting cash sweep fees was found to violate Sections 206(2) and 206(4).

Second, regarding the platform integration fees: While Pinnacle disclosed receipt of payments from custodians, it failed to disclose the availability of lower-cost institutional share classes that would not have generated these payments. This omission is material because a reasonable client would want to know that their adviser had a financial incentive to utilize higher-cost NTF share classes over cheaper alternatives. The failure to disclose this conflict violated Section 206(2)'s full-and-fair-disclosure standard.

Third, Pinnacle violated Rule 206(4)-7 by failing to adopt and implement written compliance policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent these disclosure failures. The CCO's June 2019 internal memo identifying the deficiency — which was overridden by general counsel without remediation — actually strengthens the case that Pinnacle had actual notice of the compliance gap yet failed to act. A reasonable compliance program would have required prompt remediation and enhanced disclosure.

The defense that existing language was 'sufficient under industry standards' is unavailing. Fiduciary duty under the Advisers Act imposes an affirmative obligation of utmost good faith and full disclosure; compliance with a perceived industry norm does not satisfy the statutory standard when material conflicts remain undisclosed. Pinnacle's conduct over approximately five years, affecting 14,800 accounts and involving tens of millions in conflicted revenue, represents a systemic fiduciary breach.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206(2) (fraud/deceit through omission); §206(4) (fraudulent/deceptive practices); Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures); SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963) (fiduciary duty of full and fair disclosure)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Pinnacle failed to disclose its direct role in setting the affiliated custodian's cash sweep fee and the upstream revenue-sharing arrangement, while simultaneously requiring clients to maintain cash balances subject to that fee.

fact_pattern:
Meridian Peak Capital Advisors, LLC ('Meridian'), a Delaware LLC registered with the SEC as an investment adviser since June 2016, serves as investment adviser to four clients: a private fund organized as a master/feeder structure called Meridian Peak Growth Fund, Ltd. (the 'Fund'), and two separately managed accounts for institutional investors. The Fund was formed as a Cayman Islands exempted company in 2015 and commenced operations with approximately $310 million in contributed assets from its U.S. feeder (Meridian Peak Growth, L.P.) and an offshore feeder (Meridian Peak Growth Offshore, Ltd.). The Fund's investors include 42 limited partners consisting of high-net-worth individuals and family offices.

From January 2018 through December 2021, Meridian's managing member, David Thornton, directed that the Fund pay $1.87 million in expenses that were properly the operating obligations of Meridian as the management company. Specifically, the Fund paid $640,000 for Meridian's annual regulatory compliance consulting fees charged by an outside compliance firm, $530,000 for legal fees incurred by Meridian in connection with its Form ADV filings and regulatory examinations, $420,000 for Meridian's office technology infrastructure and cybersecurity systems, and $280,000 for Meridian's directors and officers insurance premiums. The Fund's Confidential Private Placement Memorandum ('PPM') and Limited Partnership Agreement stated that the Fund would bear 'customary fund operating expenses, including audit, tax preparation, fund administration, and custody fees,' but made no reference to adviser-level compliance, legal, technology, or insurance costs.

Meridian did not adopt any written compliance policies or procedures addressing the allocation of expenses between the adviser and its fund clients, despite its Chief Compliance Officer, Sarah Lin, having raised the issue in an internal memo dated March 2019 recommending that such policies be implemented. Thornton acknowledged receiving Lin's memo but took no action. Quarterly investor letters sent to the LPs disclosed only aggregated 'operating expenses' without itemization, and the Fund's annual audited financial statements categorized the improperly allocated charges under a general 'professional and administrative fees' line item.
question: Did Meridian Peak Capital Advisors violate its fiduciary duties and compliance obligations under the Investment Advisers Act by using Fund assets to pay for adviser-level expenses without disclosure and by failing to adopt expense allocation policies?
answer:
Yes, Meridian violated Sections 206(2) and 206(4) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rules 206(4)-7 and 206(4)-8 thereunder. The analysis proceeds on multiple grounds.

First, Section 206(2) of the Advisers Act prohibits an investment adviser from engaging in any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit upon any client. Critically, Section 206(2) requires only negligence, not scienter. Meridian owed a fiduciary duty to the Fund and its investors to act in their best interests and to make full and fair disclosure of all material facts, particularly those relating to conflicts of interest. The Fund's PPM and organizational documents limited permissible fund-borne expenses to 'customary fund operating expenses' such as audit, tax, administration, and custody fees. By directing the Fund to pay $1.87 million in adviser-level compliance consulting, legal, technology, and D&O insurance costs — none of which were disclosed as Fund obligations — Meridian breached its fiduciary duty. Even if Thornton believed the allocation was reasonable, the undisclosed nature of the practice constitutes a material omission that operated as a fraud on the Fund and its LPs.

Second, Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-8 prohibit advisers to pooled investment vehicles from making untrue statements of material fact or omitting material facts necessary to make statements not misleading to investors. The quarterly letters and audited financials obscured the true nature of these charges by burying them in generic line items, preventing LPs from understanding they were subsidizing Meridian's own operating costs. This constitutes a material omission to investors in a pooled investment vehicle.

Third, Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7 require every registered investment adviser to adopt and implement written compliance policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of the Advisers Act. Meridian had no written expense allocation policy despite its CCO expressly recommending one. The failure to act on Lin's March 2019 memo demonstrates not merely a failure to adopt but an affirmative decision not to implement a critical compliance control. This is a standalone violation regardless of whether any substantive expense misallocation occurred.

Meridian cannot defend on the basis that the expenses ultimately benefited the Fund indirectly. The SEC has consistently held that an adviser's own regulatory and operational costs are not fund expenses unless the governing documents clearly authorize such allocations. The dispositive issue is the undisclosed deviation from offering document terms, compounded by the absence of any compliance infrastructure to prevent the violation.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Section 206(2) (fraud/deceit through negligence); Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures requirement); Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-8 (fraud on pooled investment vehicle investors); Sections 203(e) and 203(k) (remedial sanctions and cease-and-desist authority)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Meridian used Fund assets to pay $1.87 million in adviser-level compliance, legal, technology, and insurance expenses that were not authorized by the Fund's offering documents and were never disclosed to investors.

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Advisors, LLC ('Meridian') is a Denver-based registered investment adviser with approximately $620 million in discretionary assets under management as of March 2023. Meridian's Chief Investment Officer, Thomas Hartwell, founded a separate entity in 2019 called Hartwell Analytics, Inc., which developed a proprietary quantitative screening tool (the 'Screener') that assigns risk-adjusted scores to equities based on macroeconomic factors and corporate intangible asset valuations. Beginning in Q2 2020, Meridian entered into a soft dollar arrangement under Section 28(e) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, directing approximately $375,000 per year in client brokerage commissions to Hartwell Analytics for the use of the Screener. Over a four-year period (2020–2023), Meridian paid a total of approximately $1.5 million in soft dollars to Hartwell Analytics.

Meridian's three-person Compliance Committee — consisting of Hartwell, Chief Compliance Officer Sandra Orozco, and Director of Trading Kyle Prescott — approved the initial arrangement and each subsequent annual payment. The committee maintained minutes reflecting that the Screener was deemed to provide 'legitimate research value' to the portfolio management process. However, neither the committee minutes nor any internal compliance review identified the arrangement as creating a financial conflict of interest arising from Hartwell's dual role as CIO of Meridian and sole owner of Hartwell Analytics.

Meridian's Form ADV Part 2A disclosed generally that the firm 'may use soft dollar arrangements to obtain research and brokerage services that benefit client accounts,' but did not disclose: (1) that the CIO personally owned and controlled the soft dollar research vendor; (2) the specific dollar amounts flowing to the CIO's company; or (3) that the CIO was the individual who both recommended the use of the Screener and set the pricing for Meridian's use of it. Meridian's written compliance policies and procedures manual contained a generic soft dollar policy requiring that all soft dollar expenditures be for 'eligible research or brokerage services' under Section 28(e), but contained no procedures for identifying, escalating, or disclosing conflicts of interest where the soft dollar vendor was affiliated with a firm principal. In early 2024, Meridian's outside auditor flagged the arrangement during a routine review, prompting internal counsel to report the matter to the SEC.
question: Did Meridian Wealth Advisors violate Section 206(4) of the Investment Advisers Act and Rule 206(4)-7 thereunder by failing to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations arising from the conflicted soft dollar arrangement?
answer:
Yes, Meridian violated Section 206(4) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rule 206(4)-7 thereunder. The analysis proceeds as follows.

Rule 206(4)-7 requires every registered investment adviser to 'adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violation' of the Advisers Act and its rules. Under Section 206(2), an adviser has a fiduciary duty to disclose all material conflicts of interest to its clients. A conflict is material when there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable client would consider it important in making an investment decision or in evaluating the adviser's loyalty.

The pivotal issue is whether Meridian's compliance infrastructure was reasonably designed to identify and address the conflict created by directing $1.5 million in client brokerage commissions to a company owned by its own CIO. It was not. Meridian's soft dollar policy addressed only the threshold eligibility question under Section 28(e) — whether the purchased services constituted legitimate 'research' — but contained no mechanism for identifying affiliated-party transactions, escalating them for independent review, or ensuring adequate disclosure to clients.

The Knowledge Leaders Capital precedent (IA Release No. 4980) is directly on point. In that matter, the SEC found a violation of Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7 where the adviser used approximately $1 million in soft dollars over three years to pay a company owned by its CIO, and the adviser's compliance framework failed to identify the resulting conflict. The SEC emphasized that even where a management committee formally approved the expenditures and the research had legitimate value, the failure to identify the conflict as a conflict — and thus the failure to disclose it — constituted a policies-and-procedures violation.

Meridian's situation is arguably more egregious: the dollar amount was larger ($1.5 million versus approximately $1 million), the period was longer (four years versus three), and the CIO both recommended the vendor and set its pricing — a self-dealing dynamic that was never flagged. The Form ADV disclosure was generic and omitted every material particular of the arrangement. While the Compliance Committee's approval of the payments might superficially suggest oversight, the committee included the conflicted CIO himself and never characterized the arrangement as a conflict requiring disclosure.

Meridian may argue that the Screener provided genuine research value and that the arrangement fell within the Section 28(e) safe harbor. However, the Section 28(e) safe harbor protects against claims of breach of fiduciary duty for paying commissions in excess of the lowest available rate; it does not excuse the failure to disclose affiliated-party conflicts or the failure to maintain adequate compliance procedures. Legitimate research value is irrelevant to the policies-and-procedures charge.

The self-report and remediation, as in Knowledge Leaders, may mitigate sanctions but do not negate the underlying violation. Meridian violated Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206(2), §206(4); Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Policies and Procedures); Section 28(e) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (Soft Dollar Safe Harbor); Form ADV Part 2A disclosure obligations
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Meridian's written compliance policies contained no procedures for identifying, escalating, or disclosing conflicts of interest arising from soft dollar payments directed to an entity owned and controlled by the firm's own Chief Investment Officer.

fact_pattern:
Keystone Wealth Advisors, LLC ('KWA') is a registered investment adviser based in Columbus, Ohio, with approximately $1.1 billion in regulatory assets under management. KWA has been registered with the SEC since 2001. KWA is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Keystone Financial Holdings, Inc., which also owns Keystone Securities Corp. ('KSC'), a registered broker-dealer that acts as the introducing broker for KWA's advisory clients. Most of KWA's 42 investment adviser representatives are dually registered as representatives of KSC.

From January 2015 through December 2019, KWA managed approximately 3,200 advisory accounts, the majority of which were invested in mutual funds through wrap-fee and non-wrap advisory programs. During this period, KWA's IARs routinely purchased or recommended Class A shares with 12b-1 fees of 0.25% or institutional share classes with no 12b-1 fees were available for the same funds at the same custodial platform. In many cases, clients held positions in funds such as the Vanguard Growth Fund (Class A, VGSTX, 0.25% 12b-1 fee) when the Institutional class (VIGIX, no 12b-1 fee) was available with a $5,000 minimum that the clients easily met. Similarly, KWA placed approximately 480 retirement plan rollover IRA clients with average account balances of $275,000 into American Funds Class A shares when Class F-2 shares (which carry no 12b-1 fees and lower expense ratios) were readily available.

KSC, as the affiliated broker-dealer, received 12b-1 fee revenue totaling approximately $1.87 million over the five-year period, which was shared with the dually registered IARs. KWA's Form ADV Part 2A during this period stated that 'MAFM may recommend mutual funds that pay 12b-1 fees' but did not disclose that lower-cost share classes of the same funds were available to clients, nor did it disclose the specific conflict of interest arising from the financial incentive to select share classes generating 12b-1 revenue for its affiliated broker-dealer and its IARs. KWA did not maintain any written compliance policies or procedures addressing share class selection, suitability of share classes relative to cost, or best execution obligations specific to mutual fund investments. KWA was aware of the SEC's Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative announced in February 2018 but elected not to self-report.

Margaret Chen, a 68-year-old retired schoolteacher and KWA client since 2016, held $410,000 across two IRA accounts. Her IAR, David Morales, placed her entirely in Class A mutual fund shares across six fund families, generating approximately $1,025 annually in 12b-1 fees paid to KSC and shared with Morales. Institutional or no-load share classes were available for every fund in her portfolio and would have saved Ms. Chen an estimated $4,100 over the four years she held the positions.
question: Did KWA violate its fiduciary duties under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, and if so, what specific provisions were breached in connection with its mutual fund share class selection practices?
answer:
KWA violated multiple provisions of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, and its conduct constitutes a clear breach of fiduciary duty virtually identical to the violations found in the SEC's action against Mid Atlantic Financial Management, Inc. (IA Release No. 5387).

First, KWA violated Section 206(2) of the Advisers Act, which prohibits an investment adviser from engaging in any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit upon any client or prospective client. By systematically placing clients in higher-cost mutual fund share classes that generated 12b-1 fee revenue for its affiliated broker-dealer KSC and its dually registered IARs—when lower-cost share classes of the identical funds were readily available—KWA engaged in a course of business that operated as a fraud on its clients. The conflict of interest was material: the selection of more expensive share classes was driven not by client interest but by the financial incentive flowing to KSC and the IARs. The inadequate disclosure in KWA's Form ADV Part 2A, which acknowledged that it 'may recommend' 12b-1 fee funds but failed to disclose the availability of cheaper alternatives or the specific nature of the conflict, rendered the disclosure materially misleading.

Second, KWA breached its fiduciary duty of best execution. Under longstanding SEC interpretations and as articulated in the MAFM proceeding, an investment adviser has an obligation to seek best execution for its clients, which includes selecting the most cost-effective share class when multiple classes of the same fund are available and the client is eligible. Placing Ms. Chen and approximately 3,200 other clients in Class A shares when institutional or no-12b-1-fee classes were available constitutes a failure to meet this obligation.

Third, KWA violated Section 206(4) of the Advisers Act and Rule 206(4)-7 thereunder, which require registered investment advisers to adopt and implement written compliance policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of the Advisers Act. KWA's complete absence of written policies addressing share class selection, cost-comparative analysis, or conflict mitigation in mutual fund investments represents a direct violation of this compliance rule.

KWA cannot plausibly claim adequate disclosure as a defense. Generic language acknowledging the possibility of 12b-1 fee recommendations is insufficient under SEC standards; the adviser must specifically disclose the conflict arising from the financial incentive to select more expensive share classes and the availability of cheaper alternatives. Furthermore, KWA's decision not to self-report under the SCSD Initiative, which offered favorable settlement terms, is likely to result in more severe remedial sanctions, including disgorgement of the full $1.87 million in 12b-1 fees plus prejudgment interest, civil penalties, and a censure.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206(2) (fraud or deceit upon clients); §206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures); fiduciary duty of best execution; Rule 12b-1 under the Investment Company Act of 1940; SEC Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative (Feb. 2018); Form ADV Part 2A disclosure obligations under Rule 204-3
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: KWA systematically selected mutual fund share classes that generated 12b-1 fee revenue for its affiliated broker-dealer and dually registered IARs when lower-cost share classes of the same funds were available to clients, without adequately disclosing this conflict of interest.

fact_pattern:
Ridgeline Capital Partners, LLC ('Ridgeline') is a registered investment adviser based in Boston, Massachusetts, with approximately $1.2 billion in assets under management as of December 31, 2022. Ridgeline serves as the investment adviser to three private equity funds: Ridgeline Growth Fund II, L.P. ('Fund II,' vintage 2015, $320 million committed capital), Ridgeline Growth Fund III, L.P. ('Fund III,' vintage 2018, $410 million committed capital), and Ridgeline Growth Fund IV, L.P. ('Fund IV,' vintage 2021, $470 million committed capital). Each fund's limited partnership agreement requires that potential conflicts of interest involving Ridgeline's principals be disclosed to an independent Advisory Committee composed of limited partners, which has the authority to review and approve or waive such conflicts.

From 2016 through 2023, Ridgeline engaged DataVantage Solutions, Inc. ('DataVantage'), a cybersecurity and IT consulting firm, to perform operational and cybersecurity due diligence assessments on prospective portfolio company acquisitions. Ridgeline consistently touted its proprietary due diligence methodology — including its relationship with DataVantage — as a key competitive differentiator when marketing Fund III and Fund IV to prospective limited partners. In Fund III's Private Placement Memorandum, Ridgeline described DataVantage as an 'independent, best-in-class cybersecurity diligence partner' that provides 'unbiased assessments of target companies' technology infrastructure.' The cost of DataVantage's due diligence services — averaging $175,000 per engagement — was charged to the respective fund as a fund expense.

Unbeknownst to the funds' limited partners and Advisory Committees, three senior principals of Ridgeline — Managing Partner Thomas Calloway, Partner Sarah Whitfield, and Partner David Ostrowski — each made personal investments of $250,000 in DataVantage's Series A preferred equity round in 2014, collectively holding approximately 8% of DataVantage's outstanding equity. Furthermore, Thomas Calloway's brother-in-law, Richard Novak, is the co-founder and CEO of DataVantage, and Sarah Whitfield has occupied one of DataVantage's five board seats since 2015. These relationships were never disclosed to any fund's Advisory Committee, nor were they referenced in any PPM, annual report, or investor communication until November 2023, when an incoming compliance officer identified the issue during an internal review. Ridgeline's principals did not receive any referral fees, kickbacks, or preferential pricing from DataVantage, and Ridgeline asserts that DataVantage was selected solely on merit and that its pricing was at or below market rates for comparable services.

After discovering the omission, Ridgeline voluntarily disclosed the relationships to the Advisory Committees and limited partners, engaged outside counsel to conduct a retrospective review, and self-reported the matter to the SEC's Division of Enforcement. Approximately $4.9 million in aggregate DataVantage fees had been charged across the three funds over the seven-year period.
question: Did Ridgeline Capital Partners violate its fiduciary duties and the Investment Advisers Act by failing to disclose the personal and financial relationships between its principals and DataVantage Solutions to the funds' Advisory Committees and investors, even though Ridgeline's principals did not financially profit from the engagement of DataVantage?
answer:
Yes, Ridgeline Capital Partners violated its fiduciary duties and the Investment Advisers Act. The absence of direct financial profit to Ridgeline's principals from the DataVantage engagement is not a defense. The analysis proceeds as follows:

Section 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 prohibits an investment adviser from engaging in any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit upon any client. This provision does not require scienter; negligent conduct is sufficient. A registered investment adviser owes its clients an affirmative duty of utmost good faith and full and fair disclosure of all material facts, particularly those relating to potential conflicts of interest. Here, Ridgeline's three senior principals held a collective 8% equity stake in DataVantage, one principal sat on DataVantage's board, and a managing partner's brother-in-law was DataVantage's CEO. These personal and financial entanglements created potential conflicts that could influence Ridgeline's selection and continued use of DataVantage for fund-expensed due diligence engagements. The fund governing documents explicitly required disclosure of such conflicts to the Advisory Committees — a requirement Ridgeline failed to satisfy for approximately seven years. The fact that Ridgeline affirmatively described DataVantage as 'independent' and 'unbiased' in its PPM compounded the violation by rendering otherwise incomplete disclosures materially misleading.

Section 206(4) of the Advisers Act and Rule 206(4)-8 thereunder specifically address fraud on investors in pooled investment vehicles. Rule 206(4)-8(a)(2) makes it unlawful for an adviser to pooled investment vehicles to 'omit a material fact necessary to make the statements made, in the light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading, to any investor or prospective investor in the pooled investment vehicle.' Ridgeline's PPM disclosures touting DataVantage as independent while omitting the principals' equity stakes, board seat, and familial relationship constitute precisely the type of material omission this rule targets.

The SEC has consistently held — as illustrated by the Centre Partners Management proceeding (IA Release No. 4604) — that the absence of actual financial profit from the conflicted relationship does not negate the violation. The duty to disclose attaches to potential conflicts of interest, not solely to realized economic harm. The fact that DataVantage's pricing may have been competitive is similarly immaterial to the disclosure obligation; investors and Advisory Committees were entitled to this information to make their own informed assessments.

Ridgeline's voluntary self-report, remediation, and cooperation may serve as mitigating factors in the SEC's determination of sanctions, but they do not eliminate the underlying violations of Sections 206(2) and 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-8.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206(2) (fraud or deceit on clients through negligent conduct); §206(4) and Rule 206(4)-8 (material omissions to investors in pooled investment vehicles); fiduciary duty of full and fair disclosure of material conflicts of interest
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Ridgeline failed to disclose to fund Advisory Committees and investors the personal equity investments, board membership, and familial relationship between its principals and a service provider whose fees were charged to the funds, rendering its affirmative characterization of the service provider as 'independent' materially misleading.

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners, LLC ('Meridian') is a registered investment adviser headquartered in Scottsdale, Arizona, with approximately $2.1 billion in regulatory assets under management as of its most recent Form ADV filing dated March 31, 2020. Meridian is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Meridian Financial Holdings, Inc., which also owns Meridian Brokerage Services, LLC ('MBS'), a registered broker-dealer. Meridian's investment adviser representatives ('IARs') are also registered representatives of MBS.

From January 2015 through June 2019, Meridian's IARs routinely placed advisory clients—including 412 retirement accounts (IRAs and 401(k) rollovers) and 238 taxable accounts held by moderate-risk, income-oriented investors—into Class A shares of various mutual funds offered by American Funds, Franklin Templeton, and PIMCO. These Class A shares carried 12b-1 fees ranging from 0.15% to 0.25% annually. In each instance, lower-cost institutional share classes or 'clean' share classes of the identical funds were available to these clients through Meridian's custodial platform at National Financial Services, LLC ('NFS'), Meridian's clearing broker. The institutional share classes carried no 12b-1 fees and had expense ratios that were, on average, 22 basis points lower. MBS received the 12b-1 fee payments from the fund companies, totaling approximately $1,487,320 over the relevant period, which were then partially shared with the IARs as additional compensation.

Meridian's Form ADV Part 2A, Item 10, disclosed that 'affiliated persons may receive compensation from mutual fund companies,' but did not specifically identify that MBS received 12b-1 fees when clients were placed in higher-cost share classes, nor did it explain that lower-cost share classes of the same funds were available through the firm's custodial platform. The Form ADV did not describe the specific conflict of interest arising from the financial incentive to recommend share classes generating 12b-1 revenue to the affiliated broker-dealer. Additionally, NFS maintained a no-transaction-fee ('NTF') mutual fund program, and NFS agreed to share with MBS a portion of the shareholder servicing fees it received from fund companies participating in the NTF program. These revenue-sharing payments to MBS totaled $523,670 over the same period. Meridian's Form ADV made no reference to these revenue-sharing arrangements or the conflicts they created.

Meridian's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Hoffman, had drafted compliance policies in 2014 that addressed suitability of mutual fund recommendations generally, but these policies contained no procedures for evaluating share class selection, comparing available share classes on the custodial platform, or identifying and disclosing conflicts arising from 12b-1 fees or revenue-sharing arrangements. No periodic review of share class selection was conducted during the entire relevant period. When the SEC's Office of Compliance Inspections and Examinations conducted an examination in August 2019, it flagged these issues, prompting Meridian to begin transitioning affected clients to lower-cost share classes and to enhance its Form ADV disclosures.
question: Did Meridian Wealth Partners violate its fiduciary obligations under the Investment Advisers Act by placing advisory clients in higher-cost mutual fund share classes that generated 12b-1 fee revenue for its affiliated broker-dealer without adequate disclosure, and by failing to adopt compliance policies addressing share class selection?
answer:
Yes, Meridian Wealth Partners violated Sections 206(2), 206(4), and 207 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, as well as Rule 206(4)-7 thereunder. The analysis proceeds as follows:

First, Section 206(2) prohibits an investment adviser from engaging in any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit upon any client. As a registered investment adviser, Meridian owed a fiduciary duty to its clients, which includes obligations of full and fair disclosure of all material conflicts of interest. The receipt of $1,487,320 in 12b-1 fees by affiliated broker-dealer MBS—fees generated specifically because Meridian's IARs selected higher-cost share classes over available lower-cost alternatives of the same funds—constituted a material conflict of interest. Meridian's Form ADV disclosure that 'affiliated persons may receive compensation from mutual fund companies' was materially inadequate because it failed to identify the specific nature of the conflict: that lower-cost share classes were available and that the firm had a financial incentive to select higher-cost classes. Similarly, the $523,670 in revenue-sharing payments from NFS to MBS was entirely undisclosed. Under SEC precedent, including the Capital Analysts proceeding (IA Release No. 5009), an adviser must disclose specific conflicts with sufficient particularity to allow clients to provide informed consent. Generic boilerplate language is insufficient.

Second, Meridian breached its duty of best execution under Section 206(2) by systematically investing clients in share classes with higher expense ratios when identical, lower-cost alternatives were readily accessible on its own custodial platform. The 22-basis-point average cost differential across 650 accounts over more than four years represents a meaningful economic harm to clients.

Third, Section 207 makes it unlawful for an adviser to make untrue statements of material facts or omit material facts in filings with the Commission. Meridian's Form ADV omitted material information about the 12b-1 fee conflict and the revenue-sharing arrangement, rendering its disclosures materially misleading.

Finally, Rule 206(4)-7 requires every registered adviser to adopt and implement written compliance policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of the Advisers Act. Meridian's compliance manual contained no procedures for evaluating share class selection, monitoring whether lower-cost share classes were available, or ensuring disclosure of conflicts arising from differential compensation. CCO Hoffman's failure to address these issues in the written compliance program constitutes a standalone violation, regardless of whether substantive fraud occurred.

Meridian cannot defend by arguing that clients received the benefit of the underlying fund strategy, because the fiduciary duty extends to the costs borne by clients. The post-examination remediation, while appropriate, does not retroactively cure the violations during the relevant period.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206(2) (fraud/deceit on clients); §206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures); §207 (material misstatements/omissions in SEC filings); SEC fiduciary duty of disclosure and best execution for registered investment advisers
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Meridian failed to disclose with adequate specificity that its affiliated broker-dealer received 12b-1 fees and revenue-sharing payments when clients were placed in higher-cost mutual fund share classes, despite the availability of lower-cost share classes of the same funds on the firm's custodial platform.

fact_pattern:
Piedmont Wealth Partners, LLC ('Piedmont') is a dually registered investment adviser and broker-dealer headquartered in Charleston, South Carolina, registered with the SEC since 2011. As of its March 2023 Form ADV filing, Piedmont reported approximately $420 million in regulatory assets under management across roughly 1,800 advisory accounts, many of which are held by retail investors including retirees and small business owners.

From January 2020 through December 2022, Piedmont's investment advisory representatives routinely purchased Class A shares of several mutual fund families—including the Meridian Growth Fund, Coastal Balanced Fund, and Summit Total Return Fund—for advisory clients' fee-based wrap accounts. These Class A shares carried 12b-1 fees ranging from 25 to 35 basis points. Each of these funds simultaneously offered Class I (Institutional) shares with no 12b-1 fees and lower total expense ratios, for which the advisory clients were eligible based on the custodial platform's minimum investment thresholds and Piedmont's status as a registered investment adviser. Over the relevant period, Piedmont received approximately $312,000 in 12b-1 fee revenue from its custodian, which was remitted to the firm's broker-dealer side.

Piedmont's Form ADV Part 2A, last amended in March 2021, stated that 'the Firm may receive compensation from mutual fund companies in the form of distribution or servicing fees,' but did not disclose the specific conflict of interest arising from the selection of 12b-1 fee-paying share classes over available lower-cost share classes of the same funds. The brochure did not address that Piedmont had a financial incentive to recommend or hold share classes that generated additional revenue to the firm. Piedmont's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Kessler, was aware that institutional share classes were available but did not update the firm's policies or disclosures, believing the general language in the ADV was sufficient.

Client Margaret Holbrook, age 71, a retired schoolteacher with a $380,000 advisory account, held $145,000 in Class A shares of the Meridian Growth Fund throughout this period. Had she been placed in Class I shares, she would have saved approximately $507 annually in fund-level expenses. Across all affected clients, aggregate excess fees attributable to higher-cost share classes totaled approximately $189,000 over the three-year period.
question: Did Piedmont Wealth Partners violate its fiduciary duties under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 by placing advisory clients in 12b-1 fee-paying mutual fund share classes when lower-cost institutional share classes of the same funds were available, and by failing to adequately disclose the associated conflicts of interest?
answer:
