Harmon has no viable defense — neither the absence of formal registration of HFS during part of the relevant period nor any claimed ignorance of the fee schedule negates the deliberate misappropriation and fraud.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Sections 206(1) and 206(2); Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5; Securities Act of 1933, Section 17(a); Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Section 203(f) (remedial sanctions)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Harmon solicited funds from an elderly client under the pretense of securities investments and instead converted $247,500 entirely to personal use, constituting classic misappropriation in breach of his fiduciary duty.

fact_pattern:
Pinnacle Wealth Partners, LLC ('Pinnacle') is a dually registered investment adviser and broker-dealer headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, with approximately $4.2 billion in regulatory assets under management. From March 2015 through June 2018, Pinnacle's financial advisers managed roughly 6,400 advisory accounts under a wrap-fee program called 'Pinnacle Select.' Within these accounts, advisers routinely allocated client assets to mutual funds across equity, fixed income, and balanced categories.

During this period, Pinnacle advisers purchased or held Class A shares of the Vanguard Growth Fund, the American Funds EuroPacific Growth Fund, and the PIMCO Total Return Fund for 2,310 advisory clients. These Class A shares carried 12b-1 fees ranging from 25 to 50 basis points annually. However, each of these funds offered lower-cost institutional share classes ('Class I' or 'Institutional Class') that charged no 12b-1 fees and for which these advisory clients were eligible based on account size minimums and the clients' status as participants in an advisory program. Pinnacle and its associated persons collectively received approximately $3.7 million in 12b-1 fee revenue over the three-year period from these higher-cost share class placements.

Pinnacle's Form ADV Part 2A, filed annually during this period, contained only a generic statement that 'Pinnacle may receive compensation from mutual fund companies in connection with the sale of fund shares,' but did not specifically disclose the conflict of interest arising from the selection of 12b-1 fee-paying share classes over available lower-cost alternatives. The Form ADV did not explain that Pinnacle advisers had a financial incentive to recommend or hold share classes that generated 12b-1 fees for the firm, nor did it disclose that clients were eligible for institutional share classes with meaningfully lower expense ratios. Pinnacle's Chief Compliance Officer, David Hargrove, was aware that the firm received 12b-1 revenue but did not flag the share class selection practices or the deficient disclosure as a compliance concern during annual reviews.

In August 2018, after the SEC announced its Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative, Pinnacle conducted an internal review and identified the issue but elected not to self-report. The SEC's Office of Compliance Inspections and Examinations subsequently examined Pinnacle in early 2019 and referred findings to the Division of Enforcement.
question: Did Pinnacle Wealth Partners breach its fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 by selecting higher-cost mutual fund share classes that paid 12b-1 fees to the firm without adequate disclosure to advisory clients, and what enforcement consequences should it anticipate?
answer:
Pinnacle Wealth Partners violated Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Section 206(2) makes it unlawful for any investment adviser to engage in any transaction, practice, or course of business which operates as a fraud or deceit upon any client or prospective client. Section 206(1) prohibits the use of any device, scheme, or artifice to defraud clients. The SEC has consistently held that an investment adviser's fiduciary duty encompasses both an affirmative duty of utmost good faith and full and fair disclosure of all material facts, as well as a duty to seek best execution and avoid conflicts or, where conflicts exist, to fully disclose them.

The facts here closely parallel the conduct at issue in In re BB&T Securities, LLC (IA Release No. 5165, March 11, 2019). Like BB&T, Pinnacle purchased, recommended, or held mutual fund share classes that charged 12b-1 fees when lower-cost institutional share classes of the same funds were available and for which clients were eligible. Pinnacle and its associated persons received approximately $3.7 million in 12b-1 fees — compensation that created a direct, material conflict of interest. The firm's Form ADV Part 2A disclosure was inadequate: a generic reference to possible compensation from fund companies fails to satisfy the adviser's obligation to provide 'full and fair disclosure' of the specific conflict arising from share class selection. Under SEC guidance and precedent, an adviser must disclose (a) the receipt of 12b-1 fees, (b) that the firm has a financial incentive to select share classes paying such fees, and (c) that lower-cost share classes exist for which clients are eligible. Pinnacle's disclosure met none of these specific requirements.

Notably, Pinnacle's situation is likely to result in more severe sanctions than BB&T's because Pinnacle did not self-report under the SCSD Initiative. The Division of Enforcement explicitly designed the SCSD Initiative to incentivize self-reporting with standardized, favorable settlement terms — typically limited to disgorgement with prejudgment interest and no civil penalties. BB&T received this favorable treatment. By declining to self-report, Pinnacle forfeited the presumptive benefit of the Initiative. The SEC will likely seek disgorgement of the full $3.7 million in 12b-1 fees, prejudgment interest, and civil monetary penalties under Section 203(e) of the Advisers Act. The Commission may also impose a cease-and-desist order under Section 203(k) and require Pinnacle to retain an independent compliance consultant. CCO Hargrove's awareness of the 12b-1 revenue without flagging the disclosure deficiency may also expose the firm to heightened scrutiny regarding its compliance program under Rule 206(4)-7.

No viable defense exists: neither the absence of client complaints nor the generic ADV disclosure cures the fiduciary breach. The conflict was material, ongoing, and insufficiently disclosed.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§ 206(1), 206(2), 203(e), 203(k); Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Programs); Investment Company Act Rule 12b-1; SEC Form ADV Part 2A disclosure requirements; SEC Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative (SCSD Initiative)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Pinnacle selected and held 12b-1 fee-paying mutual fund share classes for advisory clients when lower-cost institutional share classes were available, while failing to adequately disclose the resulting conflict of interest in its Form ADV or otherwise.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Trent Holloway (CRD No. 5876321) has been a registered representative since 2006, most recently associated with Ridgeline Capital Partners, a mid-size FINRA member firm headquartered in Denver, Colorado. In March 2023, a FINRA arbitration panel rendered a $642,800 monetary award against Holloway in favor of a former colleague, Danielle Chen, arising from an industry dispute. Chen had alleged that Holloway wrongfully diverted commissions and forfeiture credits owed to her under a branch revenue-sharing agreement from 2019 to 2021, totaling $487,000 in compensatory damages, $105,800 in prejudgment interest, and $50,000 in attorneys' fees.

Holloway did not file a motion to vacate the award in any court of competent jurisdiction within the 30-day payment window prescribed by FINRA Rule 13904(j). On June 15, 2023, FINRA's Department of Enforcement served Holloway with a Rule 9554 suspension notice, advising him that failure to pay the Award within 21 days would result in suspension from association with any FINRA member firm. On July 2, 2023, Holloway timely requested a hearing before the Office of Hearing Officers, asserting a single defense: bona fide inability to pay the Award.

At the hearing held on October 4, 2023, Enforcement introduced evidence that Holloway owned a rental property in Lakewood, Colorado, with approximately $310,000 in equity, maintained a brokerage account at Fidelity holding $118,400 in diversified equity mutual funds, and had received $97,000 in net compensation from Ridgeline Capital Partners during the six months following the Award. Holloway also disclosed a checking account with a $14,200 balance and a 401(k) with $203,000 in assets. Holloway's monthly living expenses, documented through bank statements, totaled approximately $6,800. Holloway argued that liquidating his rental property would take months, that the 401(k) was retirement-protected, and that he needed his brokerage account for emergencies. He did not offer any partial payment, nor did he attempt to negotiate a settlement or installment plan with Chen.

Holloway's total identifiable liquid and semi-liquid assets exceeded $435,600, and his total net worth—including real property equity—exceeded $745,000. Despite these resources, Holloway made no effort to satisfy even a portion of the $642,800 Award in the seven months since it was issued.
question: Has Holloway established a bona fide inability to pay the arbitration award sufficient to avoid suspension under FINRA Rule 9554, and what is the likely outcome of the expedited proceeding?
answer:
Holloway has not established a bona fide inability to pay and will be suspended from associating with any FINRA member firm in any capacity.

Under FINRA Rule 13904(j), all monetary arbitration awards must be paid within 30 days of receipt unless a motion to vacate has been filed in a court of competent jurisdiction. Holloway did not file any such motion. When FINRA served the Rule 9554 suspension notice, Holloway's sole available defense—given that this was an industry (not customer) dispute—was bona fide inability to pay. See William J. Gallagher, Exchange Act Release No. 47501 (Mar. 14, 2003); SR-FINRA-2010-014, Exchange Act Release No. 62211 (June 2, 2010) (confirming the inability-to-pay defense remains available for industry arbitration awards).

The burden of proving bona fide inability to pay rests squarely on the respondent. The defense requires demonstrating that the respondent genuinely lacks the financial capacity to pay the award or make a meaningful payment toward it. Here, the evidence overwhelmingly undermines Holloway's claim. His identifiable liquid and semi-liquid assets—including $118,400 in a brokerage account and $14,200 in checking—total over $132,000 in readily accessible funds. His rental property equity of $310,000 could be accessed through a home equity line of credit or sale. His 401(k) balance of $203,000, while potentially subject to tax penalties, is not legally inaccessible. His post-award compensation of $97,000 over six months further demonstrates ongoing earning capacity.

Critically, Holloway made no partial payment whatsoever, nor did he attempt to negotiate a settlement or installment arrangement with Chen under FINRA By-Laws, Article VI, Section 3(b)—either of which would have demonstrated good faith. The Hearing Officer will view the total absence of any effort to satisfy even a portion of the Award as fatal to the inability defense. FINRA precedent consistently holds that a respondent who possesses assets substantially exceeding a meaningful fraction of the award cannot credibly claim inability to pay.

The suspension will remain in effect until Holloway: (1) pays the Award in full; (2) enters into a written settlement agreement with Chen and remains current on its terms; or (3) files a bankruptcy petition or obtains a bankruptcy discharge of the debt. Holloway will also be ordered to pay hearing costs under FINRA Rule 9554. His failure to take any affirmative step toward satisfying the Award, despite ample financial resources, is the determinative factor.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 9554(a), (c), (d), (e); FINRA Rule 13904(j); FINRA By-Laws Article VI, Section 3(b); NASD Notice to Members 00-55; William J. Gallagher, Exchange Act Release No. 47501, 2003 SEC LEXIS 599 (Mar. 14, 2003); SR-FINRA-2010-014, Exchange Act Release No. 62211, 2010 SEC LEXIS 1800 (June 2, 2010)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Holloway possessed identifiable liquid and semi-liquid assets exceeding $435,600 and total net worth exceeding $745,000, yet made no payment or partial payment toward the $642,800 arbitration award, defeating any claim of bona fide inability to pay.

fact_pattern: Pinnacle Wealth Advisors, LLC ('PWA') is a registered investment adviser based in Scottsdale, Arizona, with approximately $4.8 billion in regulatory assets under management as of December 2023. The firm's founder and CEO, Marcus D. Brennan, owns 72% of the firm's equity. In March 2022, PWA engaged a popular local podcast host, Tyler Garrison, to produce weekly sponsored segments promoting PWA's comprehensive wealth management services. The engagement agreement specified that Garrison would read pre-approved scripts prepared by PWA's marketing department. However, in September 2022, Garrison became a client of PWA, opening a managed account with an initial deposit of $1.2 million. Beginning in October 2022, Garrison started ad-libbing during the sponsored segments, incorporating personal anecdotes about his experience as a PWA client, including statements such as 'Since I moved my portfolio to Pinnacle, I've seen returns I never thought possible—Marcus and his team are the real deal' and 'My account grew 14% in the first six months—these guys actually deliver.' These unscripted endorsements aired weekly through August 2023, reaching an estimated audience of 185,000 listeners per episode. PWA's written policies and procedures manual required all advertisements to be pre-approved by the firm's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Holt, and copies of all advertising materials to be maintained in the firm's records. Despite this policy, PWA did not obtain recordings of the podcast episodes from October 2022 through August 2023, and Holt was unaware that Garrison had become a client or that his endorsements had shifted from scripted content to personal testimonials. Separately, from January 2022 through June 2023, Brennan maintained two brokerage accounts at an outside broker-dealer—one in his wife's name and one in a family trust—in which he exercised full trading discretion. These accounts held positions in several securities also held in PWA client portfolios, including concentrated positions in three small-cap equities. Brennan did not disclose these accounts to Holt or report the holdings and transactions as required by PWA's Code of Ethics, which mandated quarterly transaction reports and annual holdings reports for all 'access persons,' a category that expressly included Brennan. The accounts were discovered only when an external compliance consultant conducted a review in July 2023.
question: Did PWA and Brennan violate the Investment Advisers Act and applicable rules in connection with the podcast testimonials, the failure to monitor advertising, the recordkeeping deficiencies, and Brennan's failure to report personal securities accounts under the firm's Code of Ethics?
answer:
Yes, PWA and Brennan committed multiple violations of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and the rules thereunder, closely paralleling the violations found in In the Matter of Creative Planning, Inc. (IA Release No. 5035).

First, PWA violated Section 206(4) of the Advisers Act and Rule 206(4)-1(a)(1), which at the time prohibited any advertisement that referred, directly or indirectly, to any testimonial of any kind concerning the investment adviser or any advice, analysis, report, or other service rendered by the adviser. Garrison's unscripted, personal endorsements—describing his own positive experience as a PWA client, including specific performance figures—constitute textbook client testimonials. The fact that the testimonials originated with the podcast host rather than being scripted by PWA does not relieve the firm of liability; PWA engaged Garrison for sponsored content and bore the obligation to monitor what was broadcast under its name. The testimonials aired weekly for approximately 11 months, constituting hundreds of prohibited advertisements.

Second, PWA violated Rule 206(4)-7 under Section 206(4), which requires every registered adviser to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of the Advisers Act. Although PWA's compliance manual required pre-approval and archiving of advertisements, the firm failed to implement those procedures. PWA never obtained recordings of the podcast episodes, never monitored whether Garrison deviated from approved scripts, and the CCO was entirely unaware of the testimonial content. A policy that exists on paper but is not enforced is tantamount to having no policy at all.

Third, PWA violated Section 204 and Rule 204-2(a)(11), which require advisers to maintain copies of all advertisements. PWA's failure to obtain and preserve recordings of the podcast segments from October 2022 through August 2023 constitutes a books-and-records violation.

Fourth, PWA violated Section 204A and Rule 204A-1, which require advisers to establish, maintain, and enforce a written code of ethics that includes, among other things, requirements for access persons to report personal securities holdings and transactions. Brennan, as CEO and majority owner, was unquestionably an 'access person.' His failure to report the two outside brokerage accounts—which he controlled and which held overlapping positions with client portfolios—for approximately 18 months directly contravened the Code of Ethics. Brennan caused PWA's violation of Rule 204A-1 because his personal non-disclosure was the operative conduct that prevented the Code from functioning as designed.

The 'willfulness' standard under the Advisers Act requires only that the respondent knew what he or she was doing, not that the respondent was aware of violating a specific rule. Brennan knew he maintained the accounts and chose not to report them. PWA knew it engaged a spokesperson and failed to monitor the content. No scienter defense is available. Both respondents face potential sanctions under Sections 203(e) and 203(k), including censure, disgorgement, civil penalties, and a cease-and-desist order.
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: PWA's failure to monitor its sponsored podcast content allowed hundreds of prohibited client testimonials to air over 11 months, while its CEO simultaneously concealed reportable personal securities accounts from the firm's compliance function.

fact_pattern:
Michael Trevino, CRD No. 5621478, was a General Securities Representative registered through Pinnacle Wealth Advisors, LLC (CRD No. 18294) from March 2015 through October 2024. On November 2, 2024, Pinnacle filed a Form U5 stating that Trevino 'voluntarily resigned while under internal review for potential violations of firm policy, including undisclosed borrowing arrangements with clients and use of unapproved personal communication channels.' Specifically, the firm's internal compliance review had flagged that Trevino had allegedly borrowed $47,500 from a retired client, Dorothy Sanchez, age 72, in March 2023, and an additional $22,000 from a second client, George Harmon, age 68, in August 2023. Neither borrowing arrangement was disclosed to the firm or documented on any firm lending or outside business activity forms. Pinnacle's written supervisory procedures expressly prohibited borrowing from clients under any circumstances.

Following its review of Pinnacle's Form U5 filing, FINRA's Department of Enforcement opened an investigation into the alleged customer borrowing. On January 15, 2025, FINRA sent Trevino a written request pursuant to FINRA Rule 8210 to appear for on-the-record testimony at FINRA's regional office on February 20, 2025. The request was sent to Trevino's CRD address of record by certified mail and was confirmed as delivered on January 20, 2025.

Trevino retained counsel, and on February 10, 2025, his attorney sent an email to the FINRA investigating examiner stating: 'Mr. Trevino acknowledges receipt of FINRA's request for on-the-record testimony. After careful consideration, Mr. Trevino has decided that he will not appear for testimony on February 20, 2025, or at any future date. He respectfully declines to participate further in this investigation.' FINRA staff followed up with a second letter on February 25, 2025, reiterating the obligation to comply and providing a rescheduled date of March 18, 2025. Trevino's counsel responded on March 5, 2025, confirming that Trevino would not appear under any circumstances. Trevino is no longer registered with any FINRA member firm but has not filed a Form BDW or otherwise formally withdrawn from FINRA jurisdiction.

The underlying borrowing allegations have not been adjudicated, and no customer complaints have been filed to date.
question: Did Michael Trevino violate FINRA Rules 8210 and 2010 by refusing to appear for on-the-record testimony, and what sanctions are appropriate even though he is no longer registered with a FINRA member firm?
answer:
Trevino violated both FINRA Rule 8210 and FINRA Rule 2010. The analysis is straightforward and well-established in FINRA enforcement precedent.

First, FINRA Rule 8210(a)(1) authorizes FINRA to require any person associated with a member, or any person subject to FINRA's jurisdiction, to provide information orally and to testify under oath at a location specified by FINRA staff with respect to any matter involved in a FINRA investigation. FINRA Rule 8210(c) explicitly states that no person shall fail to provide information or testimony pursuant to the rule. Trevino received a properly served, written request for on-the-record testimony, acknowledged receipt through counsel, and affirmatively refused to appear—not once, but twice. His refusal was unequivocal and unconditional. There is no Fifth Amendment privilege that excuses compliance with FINRA Rule 8210 testimony requests in the self-regulatory context, as FINRA is not a government actor and the testimony is part of a private regulatory proceeding. Even if Trevino harbored concerns about potential criminal exposure, the proper course would have been to appear and assert the privilege question by question, not to refuse to appear entirely.

Second, a violation of FINRA Rule 8210 independently constitutes a violation of FINRA Rule 2010, which requires associated persons to observe high standards of commercial honor and just and equitable principles of trade. Refusing to cooperate with a regulatory investigation is fundamentally inconsistent with these obligations.

Regarding jurisdiction, Trevino's departure from Pinnacle does not insulate him. Under Article V, Section 4 of FINRA's By-Laws, FINRA retains jurisdiction over former associated persons for two years following the termination of their registration, provided the investigation concerns conduct that occurred during the period of registration. Here, the investigation was opened within that window, and the underlying conduct allegedly occurred while Trevino was registered.

As to sanctions, FINRA's Sanction Guidelines treat a complete refusal to appear for on-the-record testimony as among the most serious violations, warranting a bar from association in all capacities as the standard sanction. This is because FINRA's ability to regulate the industry depends entirely on its capacity to investigate misconduct, and a flat refusal to testify renders the investigatory process meaningless. A bar is appropriate regardless of whether the underlying borrowing allegations are ultimately proven, because the refusal itself is an independent and complete violation. Trevino's bar would also render him statutorily disqualified under Section 3(a)(39) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 8210(a)(1) and (c) (obligation to provide testimony); FINRA Rule 2010 (standards of commercial honor); Article V, Section 4 of FINRA By-Laws (continuing jurisdiction over former associated persons); FINRA Rule 8310 (sanctions); Section 3(a)(39) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (statutory disqualification)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Trevino's unequivocal and repeated refusal to appear for FINRA-requested on-the-record testimony, despite acknowledged receipt of the requests, constitutes a complete violation of FINRA Rule 8210 warranting a bar.

fact_pattern:
Piedmont Wealth Advisors, Inc. is a small FINRA member firm headquartered in Greensboro, North Carolina, registered since 1988. The firm has 9 registered representatives operating out of a single office, primarily serving retail customers in retirement and investment planning. The firm's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Lowell, has held the role since 2017.

When Regulation Best Interest took effect on June 30, 2020, Piedmont's existing written supervisory procedures (WSPs) were not updated to specifically address Reg BI obligations. Instead, the firm relied on its pre-existing suitability procedures under FINRA Rule 2111 and added a single paragraph to its compliance manual stating that 'all associated persons shall act in the best interest of their customers when making recommendations.' No provisions were added addressing the Care Obligation, the Disclosure Obligation, the Conflict of Interest Obligation, or the Compliance Obligation as specifically set forth in Exchange Act Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i)-(iv).

Between July 2020 and September 2023, three of Piedmont's registered representatives—Marcus Hale, Donna Fitzgerald, and Ray Chen—collectively made over 640 securities recommendations to approximately 115 retail customers. These recommendations included variable annuities with surrender periods of 7-10 years, Class A mutual fund shares with front-end loads averaging 5.25%, and various proprietary bond funds that generated higher commissions for the firm than comparable third-party alternatives. Marcus Hale alone recommended $3.8 million in variable annuity purchases, several to customers over age 70 with moderate risk profiles.

During a FINRA cycle examination in October 2023, examiners found that Piedmont had no written policies or procedures addressing how associated persons should identify, disclose, or mitigate conflicts of interest related to compensation differentials between product types. The firm had no process for documenting the basis for recommendations, no procedure to evaluate reasonably available alternatives, and no mechanism for supervisory review specifically tied to Reg BI's component obligations. Sandra Lowell acknowledged that the firm had intended to hire an outside compliance consultant to draft Reg BI-specific procedures but never followed through due to budget constraints. In January 2024, Piedmont engaged outside counsel and adopted new WSPs, but these procedures still lacked provisions for identifying and disclosing conflicts of interest arising from the firm's revenue-sharing arrangements with two mutual fund families.
question: Did Piedmont Wealth Advisors violate Regulation Best Interest's Compliance Obligation and Conflict of Interest Obligation by failing to establish and maintain written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI, and do the January 2024 updated procedures cure the violation?
answer:
Piedmont Wealth Advisors violated Exchange Act Rule 15l-1(a)(1) and (a)(2)(iii)-(iv), as well as FINRA Rules 3110 and 2010. The analysis proceeds through several layers.

First, Reg BI's Compliance Obligation under Exchange Act Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iv) requires a broker-dealer to establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI. As the SEC's Adopting Release (Exchange Act Release No. 86031, 84 FR 33318 at 33397) makes clear, these procedures must be designed to prevent violations, detect violations that have occurred, and promptly correct them. Piedmont's approach—adding a single generic sentence about acting in customers' best interests to its existing suitability manual—is materially insufficient. A vague aspirational statement does not constitute written procedures 'reasonably designed' to operationalize the four component obligations of Reg BI (Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance). This mirrors the deficiency found in the Alexander Investment Services AWC, where similarly non-specific references to best interest obligations were deemed violative.

Second, the Conflict of Interest Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iii) independently requires written policies and procedures reasonably designed to identify and, at a minimum, disclose all conflicts of interest associated with recommendations. Piedmont had no process for identifying compensation differentials between proprietary bond funds and third-party alternatives, no procedure for disclosing revenue-sharing arrangements, and no mechanism for evaluating whether such conflicts influenced recommendations. The 640 recommendations made over three years, including variable annuities generating significant commissions and Class A shares with 5.25% loads, occurred without any conflict-of-interest framework.

Third, FINRA Rule 3110 requires a supervisory system reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws. The absence of Reg BI-specific supervisory procedures—no documentation requirements, no supervisory review criteria tied to Reg BI's component obligations—constitutes a clear Rule 3110 violation. These violations also independently violate FINRA Rule 2010's requirement to observe high standards of commercial honor.

Finally, the January 2024 remediation does not cure the historical violation. The firm was non-compliant for over three years during which hundreds of recommendations were made. Moreover, the updated WSPs themselves remain deficient because they still fail to address conflicts arising from revenue-sharing arrangements, meaning the violation is ongoing. Budget constraints are not a defense to regulatory obligations that have been in effect since June 30, 2020.
applicable_standard: Exchange Act Rule 15l-1(a)(1), Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iii) (Conflict of Interest Obligation), Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iv) (Compliance Obligation); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor); SEC Adopting Release No. 86031, 84 FR 33318
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The firm failed for over three years to adopt written policies and procedures specifically addressing any of Reg BI's component obligations, relying instead on a single generic best-interest sentence grafted onto its legacy suitability procedures.

fact_pattern:
Pinnacle Securities Group, LLC (CRD No. 287445) is a mid-sized introducing broker-dealer headquartered in Miami, Florida, with 85 registered representatives operating across two branch offices. The firm primarily serves high-net-worth Brazilian and Colombian nationals seeking U.S. investment exposure. Between September 2019 and April 2020, Pinnacle recommended three separate private placement offerings to approximately 140 customers, generating approximately $47 million in total sales and $2.8 million in commissions.

The first offering, Meridian Real Estate Income Fund LP, was a $20 million Regulation D offering purporting to invest in distressed commercial real estate in secondary U.S. markets. The second, Solaris Digital Infrastructure Notes, was a $15 million offering of unsecured promissory notes funding cryptocurrency mining facilities in Paraguay. The third, Crestview Agriculture Holdings LLC, was a $12 million offering for farmland acquisition in the Midwest. For each offering, the issuers provided Pinnacle with private placement memoranda (PPMs), subscription agreements, and marketing materials.

Pinnacle's head of due diligence, Marcus Wellford, reviewed only the PPMs and issuer-provided financial projections. He did not independently verify the issuers' financial statements, did not conduct background checks on the principals of any of the three offerings, did not analyze the underlying asset valuations, and did not visit any of the physical operations or engage third-party experts. For the Solaris offering in particular, Wellford acknowledged in internal emails that he had 'limited understanding of the crypto mining economics' but approved the product for sale based solely on a 45-minute conference call with the issuer's CEO. The firm's written supervisory procedures contained only a generic two-paragraph section on private placement due diligence that did not specify required steps, assign responsibilities, or establish documentation requirements. The designated supervisory principal, Andrea Chen, approved each offering for sale after reviewing Wellford's one-page summary memos, which contained no risk analysis. Four months after the offerings closed, Solaris defaulted on its note obligations, and Crestview's principals were charged by the SEC with fraud.
question: Did Pinnacle Securities Group violate FINRA Rules 2111 and 3110 by recommending the three private placements without conducting adequate reasonable-basis due diligence and by failing to maintain a supervisory system reasonably designed to ensure compliance with the suitability rule?
answer:
Yes, Pinnacle Securities Group violated both FINRA Rule 2111 (through Rule 2010) and FINRA Rule 3110 (through Rule 2010). The analysis proceeds on two independent grounds.

First, regarding reasonable-basis suitability under FINRA Rule 2111 and Supplementary Material .05: The reasonable-basis obligation requires that a firm or associated person, based on reasonable diligence, have a reasonable basis to believe that a recommendation is suitable for at least some investors. Rule 2111.05 specifies that the diligence must provide an understanding of the potential risks and rewards associated with the recommended security, and that the rigor of diligence varies with the complexity and risks of the product and the firm's familiarity with it. Private placements—particularly those involving distressed real estate, cryptocurrency mining, and farmland—are complex, illiquid, high-risk securities that demand heightened due diligence.

Pinnacle's due diligence was deficient in virtually every respect. Wellford relied exclusively on issuer-provided materials without independent verification of financials, did not conduct background checks on principals (a critical failure given the subsequent fraud charges against Crestview's principals), did not assess underlying asset valuations, and did not engage third-party experts. For Solaris, his own email admission that he had 'limited understanding of the crypto mining economics' is dispositive evidence that the firm lacked the requisite understanding of risks and rewards. A 45-minute issuer call cannot substitute for substantive independent analysis of a novel and opaque investment structure. These facts closely mirror the XP Investments AWC, where FINRA found violations based on analogous failures to conduct reasonable diligence on private placements before recommending them to customers.

Second, regarding supervisory failures under FINRA Rule 3110: The firm must establish and maintain a supervisory system, including written supervisory procedures, reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable rules. Pinnacle's WSPs contained only a generic two-paragraph section on private placement due diligence with no specified steps, no assigned responsibilities, and no documentation requirements. Principal Andrea Chen's approval based solely on one-page summary memos lacking risk analysis demonstrates that the supervisory review was pro forma rather than substantive. The absence of a structured framework ensured that no meaningful check existed on the quality of due diligence.

Pinnacle cannot defend by arguing that the products ultimately performed well (Meridian may not have caused losses), because reasonable-basis suitability is measured at the time of recommendation, not by outcome. The $47 million in customer exposure and $2.8 million in commissions underscore the materiality of the violations. Both the substantive suitability violation and the supervisory failure independently constitute violations of FINRA Rule 2010's ethical standards requirement.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Rule 2111 Supplementary Material .05 (Reasonable-Basis Obligation); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The firm recommended three complex private placements without independently verifying issuer financials, conducting principal background checks, or analyzing underlying asset valuations, relying solely on issuer-provided materials despite acknowledging a lack of understanding of the investment economics.

fact_pattern:
Margaret Kensington, age 82, has been a client of registered representative David Sorensen at Lakeview Financial Group, a FINRA member firm, since 2003. Mrs. Kensington's account held approximately $1.4 million in diversified municipal bonds, blue-chip equities, and money market funds, consistent with her documented moderate-conservative risk tolerance and income-oriented investment objective. Her designated trusted contact person on file was her daughter, Linda Kensington-Park, listed pursuant to FINRA Rule 4512(a)(1)(F).

In March 2023, during a routine quarterly review call, Sorensen noticed that Mrs. Kensington was repeating questions she had asked minutes earlier, could not recall the purpose of the call despite having scheduled it herself, and expressed confusion about whether her late husband—who had passed away in 2019—would be joining the call. Three days later, Mrs. Kensington called Sorensen's office and requested the liquidation of her entire equity portfolio ($620,000) to wire the proceeds to an individual named 'Pastor Michael' at a church she had never previously mentioned, claiming she had been 'blessed' and needed to fulfill a 'divine financial covenant.' This pattern was entirely inconsistent with her prior investment behavior and instructions over the preceding 20 years.

Sorensen immediately escalated the matter to his branch manager, Patricia Hollis, documenting his observations and concerns in the firm's senior investor tracking system. Hollis contacted the firm's Elder Client Initiatives (ECI) team, which reviewed the case within 24 hours. The ECI team recommended placing a temporary hold on the disbursement under the firm's written supervisory procedures implementing FINRA Rule 2165, and Sorensen contacted Linda Kensington-Park as the trusted contact to discuss the situation. Linda confirmed her mother had recently been diagnosed with early-stage Alzheimer's disease and that the 'Pastor Michael' individual had been visiting her mother's assisted living facility. The firm also filed a suspicious activity report and notified the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services Adult Protective Services division. The temporary hold was maintained for 15 business days while the family obtained legal guardianship. The liquidation request was ultimately not processed.
question: Did David Sorensen and Lakeview Financial Group comply with FINRA rules and effective practices regarding the identification and response to potential financial exploitation and diminished capacity of a senior investor?
answer:
Yes, Sorensen and Lakeview Financial Group acted in full compliance with applicable FINRA rules and exemplified the effective practices promoted by FINRA for working with senior investors.

First, the firm had properly obtained a trusted contact person designation for Mrs. Kensington pursuant to FINRA Rule 4512(a)(1)(F), which requires member firms to make reasonable efforts to obtain the name and contact information of a trusted contact person upon account opening or updating. This foundational step proved critical in enabling the firm's response. The trusted contact is not an authorized party on the account but rather a resource the firm may contact when there are concerns about the customer's health, welfare, or potential financial exploitation—precisely how it was used here.

Second, the firm appropriately invoked FINRA Rule 2165, which permits a member firm to place a temporary hold on a disbursement of funds or securities from the account of a 'specified adult' (defined as a person age 65 or older, or a person age 18 or older who the firm reasonably believes has a mental or physical impairment that renders the individual unable to protect his or her own interests). The rule requires that the firm reasonably believe that financial exploitation has occurred, is occurring, has been attempted, or will be attempted. Here, the red flags were compelling: Mrs. Kensington exhibited clear signs of cognitive decline during the call, made a request wholly inconsistent with 20 years of documented investment behavior, and the beneficiary of the proposed wire was an unknown third party soliciting funds through what appeared to be an affinity-based exploitation scheme. Under Rule 2165(b)(1), the temporary hold may last up to 15 business days, with an extension of up to 10 additional business days if warranted.

Third, Sorensen's detailed contemporaneous documentation of his observations satisfies the firm's obligations under FINRA Rule 4511 (Books and Records) and the internal escalation to the branch manager and ECI team reflects sound supervisory practices under FINRA Rule 3110. The filing of a suspicious activity report and referral to Adult Protective Services further demonstrates adherence to both regulatory obligations and FINRA's stated effective practices for elder financial exploitation cases.

Finally, Sorensen's conduct throughout was consistent with FINRA Rule 2010's requirement to observe high standards of commercial honor and just and equitable principles of trade. Rather than processing a transaction that would have generated commissions, he prioritized his client's welfare. This case illustrates the precise framework FINRA has encouraged firms to adopt: trained representatives who recognize warning signs, established escalation protocols, functional ECI teams, and proper use of trusted contact and temporary hold provisions.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2165 (Financial Exploitation of Specified Adults); FINRA Rule 4512(a)(1)(F) (Trusted Contact Person); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Rule 4511 (General Requirements for Books and Records); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The firm's prompt recognition of cognitive decline indicators and proper invocation of FINRA Rule 2165's temporary hold mechanism, combined with timely contact of the designated trusted contact person and referral to Adult Protective Services, constituted a model response to suspected elder financial exploitation.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Reilly, a registered representative with Eastgate Capital Partners (a FINRA member firm), has been licensed since 2009 and primarily serves retail clients in the greater Philadelphia area. In September 2012, Reilly began working with a new client, Dorothy Albrecht, a 74-year-old retired schoolteacher. Albrecht opened a brokerage account with Eastgate after her husband passed away and she received a $430,000 life insurance payout. During the new account process, Albrecht completed a customer profile form indicating that her investment objectives were 'income and preservation of capital,' her risk tolerance was 'conservative,' her annual income from Social Security and a small pension was $38,000, her liquid net worth aside from the insurance proceeds was approximately $85,000, her time horizon was '5-10 years,' and she had no prior investment experience beyond certificates of deposit and a savings account.

Between October 2012 and March 2013, Reilly recommended and executed a series of transactions in Albrecht's account. He placed approximately $175,000 into a leveraged closed-end bond fund that employed 35% structural leverage and had experienced significant NAV volatility, $95,000 into a non-traded REIT with a seven-year lockup period and limited redemption provisions, and $60,000 across three separate high-yield (junk) bond ETFs. Reilly also recommended that Albrecht invest $40,000 in a speculative small-cap biotech stock that he described to her as a 'ground floor opportunity.' In total, approximately $370,000 of the $430,000 in proceeds—roughly 86% of the insurance payout—was directed into products carrying material risk of principal loss, illiquidity, or both.

Reilly's internal notes from the October 2012 meeting stated only: 'Client wants growth to supplement retirement income. Discussed various options.' He did not document any discussion of the specific risks of leveraged funds, non-traded REITs, high-yield bonds, or speculative equities, nor did he note any assessment of how these products aligned with Albrecht's stated conservative risk tolerance, limited investment experience, or liquidity needs. Eastgate's compliance department did not flag any of the transactions at the time, and the firm's supervisory review procedures relied on a single quarterly exception report that only flagged accounts with more than 15 trades per month, which Albrecht's account did not trigger.
question: Did Marcus Reilly violate FINRA Rule 2111's customer-specific suitability obligation by recommending leveraged funds, a non-traded REIT, high-yield bond ETFs, and a speculative biotech stock to Dorothy Albrecht?
answer:
Yes, Marcus Reilly violated FINRA Rule 2111's customer-specific suitability obligation, and Eastgate Capital Partners likely violated FINRA Rule 3110's supervisory obligations. The analysis proceeds as follows.

FINRA Rule 2111(a) requires that a broker have a reasonable basis to believe that a recommended transaction or investment strategy involving a security or securities is suitable for the customer, based on information obtained through reasonable diligence to ascertain the customer's investment profile. Rule 2111 codifies three distinct suitability obligations: reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative. The customer-specific obligation—the primary basis for violation here—requires the broker to have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is suitable for the particular customer based on that customer's investment profile, which under Rule 2111 explicitly includes age, investment experience, time horizon, liquidity needs, risk tolerance, financial situation and needs, tax status, investment objectives, and other investments.

Applying these factors to Albrecht's profile reveals a stark mismatch. She was 74 years old, had zero investment experience beyond CDs and savings, stated her objectives as income and capital preservation, identified her risk tolerance as conservative, had a 5-10 year time horizon, and had modest income of $38,000 per year. A leveraged closed-end bond fund with 35% structural leverage carries amplified downside risk wholly inconsistent with capital preservation. The non-traded REIT's seven-year lockup is incompatible with a 74-year-old client's liquidity needs and time horizon. High-yield bond ETFs carry material credit and principal risk, and a speculative biotech stock is antithetical to conservative objectives. Moreover, concentrating 86% of the insurance proceeds—which represented the vast majority of her investable assets—in these products left Albrecht with insufficient liquid, conservative reserves.

Reilly's documentation failures compound the violation. Regulatory Notice 12-25 emphasizes that while FINRA generally permits a risk-based approach to documentation, the obligation to perform and evidence reasonable diligence is paramount, particularly with complex products sold to inexperienced, elderly clients. Reilly's one-sentence note fails to demonstrate any analysis of product-specific risks relative to Albrecht's profile.

Additionally, Eastgate's supervisory framework under FINRA Rule 3110 was deficient. A quarterly exception report keyed solely to trade frequency would never capture concentrated, unsuitable allocations in a low-trade-count account. This represents a failure to establish and maintain a system reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and FINRA rules.

No plausible defense exists. The customer's documented profile directly contradicts every material recommendation. The volume of unsuitable investments was not a single misjudgment but a systematic pattern over six months. Both Reilly and Eastgate bear responsibility under Rules 2111 and 2010 (standards of commercial honor and just and equitable principles of trade).
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), including customer-specific suitability under Rule 2111(a) and the investment profile factors enumerated therein; FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Just and Equitable Trade); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Regulatory Notices 11-02, 11-25, and 12-25
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Reilly recommended high-risk, illiquid, and speculative products comprising 86% of a 74-year-old conservative, inexperienced client's investable assets without any documented analysis of how those products aligned with her stated investment profile.

fact_pattern:
QuickTrade Securities LLC is a FINRA member firm headquartered in Austin, Texas, offering self-directed online brokerage services to approximately 850,000 retail customers through a mobile application. The firm has been a FINRA member since 2012 and employs 45 registered representatives across two branch offices.

In March 2020, the firm's lead software engineer, David Calloway (CRD #7234891), designed and deployed a customer analytics database hosted on a third-party cloud platform, Amazon Web Services (AWS), outside of QuickTrade's primary corporate data security perimeter. This database contained nonpublic personal information (NPI) of all firm customers, including full legal names, Social Security numbers, brokerage account numbers, portfolio holdings, account balances, and transaction histories. The database was secured with its own set of login credentials and two-factor authentication, separate from the firm's internal single sign-on (SSO) system. Calloway was the sole person who regularly accessed and maintained the database.

QuickTrade maintained written supervisory procedures (WSPs) that required the firm's IT department to disable all systems access for departing employees within 24 hours of separation, and to conduct quarterly audits of access logs across all firm platforms. The firm's cybersecurity policy, updated in January 2020, also required the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Rachel Nguyen, to maintain a comprehensive inventory of all databases containing customer NPI. However, the AWS-hosted analytics database was never added to the firm's official systems inventory, and it was never included in the quarterly access audits.

On September 15, 2021, Calloway resigned from QuickTrade. The firm's IT department promptly terminated his access to the firm's internal network, email, CRM, and order management systems. However, because the AWS analytics database was not on the firm's systems inventory, no one disabled Calloway's AWS credentials. Between September 16, 2021, and February 28, 2022—a period of approximately five and a half months—Calloway logged into the database on 14 separate occasions and downloaded CSV reports containing the NPI of approximately 312,000 customers. The unauthorized access was discovered on March 1, 2022, when a junior developer noticed anomalous login activity while performing an unrelated migration of the database into the firm's internal infrastructure. QuickTrade self-reported the incident to FINRA on March 8, 2022, and subsequently notified affected customers on April 2, 2022.
question: Did QuickTrade Securities LLC violate Regulation S-P Rule 30(a), FINRA Rule 3110, and FINRA Rule 2010 by failing to include the external customer analytics database in its systems inventory and off-boarding procedures, resulting in prolonged unauthorized access by a former employee?
answer:
QuickTrade Securities LLC violated Regulation S-P Rule 30(a), FINRA Rule 3110(a) and (b), and FINRA Rule 2010. The analysis proceeds as follows.

First, Rule 30(a) of Regulation S-P (17 C.F.R. § 248.30(a)) requires broker-dealers to adopt written policies and procedures that address administrative, technical, and physical safeguards for the protection of customer records and information. These safeguards must be reasonably designed to (i) ensure the security and confidentiality of customer records, (ii) protect against anticipated threats or hazards to the security of such records, and (iii) protect against unauthorized access to or use of customer records that could result in substantial harm or inconvenience to any customer. QuickTrade's failure to include the AWS-hosted analytics database—which contained NPI for 850,000 customers including Social Security numbers and account holdings—in its official systems inventory and off-boarding procedures rendered its written safeguards unreasonable. The firm's existing cybersecurity policy required a comprehensive inventory of NPI-containing databases, but the CISO never ensured compliance with this requirement. The result was precisely the harm Rule 30(a) is designed to prevent: a former employee accessed NPI of 312,000 customers over five and a half months.

Second, FINRA Rule 3110(a) requires member firms to establish and maintain a supervisory system reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and regulations. Rule 3110(b) further requires written supervisory procedures that are maintained and enforced. QuickTrade's supervisory system was deficient in two respects: (1) the quarterly access audits mandated by the WSPs did not encompass the AWS database, and (2) the off-boarding process did not account for external platforms with separate access credentials. The firm had written procedures that facially addressed these risks, but the procedures were not enforced with respect to the analytics database. Having a policy on paper that is not operationally implemented fails the 'reasonably designed' standard under Rule 3110.

Third, violations of Regulation S-P and FINRA Rule 3110 constitute independent violations of FINRA Rule 2010, which requires member firms to observe high standards of commercial honor and just and equitable principles of trade. The firm's systemic failure to safeguard sensitive customer data falls below these standards.

The firm's self-report and subsequent remediation—migrating the database internally and notifying customers—are mitigating factors that FINRA may consider in determining sanctions, but they do not negate the underlying violations. The defense that the database had its own two-factor authentication is unavailing; the safeguard became meaningless once the sole authorized user departed and retained valid credentials. The pivotal failure was the gap between written policy and operational execution, a recurring theme in Regulation S-P enforcement.
applicable_standard: Regulation S-P Rule 30(a) (17 C.F.R. § 248.30(a)); FINRA Rule 3110(a) (supervisory systems); FINRA Rule 3110(b) (written supervisory procedures); FINRA Rule 2010 (standards of commercial honor and just and equitable principles of trade)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The firm failed to include an externally hosted database containing customer NPI in its systems inventory and employee off-boarding procedures, allowing a former employee to retain and exploit access credentials for over five months after separation.

fact_pattern:
Coastal Edge Financial Group ('CEFG'), a FINRA member broker-dealer registered with the SEC, operates out of Fort Lauderdale, Florida, with approximately 38 registered representatives serving roughly 2,200 retail customers. In January 2025, CEFG filed its Form CRS (Client Relationship Summary) with the SEC and began delivering it to new and prospective retail investors. The Form CRS was drafted by CEFG's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Whitfield, who had recently joined the firm from an investment advisory practice and had limited experience with broker-dealer-specific disclosure requirements.

Upon examination by FINRA in April 2025, several deficiencies were identified. First, CEFG's Form CRS stated that the firm 'may provide ongoing monitoring of your brokerage account as part of our standard services,' but in practice, CEFG did not offer systematic account monitoring; representatives only reviewed accounts sporadically when customers called in with complaints. The firm had no written supervisory procedures governing account monitoring, no technology platform to flag account drift, and no documented review schedule. Second, the Form CRS fee disclosure section stated that 'commissions and transaction fees are the primary costs you will incur,' but failed to disclose that CEFG earned revenue-sharing payments from three preferred mutual fund families—Apex Growth Funds, Meridian Income Partners, and Trident Capital Series—amounting to approximately $485,000 in 2024. These revenue-sharing arrangements incentivized representatives to recommend products from these families, and 67% of mutual fund transactions by dollar volume in 2024 involved these three families. Third, the 'Conflicts of Interest' section of the Form CRS listed proprietary products as a conflict but described it only as 'we may earn higher fees from certain products,' without specifying the nature of the revenue-sharing arrangement or quantifying its magnitude. Fourth, the Conversation Starters section omitted several SEC-mandated questions, including 'Given my financial situation, should you choose an investment advisory service? Why or why not?'

During the examination, representative Marcus Delano was found to have recommended Apex Growth Aggressive Fund (Class A shares with a 5.25% front-end load) to 14 retail customers between February and March 2025 without disclosing the revenue-sharing arrangement, even though lower-cost index ETF alternatives were available and more suitable for several of these customers, including three retirees with conservative risk profiles and account sizes under $50,000. Sandra Whitfield acknowledged during the examination that she had not reviewed the SEC's Form CRS instructions in detail and had relied on a template from CEFG's prior compliance consultant, which had not been updated since 2020.
question: Did CEFG's Form CRS disclosures and its representatives' related conduct violate applicable SEC and FINRA rules, and what are the specific regulatory bases for each deficiency?
answer:
CEFG's Form CRS and associated conduct contain multiple violations of SEC Form CRS requirements under Regulation Best Interest, FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade), FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision), and potentially FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) and SEC Rule 15l-1 (Reg BI).

First, the misleading account monitoring disclosure violates Form CRS requirements under SEC Rule 17a-14 and the Form CRS Instructions. The SEC requires that broker-dealers accurately describe the scope of services offered. By stating that CEFG 'may provide ongoing monitoring' when no systematic monitoring infrastructure existed, CEFG created a materially misleading impression that could cause retail investors to believe their accounts were being supervised. This also implicates FINRA Rule 2010, as making misleading statements to customers falls below the standards of commercial honor.

Second, the failure to disclose revenue-sharing arrangements in the fee section violates Reg BI's Disclosure Obligation under Exchange Act Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i), which requires broker-dealers to provide full and fair disclosure of all material facts relating to the scope and terms of the relationship, including conflicts of interest. Revenue-sharing payments of $485,000 annually, driving 67% of mutual fund volume toward three preferred families, constitute a material conflict that must be specifically disclosed—not buried in a vague reference to 'higher fees from certain products.' The Form CRS Instructions specifically require disclosure of third-party payments that create incentives.

Third, the omission of mandated Conversation Starters violates the Form CRS Instructions, which prescribe specific questions that must appear verbatim. This is a technical but important violation, as these prompts are designed to empower retail investors to engage with their financial professionals about key decision points.

Fourth, representative Delano's recommendations of high-load Class A mutual fund shares to conservative retirees, without disclosing the revenue-sharing incentive and without considering lower-cost alternatives, violates Reg BI's Care Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii) and the Conflict of Interest Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iii). The Care Obligation requires reasonable diligence to understand available alternatives and ensure that a recommendation is in the customer's best interest. Recommending a 5.25% front-end load fund to retirees with sub-$50,000 accounts when suitable lower-cost ETFs existed fails this standard.

Finally, Sandra Whitfield's failure to review updated regulatory guidance and CEFG's lack of written supervisory procedures for account monitoring and Form CRS compliance violate FINRA Rule 3110(a) and (b), which require firms to establish, maintain, and enforce reasonably designed supervisory systems and written procedures. Reliance on an outdated template without independent verification is insufficient. No good-faith defense excuses these systemic failures.
applicable_standard: SEC Rule 17a-14 (Form CRS delivery); Exchange Act Rule 15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest) — Disclosure Obligation §15l-1(a)(2)(i), Care Obligation §15l-1(a)(2)(ii), Conflict of Interest Obligation §15l-1(a)(2)(iii); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Rule 3110(a) and (b) (Supervision); SEC Form CRS Instructions (June 2019, as amended)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: CEFG's Form CRS affirmatively misrepresented its account monitoring services and failed to disclose material revenue-sharing conflicts that drove the majority of its mutual fund recommendations, undermining the core Reg BI disclosure and conflict-of-interest obligations.

fact_pattern:
Meridian Capital Partners, LLC (CRD #28491), a mid-sized broker-dealer headquartered in Stamford, Connecticut with approximately 85 registered representatives and 12,000 customer accounts, engaged DataBridge IT Solutions ('DataBridge') as a third-party service provider in March 2021 to manage its cloud-hosted customer relationship management (CRM) system and trade blotter infrastructure. DataBridge was granted administrative-level access to Meridian's production environment, including databases containing customers' Social Security numbers, dates of birth, account numbers, and financial holdings. Meridian's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Whitfield, had been informed during a FINRA cycle examination concluding in September 2020 that the firm needed to strengthen its cybersecurity controls, specifically by implementing multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users with access to production systems, logging all third-party access sessions, and conducting periodic access reviews. In response, Whitfield oversaw the rollout of MFA for all 85 registered representatives and 14 internal operations staff by January 2021. However, when DataBridge was onboarded two months later, Whitfield's team exempted the vendor from MFA requirements because DataBridge's lead engineer, Rajiv Menon, complained that MFA tokens interfered with his automated maintenance scripts. No compensating controls—such as IP whitelisting, session logging, or enhanced monitoring—were implemented for DataBridge's access. Additionally, Meridian never established a system to monitor or log DataBridge's access sessions to the production environment.

On August 14, 2022, an unauthorized actor compromised Menon's workstation through a phishing attack and used his administrative credentials to access Meridian's production databases over a 72-hour period, exfiltrating the non-public personal information (NPI) of approximately 4,300 customers, including account balances ranging from $15,000 to $3.2 million. The breach was discovered on August 17, 2022 when an internal IT analyst noticed anomalous data transfer volumes. Meridian activated its incident response plan, engaged CrowdStrike for forensic analysis, self-reported to FINRA on August 19, 2022, and notified all affected customers by September 5, 2022 in accordance with state breach notification laws.

Despite the remedial measures, FINRA's Department of Enforcement initiated an investigation and found that for the 17-month period between DataBridge's onboarding and the breach, Meridian had failed to require MFA for DataBridge, failed to log or monitor DataBridge's access to production systems, and had no written supervisory procedures addressing third-party vendor cybersecurity controls—all after being specifically warned by FINRA examiners about these precise deficiencies.
question: Did Meridian Capital Partners violate the Safeguards Rule and FINRA supervisory obligations by exempting its third-party service provider from multi-factor authentication and failing to monitor the provider's access to customer data, even though the firm implemented MFA for its internal personnel and responded appropriately after the breach was discovered?
answer:
Yes, Meridian Capital Partners violated Rule 30(a) of Regulation S-P (the Safeguards Rule) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as well as FINRA Rules 3110 (Supervision) and 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade). The firm's post-breach remediation, while commendable, does not cure the underlying supervisory failures that existed for 17 months.

The Safeguards Rule, codified at 17 C.F.R. § 248.30(a), requires every broker-dealer to adopt written policies and procedures reasonably designed to safeguard customer records and information, including protecting against unauthorized access to or use of such records that could result in substantial harm or inconvenience to customers. The rule does not prescribe specific technologies but imposes an obligation of reasonableness given known risks. Here, Meridian was on explicit notice from FINRA examiners that its cybersecurity program needed to address third-party access controls, including MFA and access logging. By exempting DataBridge from MFA solely because of the vendor engineer's convenience complaint—without implementing any compensating controls such as IP restrictions, session recording, or enhanced monitoring—Meridian failed to maintain a reasonably designed safeguards program. The firm's awareness of the specific risk, combined with its failure to address it, elevates this from a mere oversight to a systemic supervisory deficiency.

Under FINRA Rule 3110(a), member firms must establish and maintain a supervisory system, including written supervisory procedures, reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and FINRA rules. Meridian's WSPs contained no provisions addressing third-party vendor cybersecurity requirements, access review schedules, or escalation procedures when vendors resist security controls. This gap is particularly egregious given the prior examination findings. FINRA Rule 3110(b) further requires WSPs to be tailored to the firm's business; a firm that grants administrative access to outside vendors without corresponding written controls has failed this requirement.

Meridian's self-reporting, prompt incident response, customer notification, and subsequent remediation (implementing MFA for all third parties and deploying endpoint detection and response tools) would appropriately be treated as mitigating factors under FINRA's Sanction Guidelines §2.3, potentially reducing monetary sanctions. However, mitigation does not constitute a defense to the underlying violation. The firm's decision to exempt DataBridge after being warned by FINRA examiners could be viewed as an aggravating factor under the Guidelines, as it reflects a disregard of prior regulatory guidance. A firm cannot selectively implement cybersecurity controls for internal users while leaving an administrative-access vendor unprotected and claim its safeguards program was reasonable.
applicable_standard: Rule 30(a) of Regulation S-P (17 C.F.R. § 248.30(a)) — Safeguards Rule; FINRA Rule 3110(a) and (b) — Supervision and Written Supervisory Procedures; FINRA Rule 2010 — Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade; FINRA Sanction Guidelines § 2.3 (mitigating and aggravating factors)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The firm exempted a third-party service provider with administrative access from multi-factor authentication and access monitoring despite explicit prior FINRA examination warnings to implement those exact controls, directly enabling the unauthorized breach of 4,300 customers' non-public personal information.

fact_pattern:
Clearwater Financial Partners, LLC ('Clearwater'), a FINRA member firm with 87 registered representatives, primarily serves retail customers through brokerage accounts. In June 2020, the firm adopted written supervisory procedures (WSPs) to comply with Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), which became effective on June 30, 2020. The firm's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Whitfield, drafted the procedures largely by copying template language from an industry vendor without tailoring them to Clearwater's specific business model, product offerings, or compensation arrangements.

Between July 2020 and March 2021, Clearwater representatives recommended proprietary mutual funds to approximately 340 retail customers. These proprietary funds carried expense ratios averaging 1.45%, while substantially similar third-party funds available on the firm's platform had expense ratios averaging 0.62%. Representatives received a 25-basis-point additional trailing commission for placing clients in proprietary funds versus third-party alternatives. The firm's Form CRS, filed in June 2020, disclosed that the firm 'may have conflicts of interest' but did not specifically identify the enhanced compensation for proprietary fund recommendations or quantify the differential.

During this period, registered representative Marcus DeLeon recommended proprietary Clearwater Growth Fund Class A shares to 47 retail customers, including retiree Helen Kowalski, age 72, who had $385,000 in retirement savings, a moderate risk tolerance, and an investment objective of capital preservation with income. DeLeon placed $142,000 of Kowalski's assets in the proprietary growth fund despite her stated objectives. The firm's supervisory review system consisted solely of a quarterly random sample review of 5% of new account recommendations, conducted by branch manager Terrence Hobbs, who used a checklist that did not include any fields for evaluating cost comparisons, conflict-of-interest mitigation, or reasonably available alternatives.

FINRA examiners reviewing the firm in early 2021 found that Clearwater had no automated or systematic process for comparing costs of recommended products against reasonably available alternatives, no documentation of how conflicts were mitigated at the point of recommendation, and no evidence that supervisory personnel evaluated whether the Care Obligation was satisfied for any individual recommendation.
question: Did Clearwater Financial Partners and its personnel violate Regulation Best Interest and related FINRA supervisory obligations in their handling of proprietary fund recommendations to retail customers?
answer:
Yes. Clearwater Financial Partners violated multiple components of Regulation Best Interest (SEC Rule 15l-1 under the Exchange Act) and FINRA Rules 3110 (Supervision) and 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade). The violations span all four component obligations of Reg BI.

First, the Disclosure Obligation (Reg BI Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i)) requires broker-dealers to provide full and fair disclosure of all material facts relating to the scope and terms of the relationship, including material conflicts of interest. Clearwater's Form CRS used only boilerplate language about potential conflicts without specifically disclosing the 25-basis-point enhanced trailing commission for proprietary fund sales. This differential compensation is a material conflict that must be specifically identified, not obscured behind generic disclosure. The failure to quantify or specifically describe this incentive rendered the disclosure inadequate.

Second, the Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)) requires that the broker-dealer exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the potential risks, rewards, and costs of a recommendation, and to have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the retail customer's best interest at the time it is made, without placing the financial interest of the broker ahead of the customer. DeLeon's recommendation of a growth-oriented proprietary fund to Kowalski — a 72-year-old retiree with capital preservation and income objectives — fails on its face. Moreover, the 83-basis-point expense ratio differential between the proprietary and comparable third-party funds, with no documented justification for selecting the costlier option, demonstrates that cost was not adequately considered as required under the Care Obligation.

Third, the Conflict of Interest Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iii)) requires firms to establish, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to identify, disclose, and mitigate or eliminate conflicts of interest. Clearwater's WSPs were generic vendor templates not tailored to the firm's proprietary product conflicts or enhanced compensation structure, failing to meet this standard.

Fourth, the firm's supervisory system violated FINRA Rule 3110 by implementing only a 5% random quarterly sample review with a checklist that omitted any evaluation of cost comparisons, conflict mitigation, or assessment of reasonably available alternatives. This is not a supervisory system reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI. The absence of any systematic process for comparing recommended products against lower-cost alternatives is a particularly significant deficiency that FINRA's 2021 Report specifically flagged as a key examination focus area.

Clearwater cannot defend by arguing it had written procedures in place; untailored, unenforced procedures do not satisfy the obligation to implement and supervise. The totality of these failures — inadequate disclosure, unsuitable recommendations, unmitigated conflicts, and deficient supervision — constitutes a clear pattern of non-compliance.
applicable_standard: SEC Regulation Best Interest (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i)-(iv) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Principles of Trade); Form CRS (Rule 17a-14 under the Exchange Act)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The firm failed to establish and implement policies, procedures, and a supervisory system reasonably designed to ensure compliance with Reg BI's Care and Conflict of Interest Obligations, including the absence of any systematic process for evaluating costs of recommended proprietary products against reasonably available lower-cost alternatives.

fact_pattern:
Pinnacle Wealth Advisors, Inc. (CRD No. 54892) is a mid-sized broker-dealer based in Dallas, Texas, with approximately 340 registered representatives and a predominantly retail client base. In March 2021, the firm launched a self-directed digital platform called 'Pinnacle Direct' that allowed retail customers to open accounts and trade a wide range of products, including leveraged and inverse exchange-traded products (ETPs), structured notes with knock-in/knock-out barriers, and multi-leg options strategies including iron condors and calendar spreads.

Between March 2021 and December 2021, approximately 4,200 retail customers opened Pinnacle Direct accounts. The platform's onboarding process required customers to complete a brief questionnaire consisting of five multiple-choice questions about their investment experience, risk tolerance, and time horizon. However, there was no mechanism to assess whether customers actually understood the specific characteristics and risks of complex products before granting access to trade them. Any customer who self-certified as having 'some experience' with securities and selected 'aggressive' or 'moderate' risk tolerance was automatically approved to trade the full suite of complex products, including triple-leveraged inverse ETPs and Level 4 options strategies.

Margaret Chen, age 62, a recently retired schoolteacher from Plano, Texas, with a $385,000 retirement portfolio and limited investment experience, opened a Pinnacle Direct account in June 2021. She self-certified as having 'some experience' and selected 'moderate' risk tolerance. Between June and November 2021, Chen allocated approximately $210,000 — over 54% of her liquid net worth — to positions in ProShares UltraPro Short QQQ (SQQQ), a triple-leveraged inverse ETF, and sold uncovered put options on volatile technology stocks. She held the SQQQ position for periods ranging from 3 to 11 weeks, far exceeding the single-day holding period for which the product was designed. By November 2021, Chen had realized losses of approximately $137,000.

Pinnacle's written supervisory procedures (WSPs) for Pinnacle Direct contained no specific provisions for heightened review of complex product trading by self-directed customers. The firm's compliance department did not generate exception reports for concentrated complex product positions, did not monitor holding periods for leveraged/inverse ETPs, and did not conduct any post-trade surveillance specifically tailored to complex products. The firm's Chief Compliance Officer, David Reinhardt, had raised concerns internally in February 2021 about the absence of complex product guardrails on the platform but was overruled by the firm's CEO, who stated that 'restricting product access would put us at a competitive disadvantage against Robinhood and Webull.' No additional supervisory measures were implemented.
question: Did Pinnacle Wealth Advisors violate its supervisory obligations under FINRA rules by failing to implement adequate controls and supervision over retail customers' self-directed trading in complex products on its digital platform?
answer:
Yes, Pinnacle Wealth Advisors violated FINRA Rules 3110, 2111, and 2010 through its systemic failure to establish and maintain a supervisory system reasonably designed to address the unique risks of complex product trading by retail customers on its self-directed platform.
