On September 18, 2023, the Fund's board of directors formally designated Ridgeview as the valuation designee under SEC Rule 2a-5, which became effective in September 2022. The board resolution designating Ridgeview contained only a single paragraph stating that Ridgeview "shall perform all fair value determinations in accordance with applicable law." No written policies or procedures were adopted by Ridgeview specifically addressing Rule 2a-5's requirements. Ridgeview's chief compliance officer, Sandra Whitfield, raised concerns in an October 2023 memorandum that the firm had not established written fair valuation methodologies, had not implemented any process for periodically testing the appropriateness of the valuation methodologies applied to the Fund's illiquid holdings, and had not conducted any formal evaluation of the third-party pricing service (PriceMark Analytics) used to supply evaluated prices for approximately $340 million of the Fund's structured credit positions.

Despite Whitfield's memorandum, Ridgeview's portfolio management team, led by Managing Director Thomas Kessler, continued to rely exclusively on stale PriceMark Analytics prices—some of which had not been updated for over 45 business days—without any back-testing, calibration, or cross-referencing against observable market inputs. In December 2023, an SEC examination revealed that the Fund's NAV had been overstated by approximately 1.3% (roughly $36.4 million) over a four-month period due to the use of stale and unvalidated evaluated prices for the structured credit positions. This overstatement caused shareholders who purchased during the period to pay inflated prices and caused redeeming shareholders to receive more than their pro rata share of the Fund's value, diluting remaining shareholders' interests.
question: Did Ridgeview Capital Management, as the designated valuation designee under Rule 2a-5, comply with its obligations to determine fair value in good faith for the Fund's portfolio securities lacking readily available market quotations?
answer:
Ridgeview Capital Management failed to comply with its obligations as valuation designee under SEC Rule 2a-5 in multiple material respects.

Rule 2a-5 under the Investment Company Act of 1940, adopted in the SEC's December 2020 release (IC-34128) and effective September 2022, establishes a comprehensive framework for fair value determinations. When a fund board designates its investment adviser as the valuation designee, that adviser must satisfy four core requirements: (1) periodically assess and manage material valuation risks (Rule 2a-5(a)); (2) establish and apply fair value methodologies, including the selection of methodologies and the identification of key inputs and assumptions (Rule 2a-5(a)(2)); (3) test the appropriateness and accuracy of those methodologies, including through back-testing (Rule 2a-5(a)(3)); and (4) evaluate pricing services used to provide fair value determinations or assist in deriving fair value (Rule 2a-5(a)(4)).

Ridgeview violated each of these requirements. First, the firm never adopted written fair value policies or procedures as required—the board resolution was perfunctory and delegated responsibility without any accompanying procedural framework. This contravenes the requirement to establish and apply methodologies with specificity. Second, Ridgeview conducted no periodic testing of its valuation methodologies. The use of PriceMark Analytics prices that were stale by up to 45 business days, without any back-testing or calibration against observable inputs, is a textbook failure of the testing requirement under Rule 2a-5(a)(3). Third, Ridgeview never evaluated PriceMark Analytics as a pricing service—there was no assessment of the vendor's methodology, processes, or track record, violating Rule 2a-5(a)(4). The SEC's adopting release specifically emphasized that valuation designees must evaluate pricing services' methodologies and challenge stale or anomalous prices.

The resulting 1.3% NAV overstatement ($36.4 million) directly harmed shareholders, precisely the type of dilution Section 2(a)(41) and Rule 2a-5 are designed to prevent. Sandra Whitfield's October 2023 memorandum, which was disregarded, further demonstrates that Ridgeview had actual notice of its deficiencies. Ridgeview cannot claim good faith under these circumstances. Additionally, the firm likely violated its fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act, as the failure to properly value client assets represents a breach of the duty of care owed to the Fund and its shareholders. This conduct would also implicate Rule 38a-1 under the Investment Company Act regarding compliance program adequacy.
applicable_standard: SEC Rule 2a-5 under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (17 CFR 270.2a-5); Section 2(a)(41) of the Investment Company Act of 1940; SEC Release No. IC-34128 (Dec. 3, 2020); Investment Advisers Act of 1940 fiduciary duty; Rule 38a-1 under the Investment Company Act
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Ridgeview, as the designated valuation designee, failed to establish written fair value methodologies, never tested the appropriateness of its valuation approaches, and did not evaluate its third-party pricing service, resulting in materially overstated NAV and shareholder dilution.

fact_pattern:
Greenleaf Capital Advisors, LLC is a state-registered investment adviser based in Columbus, Ohio, with approximately $185 million in assets under management across 340 client accounts. The firm's principal, Marcus Greenleaf, CFA, has been registered since 2012. In October 2023, the firm hired a new advisory representative, Diana Portillo, who previously worked at a wirehouse broker-dealer.

Between November 2023 and March 2024, Portillo managed 47 client accounts and executed approximately 310 securities transactions across those accounts. Portillo's practice involved calling clients by phone to discuss investment recommendations, obtaining verbal authorization, and then placing trades through the firm's clearing broker, National Clearing Corp. However, Portillo did not create written memoranda for the orders she placed. Instead, she relied on the clearing broker's electronic trade confirmations as the sole record of each transaction. These confirmations showed the security, quantity, price, date, and account number, but did not identify which adviser recommended the transaction, did not indicate whether the order was entered pursuant to discretionary authority, and did not reflect the terms and conditions of the original client instruction.

During a routine state examination in April 2024, examiners requested order memoranda for a sample of 50 transactions across 12 client accounts managed by Portillo. Marcus Greenleaf produced only the clearing broker's trade confirmations. When pressed, Greenleaf acknowledged the firm had no internal order ticket system and stated that Portillo had been told during onboarding to 'document everything in CRM notes,' but the CRM contained only sparse, undated entries such as 'spoke with client re: portfolio' with no reference to specific securities, order terms, or the recommending adviser. Nine of the 47 accounts held by Portillo were discretionary accounts under signed limited powers of attorney, and 23 of the 310 transactions were executed under discretionary authority, yet none of the trade records distinguished discretionary from non-discretionary orders.

Greenleaf argued in his response letter that the clearing broker confirmations constituted adequate records and that the CRM notes, taken together with the confirmations, substantially complied with the recordkeeping requirements. He also noted that no client had complained and that all trades were suitable for the clients involved.
question: Did Greenleaf Capital Advisors, LLC violate the NASAA Model Rule 203(a)-2 recordkeeping requirements with respect to the order memoranda for transactions executed by Diana Portillo?
answer:
Yes, Greenleaf Capital Advisors, LLC committed multiple violations of NASAA Model Rule 203(a)-2(a)(3), and potentially related subsections, based on the firm's failure to maintain proper order memoranda.

Model Rule 203(a)-2(a)(3) requires every registered investment adviser to make and keep a memorandum of each order given for the purchase or sale of any security, as well as any instruction received from the client concerning the purchase, sale, receipt, or delivery of a particular security, and any modification or cancellation thereof. The rule specifies that each memorandum must contain several discrete elements: (i) the terms and conditions of the order, instruction, modification, or cancellation; (ii) the identity of the person connected with the investment adviser who recommended the transaction to the client; (iii) the identity of the person who placed the order; (iv) the account for which the order was entered; (v) the date of entry; and (vi) the bank or broker-dealer through whom executed, where appropriate. Additionally, the rule explicitly mandates that orders entered pursuant to the exercise of discretionary power 'shall be so designated.'

The firm's reliance on clearing broker trade confirmations fails on multiple elements. While confirmations may capture the security, quantity, price, date, and account number, they do not identify which adviser recommended the transaction — a critical element when a firm has multiple advisory representatives like Portillo. The confirmations also do not reflect the original terms and conditions of the client's instruction (as distinct from the executed trade), nor do they designate which orders were discretionary. The CRM notes are equally deficient: sparse, undated entries without reference to specific securities or order terms cannot substitute for the detailed memoranda the rule requires.

Greenleaf's defense that the documents 'taken together' substantially comply is unavailing. The rule requires each memorandum to contain all specified elements; a patchwork of incomplete records across different systems does not satisfy this obligation. Furthermore, the absence of client complaints and the suitability of trades are irrelevant to the recordkeeping analysis — Rule 203(a)-2 imposes an independent, prophylactic obligation designed to facilitate regulatory oversight, not merely to address client harm. The failure to designate the 23 discretionary trades as such across nine accounts is a particularly serious deficiency, as it frustrates examiners' ability to monitor the exercise of discretionary authority, which carries heightened fiduciary obligations. The firm's supervisory failure — providing only informal CRM guidance rather than implementing a proper order ticket system — compounds the violation and may also implicate supervisory obligations under state law. The firm is in clear violation of Rule 203(a)-2(a)(3).
applicable_standard: NASAA Model Rule 203(a)-2(a)(3) — Recordkeeping Requirements for Investment Advisers (order memoranda requirements including identification of recommending person, terms and conditions, discretionary designation); NASAA Model Rule 203(a)-2(a)(8)-(9) (discretionary account lists and powers of attorney)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The firm failed to create order memoranda identifying the recommending adviser, the terms and conditions of client instructions, and the discretionary designation for orders executed under discretionary authority, relying instead on incomplete clearing broker confirmations.

fact_pattern:
Consolidated Life Insurance Company of New York ('Consolidated Life'), a domestic insurer licensed under the New York Insurance Law, developed a new Guaranteed Interest Contract (GIC) product in March 2023 designed for large institutional pension plan sponsors. The product, designated Form GIC-2023-07A, offered a 5-year guaranteed interest rate of 4.85% on deposits of $10 million or more, with a market value adjustment (MVA) applied to withdrawals prior to the maturity date. The product was designed by Consolidated Life's actuary, David Reinhart, FSA, MAAA, and was intended for sale to municipal pension funds and Taft-Hartley plans in the tri-state area.

Rather than submitting the GIC form to the New York Department of Financial Services (DFS) for prior approval, Consolidated Life's Vice President of Product Development, Margaret Calloway, directed the compliance team to file the form under what she described as a 'file-and-use' procedure, asserting that GICs used in the institutional market did not require prior approval because they were negotiated contracts between sophisticated parties. She relied on a 2008 internal legal memorandum that she believed authorized this approach for group annuity contracts above a $5 million threshold. The compliance officer, Brian Ostrowski, raised concerns that New York required prior approval for GIC forms regardless of the sophistication of the purchaser, but Calloway overruled him, and the product was marketed beginning April 15, 2023.

By August 2023, Consolidated Life had issued GIC-2023-07A to three municipal pension funds—the City of Rochester Employees' Retirement System ($25 million deposit), the Nassau County Police and Fire Retirement Fund ($18 million deposit), and the Westchester County Teachers' Pension Trust ($32 million deposit)—for a total of $75 million in deposits. During a routine market conduct examination in October 2023, DFS examiners discovered that Form GIC-2023-07A had never received prior approval and that the filing made through SERFF was incomplete, lacking a submission letter with the required caption identifying the product type as a Guaranteed Interest Contract, as well as the Group Annuity Summary Sheet and Memorandum of Variable Material.
question: Did Consolidated Life violate New York's product filing requirements by issuing GIC Form GIC-2023-07A without obtaining prior approval from the DFS, and what regulatory consequences could follow?
answer:
Consolidated Life clearly violated New York's prior approval requirement for Guaranteed Interest Contracts. The GIC Product Outline (last updated October 11, 2013) issued under Superintendent Benjamin M. Lawsky's authority explicitly states at Section II.A.1 that GIC forms are subject to a 'Prior Approval Requirement.' This means that no GIC policy form may be issued or delivered in New York until the Superintendent has affirmatively approved it. There is no file-and-use exception for GICs based on the sophistication of the purchaser or the size of the deposit.

Margaret Calloway's reliance on a 2008 internal legal memorandum purporting to exempt negotiated institutional contracts from prior approval has no basis in the DFS product outline or in the New York Insurance Law. Section II.B of the GIC Product Outline enumerates the available filing tracks—Prior Approval (Section II.B.1), Alternative Approval Procedure (Section II.B.2), Prior Approval with Certification Procedure (Section II.B.3), and Out-of-State Filings (Section II.B.4)—none of which authorize a file-and-use approach for domestic GIC filings. Additionally, Section II.A.2 reserves to the Superintendent 'Discretionary Authority for Disapproval,' underscoring that the regulator must have the opportunity to review and potentially reject the form before it enters the market.

The filing deficiencies compound the violation. Under Section II.E.1, the SERFF submission must include a caption identifying the product type. Section II.E.2 requires a detailed submission letter or SERFF filing description. Section II.F.1 mandates a Memorandum of Variable Material, and Section II.F.3 requires a Group Annuity Summary Sheet. Consolidated Life's incomplete SERFF submission failed on all four counts.

Brian Ostrowski's documented objection is significant: it demonstrates that the company had actual notice of the prior approval requirement and consciously disregarded it. Under New York Insurance Law § 2405 and the Superintendent's enforcement authority, Consolidated Life faces potential penalties including fines for each unapproved form issued, an order to cease and desist from further sales, and possible remedial action requiring the company to submit the form for retroactive review or to offer the three pension fund contractholders the option to rescind the contracts without market value adjustment penalties. The DFS could also refer the matter for further action if it determines a pattern of regulatory evasion. Calloway's override of the compliance officer could additionally trigger individual liability and supervisory scrutiny under the DFS's enterprise risk framework.
applicable_standard: NY DFS GIC Product Outline (2013), Sections II.A.1 (Prior Approval Requirement), II.A.2 (Discretionary Authority for Disapproval), II.B.1–B.4 (Types of Filings), II.E.1 (Caption Requirement), II.E.2 (Submission Letters/SERFF Filing Description), II.F.1 (Memorandum of Variable Material), II.F.3 (Group Annuity Summary Sheet); New York Insurance Law §§ 2405, 3201
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Consolidated Life issued a GIC product form to three institutional purchasers totaling $75 million in deposits without ever obtaining the prior approval from the New York DFS that is explicitly required for all Guaranteed Interest Contracts under the GIC Product Outline.

fact_pattern:
In October 2010, licensed insurance producer Gerald Fontaine, operating through his agency Fontaine Financial Services in Rochester, New York, met with Margaret Kowalski, a 78-year-old retired school teacher. Mrs. Kowalski had $340,000 in a bank CD that was maturing and $1,850 per month in combined Social Security and pension income. She told Fontaine she needed safe, liquid funds to cover potential nursing home costs, as her husband had recently been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and she herself had been treated for a mild stroke six months prior. She explicitly stated she wanted 'something safe like another CD, but maybe paying a little more interest.'

Fontaine recommended she place $285,000 into a 12-year surrender-period fixed indexed annuity issued by Great Northern Life Insurance Company, with a 9% surrender charge in year one declining by 0.75% annually. The annuity offered a 4% premium bonus but included a market value adjustment provision that could reduce the account value upon early withdrawal. The product had a 10% annual free withdrawal provision, but amounts exceeding that threshold would trigger the full surrender charge plus MVA. Fontaine earned a 7.5% first-year commission of $21,375 on the sale.

Fontaine completed the insurer's suitability questionnaire but listed Mrs. Kowalski's risk tolerance as 'moderate' and her liquidity needs as 'low,' despite her clear verbal statements to the contrary. He also listed her investment time horizon as '10+ years' and did not document her husband's health condition or her own recent stroke. The application was processed by Great Northern Life, which had been authorized to do business in New York and was subject to oversight by the New York State Insurance Department under Superintendent James J. Wrynn. Mrs. Kowalski's daughter discovered the annuity nine months later when trying to access funds for her father's memory care facility placement, at which point a withdrawal of $150,000 would have triggered approximately $12,825 in surrender charges plus an adverse market value adjustment estimated at $3,200.
question: Under the New York State Insurance Department's regulatory framework in effect as of 2010, including applicable NAIC-based annuity suitability standards and New York Insurance Law, did Gerald Fontaine's sale of this fixed indexed annuity to Mrs. Kowalski violate applicable suitability requirements, and what enforcement authority would the Superintendent have had?
answer:
Verdict: Gerald Fontaine's conduct constitutes a clear violation of New York's annuity suitability requirements as they existed in 2010, and the Superintendent of Insurance had broad enforcement authority to address it.

In 2010, New York had adopted Regulation 60 (11 NYCRR 224), which incorporated suitability standards for annuity transactions modeled on the NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation (Model 275). Under these provisions, an insurance producer recommending the purchase of an annuity was required to have reasonable grounds for believing the recommendation was suitable for the consumer based on facts disclosed by the consumer regarding, among other things, age, financial situation, investment objectives, intended use of the annuity, liquidity needs, risk tolerance, and existing insurance or annuity holdings.

Fontaine violated multiple elements of these suitability requirements. First, regarding liquidity needs: Mrs. Kowalski explicitly communicated a need for accessible funds to cover potential nursing home expenses. A 12-year surrender period annuity with a 9% first-year surrender charge and market value adjustment provision is fundamentally incompatible with high liquidity needs. Second, regarding risk tolerance: Fontaine falsified the suitability questionnaire by recording her risk tolerance as 'moderate' when she requested CD-like safety, and listed her liquidity needs as 'low' when they were demonstrably high. This constitutes a material misrepresentation on required documentation. Third, regarding age and time horizon: At 78 years old with documented health concerns, a 10+ year investment horizon designation was unreasonable and unsupported by the facts.

Under New York Insurance Law §§ 2110 and 2122, the Superintendent had authority to revoke, suspend, or decline to renew Fontaine's insurance producer license for, among other grounds, demonstrated untrustworthiness or incompetence in conducting business. Under § 2405 and related enforcement provisions, the Department could impose monetary penalties. The deliberate falsification of suitability documentation would also implicate Insurance Law § 4226 regarding unfair trade practices.

Fontaine cannot credibly argue the 4% premium bonus or 10% free withdrawal provision cured the suitability deficiency. The bonus was subject to the same surrender schedule, effectively acting as a recapture mechanism, and the 10% free withdrawal was grossly insufficient given Mrs. Kowalski's foreseeable need for $150,000. The $21,375 commission further evidences a conflict that should have heightened Fontaine's suitability analysis. Note that although NY Reg 187 (11 NYCRR 224, as later amended in 2018-2019) would subsequently impose a best interest standard, even the 2010 suitability standard was plainly breached here.
applicable_standard: 11 NYCRR 224 (NY Regulation 60, annuity suitability); NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation (Model 275), Sections 6(A)-(D); New York Insurance Law §§ 2110, 2122, 2405, 4226
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Fontaine deliberately misrepresented Mrs. Kowalski's liquidity needs, risk tolerance, and time horizon on the suitability questionnaire to facilitate the sale of a long-surrender-period annuity that was fundamentally incompatible with her clearly stated need for safe, accessible funds to cover imminent healthcare expenses.

fact_pattern: Patricia Lawson is a 71-year-old retired schoolteacher living in the District of Columbia. She has $340,000 in a traditional IRA, a $1,200/month pension, and receives $2,100/month in Social Security. She has no long-term care insurance and mild early-stage cognitive decline, though she remains legally competent. In March 2024, she meets with Ronald Hensley, a licensed insurance producer affiliated with Keystone Annuity Distributors, LLC, at a free dinner seminar held at a hotel in Georgetown. Hensley recommends that Patricia liquidate her entire IRA and purchase a 12-year market value adjustment (MVA) fixed indexed annuity issued by National Fidelity Life Insurance Company, with a $340,000 single premium. The annuity carries a 10-year surrender charge schedule starting at 9% and declining to 0%, and includes an income rider with a 1.10% annual charge. The guaranteed minimum surrender value would not equal the premium paid until year 11. Hensley's commission on the sale is $23,800 (7% of premium). During the meeting, Hensley fills out a suitability questionnaire but marks Patricia's risk tolerance as 'moderate growth' and her liquidity needs as 'none anticipated,' despite Patricia verbally mentioning that she might need funds within two years for possible assisted living costs. Hensley does not document Patricia's mention of potential near-term liquidity needs, does not inquire about her health status or existing insurance coverage, and does not consider any alternative products. He submits the application the same day. The insurer's home office suitability review team approves the application based solely on the questionnaire without independent verification. Patricia's niece, a financial planner, discovers the transaction 45 days later — after the D.C. free-look period has expired — and files a complaint with the D.C. Department of Insurance, Securities and Banking.
question: Did Ronald Hensley and Keystone Annuity Distributors, LLC violate the annuity suitability requirements applicable in the District of Columbia, and what are the respective obligations of the producer and the insurer under the controlling regulation?
answer:
This transaction is non-compliant and constitutes multiple violations of the District of Columbia's annuity suitability regulation. The D.C. Municipal Regulations, Title 26A, §§ 8400–8499 (adopted 2010/2011), govern suitability in annuity transactions and are based on a previous version of the NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation (#275). Notably, as reflected in the NAIC state page chart, D.C. has not adopted the most recent (2020) revised NAIC Model Regulation, meaning the older framework applies — but even under that earlier standard, the facts here reveal clear violations.

First, regarding the producer's duty: Under the NAIC Model and its D.C. counterpart, a producer must have reasonable grounds for believing that a recommendation is suitable based on facts disclosed by the consumer concerning, among other things, the consumer's age, financial situation, tax status, insurance needs, investment objectives, liquidity needs, and risk tolerance. Hensley failed this obligation in several critical respects. He recorded Patricia's liquidity needs as 'none anticipated' despite her explicit verbal disclosure of potential near-term assisted living expenses. Misrepresenting or ignoring known consumer information on the suitability form is a direct violation of the duty to make a suitable recommendation based on the consumer's actual profile. A 12-year MVA annuity with a 10-year declining surrender charge starting at 9% is fundamentally unsuitable for a 71-year-old with near-term liquidity concerns and no long-term care coverage. The surrender penalties would severely penalize Patricia if she needed funds for assisted living within two years.

Second, Hensley failed to consider alternative products or to document why this particular annuity — consuming 100% of Patricia's liquid retirement assets — was preferable. Under the model regulation framework, the recommendation must be suitable not merely in product type but in the specific allocation relative to the consumer's overall financial profile.

Third, the insurer, National Fidelity Life, bears supervisory responsibility. Under the NAIC Model §6 (and the D.C. counterpart), insurers must establish and maintain a system to supervise recommendations that is reasonably designed to detect unsuitable transactions. Approving this application based solely on the questionnaire — without independent verification or flagging the age-to-surrender-period mismatch and the 100% asset concentration — represents a failure of the insurer's supervisory system. The insurer cannot rely solely on the producer's representations when red flags are apparent on the face of the application.

Hensley and Keystone face potential disciplinary action, including license suspension or revocation, fines, and an order to rescind the transaction. National Fidelity Life faces parallel supervisory liability for its inadequate review system.
applicable_standard: D.C. MUN. REGS. tit. 26A, §§ 8400–8499 (2010/2011); NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation #275, §§ 5 (Duties of Insurers and Producers), 6 (Insurer Supervision System); prior version of NAIC Model Regulation adopted by D.C.
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Hensley deliberately failed to document and act upon Patricia's disclosed near-term liquidity needs, resulting in a recommendation of a long-surrender, illiquid annuity that consumed 100% of her retirement assets and was fundamentally unsuitable for her age, health, and financial profile.

fact_pattern:
Gerald Whitmore is a licensed insurance producer in Kansas who holds appointments with three annuity carriers. On April 15, 2022, Gerald meets with Dorothy Redmond, a 72-year-old retired schoolteacher living in Topeka. Dorothy's financial profile includes a $185,000 fixed-rate CD maturing at her local bank, a $62,000 checking/savings balance, Social Security income of $2,400/month, and a small Kansas Public Employees Retirement System (KPERS) pension of $1,100/month. Dorothy has moderate risk tolerance, no outstanding debts, and her primary financial goal is preserving principal while generating modest supplemental income to cover anticipated long-term care expenses she discussed with Gerald. She explicitly tells Gerald she wants liquidity because her husband recently passed and she is uncertain about future medical costs.

Gerald recommends a 10-year fixed indexed annuity (FIA) from Heartland Life Insurance Company with a $175,000 single premium. The product features a 10-year surrender period with declining charges starting at 12% in year one, a 10% annual free withdrawal provision, a guaranteed minimum interest rate of 0.25%, and participation in S&P 500 index gains capped at 4.5%. The product pays Gerald a 7.2% first-year commission ($12,600). Gerald completes the required suitability disclosure form but does not document any consideration of alternative products—including a 3-year or 5-year MYGA (multi-year guaranteed annuity) offered by the same carrier with much shorter surrender periods and guaranteed rates of 2.8% and 3.1%, respectively. He also fails to document why locking up 94.6% of Dorothy's liquid assets in a long-surrender product serves her stated liquidity needs.

Gerald's supervising insurer, Heartland Life, has adopted a best interest compliance framework in anticipation of Kansas adopting the revised NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation (#275). Kansas formally adopted the revised Model #275 effective January 1, 2022, incorporating the best interest standard. Heartland Life's compliance system flags the transaction due to the client's age, concentration of liquid assets, and surrender period length, but the compliance reviewer approves it after Gerald verbally assures the reviewer that Dorothy 'understood the product and wanted the higher upside potential.' No written rationale addressing the care, skill, and prudence obligations or the conflict of interest posed by the differential commission structure is placed in the file.
question: Under the revised NAIC Model #275 best interest standard as adopted by Kansas, did Gerald Whitmore and Heartland Life Insurance Company satisfy their respective obligations in recommending the 10-year fixed indexed annuity to Dorothy Redmond?
answer:
Neither Gerald Whitmore nor Heartland Life Insurance Company satisfied their obligations under the revised NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation (#275) as adopted by Kansas. The recommendation is non-compliant for multiple independent reasons.

First, under Section 6A of revised Model #275, a producer must act in the best interest of the consumer at the time of the recommendation, and this obligation encompasses four component obligations: Care, Disclosure, Conflict of Interest, and Documentation. Gerald failed virtually all of them.

Regarding the Care Obligation (Section 6B), the producer must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to know the consumer's financial situation, insurance needs, and financial objectives, and must consider reasonably available alternatives. Dorothy explicitly stated her priority was principal preservation with liquidity to cover uncertain future medical costs. Recommending a product that locks up 94.6% of her liquid assets for 10 years with a 12% first-year surrender charge directly contradicts her stated objectives. The existence of 3-year and 5-year MYGAs from the same carrier—products that would have addressed Dorothy's liquidity and preservation needs far more appropriately—demonstrates Gerald failed to evaluate reasonably available alternatives as required.

Regarding the Conflict of Interest Obligation (Section 6D), the producer must not place his financial interest ahead of the consumer's interest. The 7.2% commission ($12,600) on the 10-year FIA compared to the materially lower commissions on shorter-surrender MYGAs creates a textbook compensation conflict. Gerald made no effort to document how this conflict was identified and mitigated, as Model #275 requires.

Regarding the Documentation Obligation (Section 6E), the producer must make a written record of the basis for the recommendation. Gerald's file contains no written rationale explaining why the 10-year FIA was in Dorothy's best interest despite her liquidity needs and the availability of shorter-term alternatives.

Heartland Life also failed its insurer supervision obligations under Section 7 of Model #275, which requires the insurer to establish and maintain a system to supervise recommendations that is reasonably designed to achieve compliance with the best interest standard. The compliance system appropriately flagged the transaction, but the reviewer accepted a mere verbal assurance rather than requiring documented substantiation addressing the specific red flags. This constitutes a failure of the insurer's supervisory system.

Gerald cannot rely on the safe harbor in Section 6H (if adopted by Kansas) because that provision requires the recommendation to have been made in compliance with the substantive best interest components—which it was not. The transaction is non-compliant under revised Model #275, Sections 6A, 6B, 6D, 6E, and 7.
applicable_standard: NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation (#275), as revised February 2020, Sections 6A (Best Interest Obligation), 6B (Care Obligation), 6D (Conflict of Interest Obligation), 6E (Documentation Obligation), and Section 7 (Insurer Supervision System); Kansas adoption effective January 1, 2022; Dodd-Frank Act Section 989J (federal preemption safe harbor for state annuity suitability standards meeting NAIC model requirements)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Gerald failed to document consideration of reasonably available shorter-surrender alternatives that aligned with the client's explicitly stated liquidity needs, while recommending a product that paid him materially higher compensation—violating the care, conflict of interest, and documentation obligations under revised Model #275.

fact_pattern: Marcus Kellerman is the sole managing member of Ridgeline Capital Advisors LLC, a Nevada-based firm organized in January 2022 that provides investment advisory services exclusively to two private funds: Ridgeline Growth Fund LP and Ridgeline Opportunity Fund LP. The Growth Fund has 22 limited partners, all of whom are qualified purchasers under Section 2(a)(51) of the Investment Company Act of 1940, with a combined AUM of $78 million. The Opportunity Fund has 14 limited partners, also all qualified purchasers, with AUM of $45 million. Neither fund makes any public offering of securities, and both rely on the Section 3(c)(7) exclusion from the definition of investment company. Ridgeline Capital Advisors does not hold itself out generally to the public as an investment adviser, has no retail clients, and does not provide financial planning or advisory services to any natural person in their individual capacity. Kellerman has never registered Ridgeline Capital Advisors as an investment adviser with the Nevada Secretary of State's Securities Division. In March 2023, a routine sweep by the Nevada Securities Division flagged Ridgeline Capital Advisors as an unregistered entity providing investment advisory services within the state. During the examination, Kellerman presented documentation showing the firm's exclusive advisory relationship with the two qualifying private funds, the accreditation and qualified purchaser status of all investors, the private placement memoranda for both funds, and written compliance policies. Kellerman argued that Senate Bill No. 9, as amended during the 81st Session of the Nevada Legislature in 2021, created an exemption from state investment adviser licensing requirements for advisers to certain qualifying private funds, and that Ridgeline Capital Advisors squarely fell within that exemption. The Nevada Securities Division examiner, Diana Vasquez, must determine whether Kellerman's reliance on the exemption is proper and whether the firm's failure to register constitutes a violation of Nevada securities law.
question: Did Ridgeline Capital Advisors LLC's failure to register as an investment adviser with the Nevada Securities Division constitute a violation of Nevada securities law, given its reliance on the private fund adviser exemption created by Senate Bill No. 9 as amended during the 2021 legislative session?
answer:
Ridgeline Capital Advisors LLC is likely compliant and did not violate Nevada securities law by operating without state investment adviser registration. Senate Bill No. 9, as introduced during the 81st Session (2021) of the Nevada Legislature and referred to the Assembly Committee on Judiciary with Amendment No. 501, was specifically designed to create an exemption from licensing requirements for investment advisers to certain private funds. This legislation mirrors the federal framework established under Section 203(m) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act's private fund adviser exemption, adapted for state-level application.

The key elements of the exemption, as contemplated by SB 9 as amended, require that: (1) the adviser provides advisory services solely to one or more qualifying private funds; (2) the private funds are not required to register as investment companies under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (relying on Section 3(c)(1) or 3(c)(7) exclusions); (3) the adviser does not hold itself out generally to the public as an investment adviser; and (4) the adviser does not advise any natural persons in their individual capacity outside the private fund structure.

Applying these elements to the facts, Ridgeline Capital Advisors satisfies each criterion. First, the firm advises only Ridgeline Growth Fund LP and Ridgeline Opportunity Fund LP — both qualifying private funds relying on the Section 3(c)(7) exclusion. Second, all 36 limited partners across both funds are verified qualified purchasers, and neither fund makes a public offering. Third, Kellerman and Ridgeline do not hold the firm out to the general public as an investment adviser and have no retail advisory clients. Fourth, the firm provides no individual advisory or financial planning services to natural persons outside the fund vehicles.

Examiner Vasquez should conclude that Kellerman's reliance on the SB 9 private fund adviser exemption is well-founded, provided the firm maintains adequate documentation of investor qualifications and fund structures on an ongoing basis. A potential risk factor would arise if Ridgeline were to begin accepting non-qualified purchasers, advising individuals outside the fund structure, or engaging in general solicitation, any of which would vitiate the exemption and trigger registration obligations under NRS Chapter 90. The firm's written compliance policies and documentation further support a finding of good-faith reliance on the statutory exemption. No enforcement action is warranted.
applicable_standard: Nevada SB 9 (81st Session, 2021), as amended by Amendment No. 501 (BDR 7-423); NRS Chapter 90 (Nevada Securities Law); Section 203(m) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940; Section 3(c)(7) of the Investment Company Act of 1940; Section 2(a)(51) of the Investment Company Act (qualified purchaser definition)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Ridgeline Capital Advisors provided advisory services exclusively to qualifying private funds relying on Section 3(c)(7) exclusions and did not hold itself out to the general public as an investment adviser, satisfying all elements of the SB 9 private fund adviser exemption from Nevada state registration.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Whitfield is a registered representative associated with Pinnacle Securities LLC, a broker-dealer registered with the SEC and FINRA. Pinnacle has approximately 4,200 retail customer accounts and operates twelve branch offices across the Mid-Atlantic region. In January 2022, Marcus began offering a service he branded 'Pinnacle Strategic Portfolio Management' to a subset of approximately 85 high-net-worth clients, including Helen Carruthers, a 67-year-old retired pharmaceutical executive with $2.8 million in investable assets. Under this arrangement, Marcus entered into a written agreement with Helen in which he committed to providing ongoing portfolio monitoring, quarterly rebalancing of her equity and fixed-income allocations, and discretionary authority to execute trades in her brokerage account without prior consultation on each transaction. Helen's account agreement specified that she would pay a standard commission on each trade executed, and Marcus received no separate asset-based or flat advisory fee for the monitoring and discretionary services—Pinnacle's compliance department noted that because there was no 'special compensation,' the service fell within the broker-dealer exclusion under Section 202(a)(11)(C) of the Advisers Act.

By October 2023, Marcus had exercised discretionary authority over Helen's account on 47 separate occasions, rebalancing her portfolio across equity sectors and shifting her bond duration profile in response to interest rate expectations. He also sent her monthly written 'investment outlook' reports and proactively contacted her about three times per month to discuss macroeconomic conditions and their implications for her portfolio strategy. Helen relied exclusively on Marcus's judgment for all investment decisions and had not independently directed a single trade since signing the agreement.

During an SEC examination of Pinnacle in February 2024, examiners flagged Marcus's 'Strategic Portfolio Management' service and questioned whether the exercise of discretionary authority and the ongoing, continuous nature of the advisory relationship exceeded the 'solely incidental' prong of the broker-dealer exclusion. Pinnacle's Chief Compliance Officer, Dana Reeves, argued that because Marcus received only transaction-based commissions and no special compensation, the exclusion applied and Pinnacle had no obligation to register as an investment adviser or comply with the Advisers Act's fiduciary duty with respect to these accounts.
question: Does Marcus Whitfield's exercise of discretionary authority and provision of continuous, ongoing advisory services to Helen Carruthers fall within the 'solely incidental' prong of the broker-dealer exclusion under Section 202(a)(11)(C) of the Investment Advisers Act, thereby exempting Pinnacle Securities from investment adviser registration requirements?
answer:
No. Marcus Whitfield's conduct almost certainly exceeds the 'solely incidental' prong of the broker-dealer exclusion under Section 202(a)(11)(C) of the Investment Advisers Act, and Pinnacle Securities' reliance on the absence of special compensation is insufficient to avoid Advisers Act obligations.

The broker-dealer exclusion under Section 202(a)(11)(C) is conjunctive: a broker-dealer must satisfy both (1) the solely incidental prong—that advisory services are solely incidental to the conduct of its business as a broker-dealer—and (2) the special compensation prong—that no special compensation is received. Even if the special compensation prong is arguably satisfied because Marcus receives only standard commissions, the analysis does not end there. Both prongs must be met independently.

As articulated in Release No. IA-5249, the SEC's 2019 interpretation clarifies that the exercise of investment discretion over customer accounts is a critical factor in evaluating the solely incidental prong. The Commission has long held, dating back to Advisers Act Release No. 2 (Oct. 28, 1940) and reaffirmed in the 2019 interpretation, that when a broker-dealer exercises discretionary authority over a client's account, the advisory services are generally not 'solely incidental' to the brokerage business. Discretionary authority transforms the nature of the relationship from a transactional, recommendation-based model to one of ongoing portfolio management—a hallmark of an investment advisory relationship.

Here, Marcus held and regularly exercised discretionary authority over Helen's account on 47 occasions over approximately 21 months. He committed to ongoing portfolio monitoring and quarterly rebalancing via a written agreement. He proactively communicated investment views and Helen relied exclusively on his judgment, directing no trades independently. This is the functional equivalent of an investment advisory relationship: continuous, comprehensive, and discretionary in nature.

Dana Reeves's defense—that the absence of special compensation alone satisfies the exclusion—fundamentally misreads the statute. The exclusion's two prongs are independent requirements, not alternatives. The SEC's 2019 interpretation expressly states that even where no special compensation is received, a broker-dealer whose advisory services are not solely incidental to its brokerage business cannot rely on the exclusion. The nature and scope of the services, particularly the exercise of discretion and the ongoing, continuous character of the advisory relationship, place Marcus's activities squarely outside the solely incidental standard.

Pinnacle Securities should have registered as an investment adviser (or ensured Marcus operated through a registered investment adviser) with respect to the 'Strategic Portfolio Management' accounts, and Marcus owed a fiduciary duty under the Advisers Act to clients like Helen Carruthers. The failure to do so constitutes a violation of Section 202(a)(11) and potentially Section 203 (registration requirement) of the Advisers Act.
applicable_standard: Section 202(a)(11)(C) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 [15 U.S.C. 80b-2(a)(11)(C)]; SEC Release No. IA-5249 (Commission Interpretation Regarding the Solely Incidental Prong of the Broker-Dealer Exclusion); Advisers Act Release No. 2 (Oct. 28, 1940); Section 203 of the Advisers Act (registration requirements)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Marcus's exercise of discretionary authority over client accounts and provision of continuous, ongoing portfolio management services rendered his advisory activities not 'solely incidental' to Pinnacle's broker-dealer business, defeating the Section 202(a)(11)(C) exclusion regardless of whether special compensation was received.

fact_pattern:
Heritage Life Insurance Company ('Heritage Life') is a mid-sized life insurer domiciled in Iowa that issues both fixed indexed annuities (FIAs) and registered variable annuities across 38 states. In March 2025, Heritage Life entered into a selling agreement with Pinnacle Financial Group, a FINRA-registered broker-dealer headquartered in Ohio. Under the agreement, Pinnacle's registered representatives who also hold insurance producer licenses may sell Heritage Life's full product line, including the Heritage Horizon 10 FIA — a 10-year fixed indexed annuity with a 7% surrender charge in year one and a 2% annual premium bonus.

On June 15, 2025, Marcus Chen, a dual-licensed registered representative of Pinnacle and insurance producer in Ohio, recommended the Heritage Horizon 10 FIA to Dorothy Waverly, a 72-year-old retired schoolteacher with $340,000 in liquid savings, a modest $2,100/month pension, and Social Security income of $1,850/month. Dorothy expressed a primary need for guaranteed income and liquidity for potential healthcare expenses. Marcus recommended she allocate $280,000 — approximately 82% of her liquid assets — into the Heritage Horizon 10 FIA, citing the premium bonus and index-linked growth potential. The recommendation was processed through Pinnacle's standard Reg BI compliance workflow, which generated a CRS disclosure and a best interest obligation assessment. Pinnacle applied its Reg BI policies and procedures to the FIA sale even though Reg BI does not directly apply to unregistered fixed annuities.

Heritage Life sought to rely on the NAIC Model 275 safe harbor provision, Section 6(E), for this transaction. During its onboarding of Pinnacle in early 2025, Heritage Life verified that Pinnacle was a registered broker-dealer and confirmed that Pinnacle represented it would apply its Reg BI business rules, controls, and procedures to fixed annuity recommendations. However, Heritage Life did not independently establish any monitoring framework for Pinnacle's supervision of fixed annuity transactions. Heritage Life's compliance department did not conduct any audits of Pinnacle's supervisory systems for fixed annuity sales, nor did it request or review any transaction-level data regarding the Waverly recommendation. Heritage Life's internal compliance manual stated: 'For safe harbor transactions, Heritage Life relies entirely on the supervising broker-dealer's compliance systems and does not conduct independent review or audits of individual fixed annuity sales.'

A subsequent state regulatory examination in September 2025 flagged the Waverly transaction as potentially unsuitable given Dorothy's age, liquidity needs, and the high concentration of assets in a single long-surrender-period product. Examiners also questioned Heritage Life's supervisory framework under the safe harbor.
question: Did Heritage Life Insurance Company satisfy its obligations under the NAIC Model Regulation's safe harbor provision, specifically its Section 6(C)(1) supervisory duty and its monitoring and audit obligations under Sections 6(E)(3) and 6(C)(3)(b), with respect to the Waverly fixed indexed annuity transaction?
answer:
Heritage Life did not satisfy its obligations under the NAIC Model Regulation (Model 275-1), and its reliance on the safe harbor is deficient for multiple independent reasons.

First, under Section 6(C)(1), an insurer must have a reasonable basis to believe that an annuity recommendation meets a consumer's financial and insurance needs, regardless of whether the safe harbor applies. The NAIC guidance adopted in November 2025 explicitly states that this obligation persists 'whether that annuity is a federally registered security or a fixed annuity.' Heritage Life made no independent assessment of whether allocating $280,000 — 82% of Dorothy Waverly's liquid savings — into a 10-year FIA with a 7% year-one surrender charge was appropriate for a 72-year-old retiree whose stated primary needs included liquidity for healthcare expenses. The product's long surrender period and illiquidity profile directly conflict with Dorothy's expressed financial objectives. Heritage Life's failure to evaluate the transaction against the consumer's profile is a standalone violation of Section 6(C)(1).

Second, while Heritage Life contractually assigned supervisory functions to Pinnacle under Section 6(C)(3)(a), which is permissible, it failed to comply with Section 6(C)(3)(b), which requires the insurer to 'monitor and, as appropriate, conduct audits to assure the contracted function is properly performed.' Heritage Life's own compliance manual explicitly disclaimed any independent review or audit of individual fixed annuity sales. This blanket abdication of audit responsibility is directly contrary to the Model Regulation's requirements and the adopted guidance.

Third, under the safe harbor's monitoring requirement in Section 6(E)(3), Heritage Life was required to 'monitor the relevant conduct of the financial professional or the entity responsible for supervising the financial professional using information gathered in the normal course of an insurer's business.' Heritage Life gathered no transaction-level data on the Waverly sale, requested no supervisory reports from Pinnacle regarding fixed annuity recommendations, and had no system for flagging potentially unsuitable fixed annuity transactions. The guidance clarifies that monitoring is an affirmative, ongoing duty — not a passive assumption that the broker-dealer's systems are functioning.

Heritage Life cannot defend by arguing that Pinnacle applied Reg BI procedures to the FIA. The guidance acknowledges that broker-dealers may voluntarily extend Reg BI controls to fixed annuities, and this can form the basis for safe harbor reliance. However, the safe harbor does not eliminate the insurer's independent supervisory duties under Sections 6(C)(1), 6(C)(3)(b), and 6(E)(3). Heritage Life's total delegation without monitoring or audit constitutes a failure to meet the conditions for valid safe harbor reliance, exposing the insurer to regulatory action for supervisory deficiencies under the Model Regulation.
applicable_standard: NAIC Suitability in Annuity Transactions Model Regulation (Model 275-1), Sections 6(C)(1), 6(C)(3)(a), 6(C)(3)(b), 6(D), 6(E)(1), 6(E)(3); SEC Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR §240.15l-1); FINRA Rules 2330, 3110, 3120, 3130
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Heritage Life's compliance manual explicitly disclaimed any independent monitoring or audit of fixed annuity transactions processed under the safe harbor, directly violating its non-delegable supervisory obligations under Sections 6(C)(1), 6(C)(3)(b), and 6(E)(3) of the Model Regulation.

fact_pattern:
Margaret Olsen, age 72, is a retired schoolteacher living in Syracuse, New York, with an annual pension income of $38,000 and Social Security benefits of $22,800. In March 2017, she held a flexible premium deferred variable annuity issued by Horizon Life Insurance Company with an accumulation value of $187,400. The deferred annuity contract included guaranteed annuity purchase rates established in 2004 that were significantly more favorable than prevailing market rates, effectively guaranteeing a monthly income stream of approximately $1,215 per month if she elected to annuitize the existing contract under its guaranteed terms.

Brandon Kessler, a career agent licensed in New York and contracted with Ridgepoint Life Insurance Company, approached Margaret at a community financial literacy seminar. After a 45-minute meeting at her home on April 3, 2017, during which he collected basic information about her age, income, and desire for 'guaranteed monthly income,' Kessler recommended that Margaret surrender her Horizon deferred annuity and purchase a Ridgepoint single premium immediate annuity (SPIA) using the $187,400 surrender proceeds. The Ridgepoint SPIA would pay Margaret $1,048 per month for life—$167 less per month than the guaranteed annuitization rate available under her existing Horizon contract. Kessler earned a 4.5% commission ($8,433) on the replacement SPIA sale.

Kessler completed a Disclosure Statement (Appendix 10B to Insurance Regulation 60) but left the section comparing guaranteed annuitization rates of the existing deferred annuity blank, writing 'N/A—client is purchasing a new product.' He did not contact Horizon to obtain the guaranteed annuity purchase rates embedded in Margaret's existing contract, nor did he explain to Margaret that she could annuitize her existing contract for a higher guaranteed payment. Ridgepoint's home office compliance unit processed the replacement paperwork without flagging the incomplete disclosure or conducting an independent suitability review comparing the annuitization values. Internal training records show that Ridgepoint had not updated its agent training materials on Regulation 187's suitability requirements since 2014, and had no documented supervisory procedure requiring comparison of existing contract annuitization rates before approving a replacement immediate annuity.

Margaret did not discover the disparity until 2019, when a new financial adviser reviewed her records and informed her that she had forfeited approximately $2,004 per year in guaranteed income by surrendering the Horizon contract.
question: Did Ridgepoint Life Insurance Company and its agent Brandon Kessler violate New York Insurance Regulations 60 and 187 in connection with the replacement of Margaret Olsen's deferred annuity with a single premium immediate annuity?
answer:
Yes. Both Ridgepoint Life Insurance Company and agent Brandon Kessler violated New York Insurance Regulations 60 and 187 in multiple respects, and the fact pattern closely mirrors the conduct at issue in the DFS Consent Order against Principal Life Insurance Company.

First, regarding Regulation 60 (11 NYCRR Part 51), the regulation requires that when a replacement annuity transaction occurs, the agent and insurer must complete the Disclosure Statement prescribed in Appendix 10B, which mandates a side-by-side comparison of the existing deferred annuity and the proposed replacement immediate annuity, including guaranteed annuitization values. Kessler left the annuitization comparison section blank and wrote 'N/A,' which constitutes a failure to provide accurate and complete disclosures as required. The fact that he did not contact Horizon to obtain the guaranteed annuity purchase rates embedded in Margaret's existing contract is directly analogous to the DFS finding that Principal 'failed to obtain appropriate annuitization information for replaced deferred annuities.' Without this information, the Disclosure Statement was materially deficient, depriving Margaret of the information necessary to make an informed decision.

Second, regarding Regulation 187 (11 NYCRR Part 224), which requires that any recommendation to replace an annuity must be suitable and in the best interest of the consumer, the recommendation fails on its face. The replacement SPIA paid $167 less per month than the guaranteed annuitization option available under the existing contract. There was no documented analysis of whether the replacement was suitable, no consideration of guaranteed benefits being forfeited, and no evidence that the recommendation served Margaret's best interest rather than the agent's commission interest. Under Regulation 187, the producer and insurer must act in the best interest of the consumer, and the insurer must establish and maintain a system of supervision reasonably designed to achieve compliance.

Third, Ridgepoint's supervisory failures are material. The company processed the replacement without flagging the incomplete Appendix 10B disclosure, conducted no independent suitability review comparing annuitization values, had not updated training materials on Regulation 187 since 2014, and maintained no documented procedure requiring comparison of existing contract annuitization rates. These failures mirror the DFS findings that Principal 'failed to adequately train agents and brokers to conduct proper suitability reviews' and 'failed to maintain adequate supervisory controls.' Under both Regulations 60 and 187, the insurer bears independent responsibility for ensuring compliance.

Ridgepoint could argue the consumer signed the paperwork voluntarily, but this is not a defense when the disclosures were incomplete and the consumer was not informed of a materially better alternative embedded in her existing contract. The consumer was harmed in the amount of approximately $2,004 annually in lost guaranteed income.
applicable_standard: New York Insurance Regulation 60 (11 NYCRR Part 51), including Appendix 10B Disclosure Statement requirements; New York Insurance Regulation 187 (11 NYCRR Part 224) best interest and suitability standard for annuity transactions; New York Insurance Law § 4223(a)(1)(E) regarding guaranteed annuity purchase rates
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The agent and insurer failed to obtain and disclose the guaranteed annuitization rates available under the existing deferred annuity contract, thereby preventing the consumer from making an informed comparison and causing her to replace a more financially favorable contract with an inferior immediate annuity.

fact_pattern:
Robert Whitfield, age 63, is the sole owner and only investment adviser representative of Whitfield Wealth Strategies, LLC, a state-registered investment adviser in Oregon. The firm was organized as a single-member LLC in 2011 and manages approximately $42 million in assets under management for 87 retail clients, most of whom are retirees or pre-retirees with moderate to conservative risk profiles. Whitfield operates from a single office in Portland and employs one part-time administrative assistant, Diane Cho, who handles scheduling and basic paperwork but holds no securities licenses and has no discretionary authority over client accounts. Client assets are custodied at Schwab Advisor Services.

On February 8, 2024, Robert Whitfield suffered a severe stroke while at home and was hospitalized in critical condition. He remained incapacitated and unable to communicate for over six weeks. Diane Cho, upon learning of the hospitalization, attempted to notify clients but discovered she had no access to the firm's CRM system, email accounts, or cloud-based portfolio management software — all of which were protected by passwords known only to Whitfield. The firm's client files, including financial plans, investment policy statements, and signed advisory agreements, were stored on an encrypted laptop in Whitfield's locked home office. Cho had no written authority to act on behalf of the firm and no instructions regarding whom to contact in the event of Whitfield's incapacity.

During the six-week period, 14 clients called the office seeking portfolio rebalancing or withdrawal requests related to required minimum distributions and other time-sensitive needs. Three clients with aggregate accounts totaling $4.7 million missed RMD deadlines, incurring IRS penalties. Two other clients, including a 78-year-old widow named Patricia Gunderson with a $620,000 portfolio heavily concentrated in long-duration bonds, suffered material losses during a sharp interest rate spike because scheduled defensive rebalancing trades were never executed. No regulatory notifications were made to the Oregon Division of Financial Regulation during this period.

Upon investigation, regulators discovered that Whitfield Wealth Strategies had never adopted a written Business Continuity and Succession Plan. No designated successor adviser had been identified. No backup communication protocols existed. No arrangements had been made to ensure continuity of service in the event of the principal's death or incapacity. Whitfield's advisory agreements with clients contained no provisions addressing business interruption or succession.
question: Did Whitfield Wealth Strategies, LLC violate the NASAA Model Rule on Business Continuity and Succession Planning, and did this failure also constitute a breach of the adviser's fiduciary duty?
answer:
Whitfield Wealth Strategies, LLC is in clear violation of the NASAA Model Rule on Business Continuity and Succession Planning (Model Rule 203(a)-1A / 2002 Rule 411(c)-1A). The rule unambiguously requires that '[e]very investment adviser shall establish, implement, and maintain written procedures relating to a Business Continuity and Succession Plan.' This is not discretionary — it is a mandatory obligation applicable to all registered investment advisers, including sole proprietorships, as the Guidance expressly states that its definition of 'Adviser' includes sole proprietorships.

The firm failed on every enumerated element of the Model Rule. First, regarding Section 1 (protection, backup, and recovery of books and records), all client records were stored on a single encrypted laptop accessible only to Whitfield, with no backup protocol and no means for any other person to access them during his incapacity. Second, under Section 2 (alternate means of communications), no system existed for Diane Cho or any other person to communicate with clients, custodians, or regulators during a significant business interruption. The fact that 14 clients could not obtain service and no notification was made to the Oregon Division of Financial Regulation directly evidences this failure. Third, Section 4 (assignment of duties to qualified responsible persons) was violated because no designated successor, temporary or permanent, was identified — Cho held no licenses and had no written authority to act. Fourth, Section 5 (minimizing service disruptions and client harm) was violated as the complete absence of planning directly caused quantifiable client harm: missed RMD deadlines resulting in IRS penalties and unexecuted rebalancing trades causing material portfolio losses for clients like Patricia Gunderson.

Beyond the specific Model Rule violations, this failure also constitutes a breach of the adviser's fiduciary duty. The Commentary to the Model Rule explicitly states that '[u]pholding the obligations of the Model Rule and Guidance are also inherent to an adviser's fiduciary duty, pursuant to Section 102 of the Uniform Securities Act of 1956 and Section 502 of the Uniform Securities Act of 2002.' An adviser's fiduciary duty encompasses the duty of care, which includes prudent management of the advisory practice itself — not merely individual investment recommendations. By failing to plan for a foreseeable event (his own incapacity at age 63 as a sole practitioner), Whitfield placed every client relationship at risk. The Guidance specifically warns that '[f]ailing to address these risks with a BCP can result in harm to Advisers' clients, exposure to regulatory actions, and litigation for failure to satisfy legal, regulatory, or contractual duties.' Whitfield cannot credibly argue that his small firm size exempts him; the Model Rule explicitly requires the plan to be 'based upon the facts and circumstances of the investment adviser's business model including the size of the firm,' meaning even the smallest firms must have a plan proportionate to their operations. The firm faces potential enforcement action, client claims for damages, and possible additional liability for the failure to notify regulators.
applicable_standard: NASAA Model Rule on Business Continuity and Succession Planning (Model Rule 203(a)-1A / 2002 Rule 411(c)-1A), Sections 1-5; Uniform Securities Act of 1956, Sections 102 and 203(a); Uniform Securities Act of 2002, Sections 411(c) and 502; NASAA Guidance on Business Continuity and Succession Planning for State-Registered Investment Advisers
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The firm never established, implemented, or maintained any written Business Continuity and Succession Plan despite being a sole-practitioner firm where the principal's incapacity foreseeably would — and did — result in complete cessation of client services and direct client harm.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Ellison is a licensed insurance producer affiliated with Summit Financial Partners, a general agency based in Hartford, Connecticut. On March 15, 2020, Marcus met with Elena Vasquez, a 58-year-old school administrator residing in White Plains, New York, who was seeking to roll $340,000 from a mature fixed annuity into a new product that could provide guaranteed lifetime income beginning at age 65. Elena had moderate risk tolerance, limited investment experience beyond her 403(b) plan and the existing annuity, and expressed concern about outliving her savings given her family's history of longevity. She earned approximately $92,000 per year and had no other significant liquid assets beyond the annuity and $45,000 in a savings account.

Marcus recommended that Elena purchase a Pinnacle Index-Linked Variable Annuity issued by National Horizon Life Insurance Company, a product featuring a 10-year surrender charge schedule starting at 9%, an annual rider fee of 1.35% for the guaranteed lifetime withdrawal benefit, and a 150-basis-point annual mortality and expense charge. The product offered uncapped participation in an S&P 500 index-linked strategy with a buffer against the first 10% of losses. Marcus's commission on the sale was 7.25% of the premium, totaling $24,650. Summit Financial Partners also received a 1% override, and National Horizon Life was running a sales contest that quarter awarding a trip to Bermuda for producers exceeding $500,000 in new annuity premium; Marcus had already written $275,000 in qualifying premium before Elena's case.

During the meeting, Marcus provided Elena with the product prospectus and a standard illustration, and he verbally explained the index-linked crediting strategy. He told Elena the product would 'protect her from market downturns while giving her growth potential.' However, Marcus did not disclose the existence of the sales contest, did not disclose the override paid to Summit Financial Partners, and did not discuss any alternative products—including a traditional fixed indexed annuity with a 5-year surrender period, lower fees, and a comparable lifetime income rider offered by a competing carrier that would have paid him a 4.5% commission. Marcus documented Elena's financial profile on a suitability questionnaire but did not memorialize why the recommended product was in her best interest compared to available alternatives. The application was submitted and the policy was issued as a New York contract on April 2, 2020.
question: Did Marcus Ellison's recommendation of the Pinnacle Index-Linked Variable Annuity to Elena Vasquez satisfy the best interest standard required under New York Regulation 187?
answer:
Marcus Ellison's recommendation did not satisfy the best interest standard under New York Regulation 187 (11 NYCRR §224). The regulation, effective for life insurance transactions as of February 1, 2020, and already in effect for annuity transactions since August 1, 2019, imposes a best interest obligation on all producers recommending annuity and life insurance products involving New York-issued contracts.

Under Reg 187, Section 224.4, a producer making a recommendation must act in the best interest of the consumer. This requires, at minimum: (1) obtaining and utilizing accurate and complete consumer profile information; (2) ensuring the recommendation is based on an evaluation of the relevant suitability factors, including the consumer's financial situation, insurance needs, objectives, and risk tolerance; (3) disclosing all material conflicts of interest; and (4) documenting the basis for any recommendation, including why the specific product serves the consumer's best interest.

Marcus failed on multiple independent grounds. First, Reg 187 Section 224.4(d) explicitly prohibits compensation from being a factor that influences the recommendation. The existence of the Bermuda sales contest—which Marcus was actively pursuing and stood to qualify for with Elena's premium—creates a material conflict of interest that was never disclosed. Section 224.4(b) requires that a producer must disclose to the consumer, at the point of sale, all relevant conflicts including compensation arrangements. The 7.25% commission, the 1% override to Summit Financial Partners, and the sales contest incentive were all undisclosed material conflicts.

Second, Reg 187 requires that the producer's recommendation reflect the consumer's best interest, not merely suitability. Marcus failed to consider or present a less costly, arguably more appropriate fixed indexed annuity with a shorter surrender period, lower fees, and a comparable income rider. Given Elena's moderate risk tolerance, limited investment sophistication, concern about outliving savings, and the absence of other liquid assets, a product with a 10-year surrender schedule and market-linked loss exposure beyond a 10% buffer raises serious questions about whether it was truly in her best interest. The regulation demands more than a product that is merely 'not inappropriate'—it demands that the recommendation be in the consumer's best interest.

Third, Marcus failed to document the rationale for the recommendation as required under Section 224.4(e). While he completed a suitability questionnaire, he did not memorialize why this specific product was superior to alternatives for Elena's circumstances. This documentation failure independently violates the regulation.

Marcus cannot defend on the basis that the product was 'suitable' for Elena—Reg 187 expressly elevated the standard beyond traditional suitability for producers making recommendations. The confluence of undisclosed conflicts, failure to evaluate and present alternatives, and inadequate documentation constitutes a clear violation of New York Regulation 187's best interest standard.
applicable_standard: New York Regulation 187 (11 NYCRR §224), specifically Sections 224.4(b) (conflict disclosure), 224.4(d) (prohibition on compensation-driven recommendations), 224.4(e) (documentation requirements), and the overarching best interest standard of Section 224.4(a)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Marcus failed to disclose material compensation-related conflicts of interest—including a carrier sales contest and override payments—and allowed those undisclosed conflicts to influence his recommendation of a higher-cost product over a more suitable and less expensive alternative.

fact_pattern:
Rebecca Thornton, age 62, is a retired school administrator in Spokane, Washington, with a moderate risk tolerance, a total liquid net worth of approximately $485,000, and a stated investment objective of generating income to supplement her pension over the next three to five years before enrolling in Medicare and drawing Social Security. In March 2017, she opened a brokerage account with Pacific Ridge Financial Services, LP ('Pacific Ridge'), a broker-dealer registered in Washington since 1991 and also SEC-registered as an investment adviser. Her financial advisor, Craig Meyers (CRD #441876), recommended she invest $210,000 across four mutual fund families, all in Class A shares, each carrying a front-end load of approximately 4.75%. Craig documented Rebecca's investment time horizon as 'long-term (10+ years)' on her new account form, even though during their recorded discovery meeting Rebecca stated she anticipated needing to liquidate portions of the portfolio within two to four years to cover healthcare expenses before Medicare eligibility. Craig's branch manager, Linda Farrell, approved the transactions without questioning the discrepancy between the documented time horizon and the client's actual stated needs.

Within 18 months, by September 2018, Rebecca had liquidated approximately $145,000 of her Class A mutual fund holdings to pay for a hip replacement surgery and bridge health insurance premiums—exactly the scenario she had described in her initial meeting. The early liquidation meant Rebecca effectively paid approximately $6,887 in front-end loads on shares she held for less than two years, forfeiting the long-term cost advantage that was the primary rationale for selecting Class A shares over lower-load or no-load alternatives such as Class C shares or no-transaction-fee funds available through Pacific Ridge's advisory platform.

A subsequent multistate investigation coordinated through NASAA discovered that Pacific Ridge had no systematic supervisory procedures to flag accounts where Class A shares were recommended to clients whose documented or stated time horizons were inconsistent with the cost structure of those shares. The firm's compliance manual referenced suitability obligations under Washington's Securities Act but contained no written supervisory procedures specifically addressing share class selection relative to client-stated liquidity needs. Craig Meyers's compensation was higher on Class A share sales due to the upfront commission structure, and Pacific Ridge's internal training materials acknowledged that Class A shares were generally unsuitable for investors with short-to-intermediate holding periods.
question: Did Pacific Ridge Financial Services and its financial advisor Craig Meyers violate Washington's Securities Act and applicable suitability obligations by recommending Class A mutual fund shares to a client whose stated liquidity needs were inconsistent with the long-term holding period required to justify Class A front-end loads, and did the firm fail in its supervisory duties?
answer:
This conduct constitutes a violation of the Securities Act of Washington, RCW 21.20, specifically RCW 21.20.010 (anti-fraud provisions) and RCW 21.20.040 (registration and conduct requirements for broker-dealers and their agents), as well as FINRA Rules 2111 (Suitability) and 3110 (Supervision), which Washington incorporates by reference in its regulatory enforcement.

First, regarding the suitability violation: FINRA Rule 2111 requires that a broker-dealer or associated person have a reasonable basis to believe that a recommended transaction is suitable for the customer based on that customer's investment profile, including the customer's age, financial situation, investment objectives, time horizon, liquidity needs, and risk tolerance. Here, Rebecca Thornton explicitly communicated a three-to-five-year time horizon and anticipated liquidity needs for healthcare expenses. Craig Meyers disregarded these stated needs and instead documented a 'long-term (10+ years)' horizon to justify Class A share recommendations. Pacific Ridge's own training materials acknowledged that Class A shares are generally unsuitable for investors with short-to-intermediate holding periods because the front-end load cannot be amortized over sufficient time to produce a cost advantage over Class C or no-load alternatives. The approximately $6,887 in forfeited front-end load value is direct, quantifiable client harm.

Second, the documentation discrepancy between what Rebecca stated and what Craig recorded constitutes a potential violation of RCW 21.20.010's anti-fraud provisions, which prohibit any device, scheme, or artifice to defraud, or any act or practice that operates as a fraud upon any person. Misrepresenting a client's time horizon to justify a higher-commission product is precisely the type of conduct this provision targets.

Third, Pacific Ridge failed its supervisory obligations under FINRA Rule 3110 and RCW 21.20.040. The firm lacked written supervisory procedures to identify and flag share class recommendations inconsistent with documented or stated client time horizons. Branch manager Linda Farrell approved the transactions without reconciling the evident inconsistency.
