key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Greenfield failed to remediate nine critical and high-risk vulnerabilities identified by its own penetration testing vendor for over seven months, directly contradicting its written 30-day patch policy and resulting in a data breach affecting 2,300 clients.

fact_pattern:
Greenfield Manufacturing, Inc. sponsors a 401(k) plan with approximately 4,200 participants and $380 million in assets. The plan's named fiduciary is the Benefits Committee, chaired by CFO Diana Kowalski. In March 2024, the committee decided to replace the plan's existing QDIA — a low-cost Vanguard Target Retirement Fund series with an average expense ratio of 0.10% — with the 'RetireSecure Managed Account' product offered by Patriot Financial Services, Inc. The RetireSecure product is a managed account QDIA that includes an embedded group variable annuity component designed to provide a guaranteed lifetime withdrawal benefit beginning at age 65. The all-in fee for the RetireSecure product is 0.95% annually, inclusive of the annuity insurance charge of 0.40% and the managed account advisory fee of 0.55%.

Diana Kowalski's brother-in-law, Marcus Trent, is a regional vice president at Patriot Financial Services. Marcus made the initial presentation to the Benefits Committee in January 2024, and he personally stood to earn a $75,000 placement bonus if Greenfield adopted the RetireSecure product. The committee meeting minutes from the January and March meetings reflect only a brief notation that 'the committee reviewed managed account options with lifetime income features' and that 'the committee voted unanimously to adopt the RetireSecure Managed Account as the plan's QDIA effective July 1, 2024.' There is no documentation of any benchmarking analysis, fee comparison with the incumbent Vanguard TDF series or other managed account providers, evaluation of the annuity carrier's financial strength, or assessment of whether the lifetime income feature was appropriate given the plan's participant demographics — 62% of whom are under age 40.

Following the transition on July 1, 2024, approximately 2,900 participants who had never made an affirmative investment election were automatically moved into the RetireSecure Managed Account. Within six months, several participants complained about the higher fees and the surrender charges that would apply if they transferred out of the annuity component within seven years. The DOL's Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA) subsequently opened an investigation into the QDIA selection process.
question: Did the Greenfield Benefits Committee satisfy its ERISA fiduciary duties under the QDIA safe harbor regulations when it replaced the incumbent target date fund with the RetireSecure Managed Account as the plan's qualified default investment alternative?
answer:
The Benefits Committee almost certainly failed to satisfy its ERISA fiduciary duties, and the QDIA safe harbor under 29 CFR §2550.404c-5 likely does not protect the committee from liability.

First, the threshold issue: the QDIA regulation at 29 CFR §2550.404c-5(b) provides relief to fiduciaries for investment outcomes when participants are defaulted into a QDIA, but it does not relieve fiduciaries of their obligation to prudently select and monitor the QDIA itself. The preamble to the 2007 final QDIA regulation and subsequent DOL guidance make clear that the selection of a QDIA remains subject to the full fiduciary standards of ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) and (B) — the duties of loyalty and prudence.

Under ERISA §404(a)(1)(B), a fiduciary must act 'with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a prudent man acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use.' The committee's process was deficient in multiple respects: (1) no documented benchmarking analysis comparing the RetireSecure product against the incumbent TDF or competing managed account or lifetime income QDIAs; (2) no fee reasonableness analysis despite a nearly tenfold increase in expense ratios (0.10% to 0.95%); (3) no evaluation of participant demographics — 62% of participants are under 40, raising serious questions about the appropriateness of embedding an annuity with surrender charges for a young workforce; and (4) no assessment of the annuity carrier's financial strength ratings.

Under ERISA §404(a)(1)(A), the duty of loyalty requires fiduciaries to act 'solely in the interest of the participants and beneficiaries.' Diana Kowalski's brother-in-law Marcus Trent directly solicited the business and stood to earn a $75,000 placement bonus. While the relationship itself does not automatically constitute a prohibited transaction, the failure to disclose and manage this conflict — combined with the absence of any independent evaluation — strongly suggests the decision was influenced by considerations other than participant welfare. This implicates ERISA §406(b)(2), which prohibits a fiduciary from acting in a transaction involving the plan on behalf of a party whose interests are adverse to the plan.

The seven-year surrender charge is also problematic. As the 2024 ERISA Advisory Council report highlights, QDIA regulations were designed primarily for the accumulation phase, and embedding illiquid annuity features in a default investment constrains participant choice — a tension the Council specifically flagged. The surrender charges effectively penalize participants who later make an affirmative investment election, undermining the purpose of the QDIA framework.

The committee cannot invoke the QDIA safe harbor to shield itself because the safe harbor's prerequisite — prudent selection — was not met. The EBSA investigation will likely find breaches of ERISA §§404(a)(1)(A), 404(a)(1)(B), and potentially §406(b), exposing committee members to personal liability for losses attributable to the excessive fees.
applicable_standard: ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) (duty of loyalty); ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) (duty of prudence); ERISA §406(b)(2) (prohibited transactions — conflicts of interest); 29 CFR §2550.404c-5 (QDIA safe harbor regulation); SECURE Act §204 (lifetime income fiduciary safe harbor); DOL QDIA Final Rule (2007)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The Benefits Committee failed to document any prudent process — including fee benchmarking, demographic appropriateness analysis, or conflict-of-interest management — when replacing a low-cost TDF QDIA with a high-cost managed account product solicited by a committee member's relative who received a placement bonus.

fact_pattern: Gerald Whitmore is a licensed insurance agent affiliated with Pinnacle Insurance Marketing Group, an independent marketing organization (IMO) that distributes fixed indexed annuity (FIA) products from several carriers. On March 15, 2024, Gerald meets with Margaret Ellison, a 67-year-old recently retired public school teacher with a $410,000 traditional IRA rollover from her 403(b) plan. Margaret tells Gerald she needs reliable income to supplement her $2,100/month pension and $1,850/month Social Security benefit. She describes herself as conservative, noting she 'cannot afford to lose any of this money.' Gerald recommends she place the entire $410,000 into the Sentinel Secure Growth FIA, a product issued by Sentinel Life Insurance Company. The Sentinel Secure Growth FIA carries a 12-year surrender charge schedule beginning at 10% and declining to 0%, offers a 6.5% participation rate on the S&P 500 with a 3% floor, and includes an optional lifetime income rider with a 0.95% annual fee. Gerald earns a first-year commission of 7% ($28,700), plus a 1.25% trail commission each subsequent year. Pinnacle IMO receives an additional 1.5% override on all Sentinel product placements. Gerald does not document any consideration of alternative products, including a competing FIA from Guardian Horizon Life that offers a 7-year surrender period, a 7.25% participation rate, a 1.5% floor, and a comparable income rider at 0.75% — on which Gerald would earn only a 4.5% first-year commission. Gerald does not disclose to Margaret the specific commission differential between the two products, nor does he explain the compensation override paid to Pinnacle IMO. He provides Margaret with the Sentinel product illustration and a generic suitability form but does not memorialize why the Sentinel product was selected over alternatives. Gerald relies on PTE 84-24 to exempt the commission-based compensation he and Pinnacle receive in connection with the IRA annuity transaction.
question: Under the DOL's amended PTE 84-24 and the broader fiduciary framework applicable to IRA rollover recommendations, did Gerald Whitmore's recommendation of the Sentinel Secure Growth FIA to Margaret Ellison satisfy the conditions necessary to rely on PTE 84-24 for exemptive relief from ERISA's and the Code's prohibited transaction provisions?
answer:
Gerald Whitmore's transaction almost certainly fails to satisfy the conditions of amended PTE 84-24 and constitutes a non-exempt prohibited transaction under Code section 4975(c)(1)(D), (E), and (F).

First, under the DOL's 2024 Retirement Security Rule and the amended definition of investment advice fiduciary, Gerald is a fiduciary under Code section 4975(e)(3)(B) because he provided a recommendation to Margaret — a Retirement Investor — regarding the disposition of her IRA assets for a fee (his commission), in a context where Margaret reasonably relied on that recommendation as individualized to her. The rollover recommendation itself triggers fiduciary status. As a fiduciary, Gerald's receipt of the 7% commission and Pinnacle's receipt of the 1.5% override constitute prohibited transactions — specifically, dealing with plan assets in his own interest and receiving consideration from a party dealing with the plan (Sentinel Life) — under Code sections 4975(c)(1)(D) and (E).

To rely on PTE 84-24 as amended, Gerald must satisfy several conditions. Critically, the amended exemption requires that the Insurance Producer provide advice in accordance with the Impartial Conduct Standards, which include a best interest obligation (the advice must be prudent, loyal, and not place the financial interest of the adviser ahead of the Retirement Investor), a reasonable compensation standard, and a no-misleading-statements requirement. Gerald fails on multiple fronts.

Regarding best interest: Gerald did not consider or document any alternatives, including the Guardian Horizon product that offered materially better terms for a conservative income-seeking retiree (shorter surrender period, higher participation rate, lower rider fee). The 12-year surrender schedule is particularly problematic for a 67-year-old who may need liquidity. The absence of any documented comparative analysis demonstrates that Gerald's recommendation was driven by the substantially higher 7% commission rather than Margaret's interests, violating the loyalty and prudence components of the Impartial Conduct Standards.

Regarding disclosure: Amended PTE 84-24 requires disclosure of material conflicts of interest, including the specific compensation the Insurance Producer and related entities receive. Gerald failed to disclose the commission differential or Pinnacle's override, depriving Margaret of material information necessary to evaluate his recommendation.

Regarding documentation: The amended exemption imposes specific documentation and recordkeeping requirements. Gerald's reliance on a generic suitability form, without any written rationale for the product selection, fails these requirements.

Gerald cannot claim reliance on pre-amendment PTE 84-24 because the amended conditions apply to transactions occurring after the effective date. His conduct represents a textbook example of a conflicted recommendation where compensation incentives — not the client's retirement security — drove the product selection. The exemption is unavailable, and the transaction constitutes a non-exempt prohibited transaction subject to excise taxes under Code section 4975(a) and (b).
applicable_standard: Code §4975(c)(1)(D), (E), (F); Code §4975(e)(3)(B); ERISA §§3(21)(A)(ii), 406(b)(1), 406(b)(3); Amended PTE 84-24 (Application No. D-12060, ZRIN 1210-ZA33) — Impartial Conduct Standards (best interest, reasonable compensation, no misleading statements); PTE 84-24 disclosure and documentation conditions; DOL Retirement Security Rule (29 CFR Part 2550)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Gerald selected the higher-commission annuity product without documenting consideration of a materially superior lower-commission alternative, failing the Impartial Conduct Standards' best interest obligation required under amended PTE 84-24.

fact_pattern:
Meridian Benefits Consulting LLC is a benefits brokerage firm based in Columbus, Ohio, that provides brokerage services and consulting to employer-sponsored group health plans. In October 2021, Meridian entered into a new three-year service agreement with Trident Manufacturing Corp., an ERISA-covered group health plan sponsor with 1,200 employees and a self-funded health plan. Meridian's principal, Rebecca Talmadge, serves as the primary broker and consultant on the account. Under the arrangement, Meridian expects to receive $185,000 annually in direct compensation from Trident (paid as a flat consulting fee), plus approximately $47,000 per year in indirect compensation from PharmaCare Network, a pharmacy benefit manager, in the form of override commissions tied to Trident plan participants' prescription volume. Meridian also expects to receive approximately $12,500 annually from Apex Wellness Solutions, a third-party wellness vendor, as referral fees for steering Trident's wellness program business to Apex.

As the December 27, 2021 effective date of the new ERISA §408(b)(2)(B) disclosure requirements approached, Rebecca Talmadge consulted with Meridian's outside ERISA counsel to determine how to comply. On December 20, 2021, Meridian provided Trident's HR Director and plan fiduciary, Marcus Elwood, with a comprehensive written disclosure document. The document itemized the $185,000 direct compensation, described the expected $47,000 in override commissions from PharmaCare Network (identifying PharmaCare by name and explaining the volume-based commission structure), and disclosed the $12,500 referral fee arrangement with Apex Wellness Solutions (identifying Apex by name and the basis for the referral fee). The disclosure also included a description of all services Meridian would provide, including plan design consultation, carrier negotiations, renewal management, compliance support, and claims advocacy.

Meridian's disclosure format did not follow any DOL-prescribed template—because none existed at the time—but instead was modeled on the structure used for retirement plan service provider disclosures under 29 CFR §2550.408b-2(c). Rebecca Talmadge believed this was a reasonable approach given the absence of specific regulatory guidance for group health plan disclosures. The disclosure was provided to Marcus Elwood seven days before the service arrangement's January 1, 2022 renewal date. In February 2022, the DOL's Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA) initiated an investigation of Meridian's disclosure practices as part of a broader health plan fee transparency enforcement initiative.
question: Did Meridian Benefits Consulting LLC satisfy its disclosure obligations under ERISA §408(b)(2)(B) as interpreted under the DOL's temporary enforcement policy in FAB 2021-03, and would the DOL treat Meridian as having failed to make required disclosures?
answer:
Meridian Benefits Consulting LLC would likely be found compliant with its disclosure obligations under ERISA §408(b)(2)(B) as applied through the DOL's temporary enforcement policy announced in Field Assistance Bulletin 2021-03.

First, Meridian qualifies as a 'covered service provider' under ERISA §408(b)(2)(B) because it provides both 'brokerage services' and 'consulting' to an ERISA-covered group health plan and reasonably expects to receive well in excess of the $1,000 statutory threshold in direct and indirect compensation ($185,000 + $47,000 + $12,500 = $244,500 annually).

Second, the substantive content of Meridian's disclosure satisfies the statutory requirements. ERISA §408(b)(2)(B) requires disclosure of both direct compensation and indirect compensation, defined under §408(b)(2)(B)(ii)(I)(dd)(CC) as compensation received from sources other than the plan or plan sponsor. Meridian disclosed all three compensation streams: the $185,000 direct fee from Trident, the $47,000 in override commissions from PharmaCare Network, and the $12,500 referral fee from Apex Wellness Solutions. Each source was identified by name, the compensation amount was specified, and the basis for payment was explained. This directly addresses what FAB 2021-03 identifies as 'a significant goal of the new disclosure requirements'—enhancing fee transparency, 'especially for service arrangements that involve the payment of indirect compensation.'

Third, regarding timing, the statute requires disclosures 'reasonably in advance' of entering into the contract or arrangement. Meridian provided the disclosure on December 20, 2021, seven days before the January 1, 2022 renewal, which appears reasonable under the circumstances given the December 27, 2021 effective date of the statutory requirements.

Fourth, and most critically, FAB 2021-03 establishes a temporary enforcement safe harbor: the DOL 'will not treat [a covered service provider] as having failed to make required disclosures... as long as the person made disclosures in accordance with a good faith, reasonable interpretation of ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B).' Meridian's approach—modeling its disclosure on the established retirement plan disclosure framework under 29 CFR §2550.408b-2(c) in the absence of group health plan-specific regulatory guidance—constitutes precisely the type of good faith, reasonable interpretation contemplated by FAB 2021-03. The DOL expressly acknowledged that it was 'not issuing regulatory guidance at this time' and that 'covered service providers will adopt various methods to make the required disclosure.' Meridian's disclosure was 'reasonably designed and implemented to provide the required information and transparency,' which is the standard FAB 2021-03 states the Department will apply when analyzing compliance efforts. Meridian should be found compliant.
applicable_standard: ERISA §408(b)(2)(B); ERISA §408(b)(2)(B)(ii)(I)(dd)(CC) (indirect compensation); ERISA §408(b)(2)(B)(viii) (fiduciary conditional relief); DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2021-03 (temporary enforcement policy); Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, §202 of Title II of Division BB; 29 CFR §2550.408b-2(c) (retirement plan service provider disclosure regulation, used as analogous framework)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Meridian's comprehensive itemized disclosure of all direct and indirect compensation—including third-party override commissions and referral fees identified by source, amount, and basis—constituted a good faith, reasonable interpretation of ERISA §408(b)(2)(B) within the meaning of FAB 2021-03's temporary enforcement safe harbor.

fact_pattern:
Greenfield Manufacturing, Inc. sponsors a single-employer defined benefit pension plan with a calendar plan year. The plan has 4,200 participants and beneficiaries and held approximately $287 million in assets as of December 31, 2024. The plan administrator, Janet Kowalski, VP of Human Resources, began preparing the 2024 annual funding notice in early February 2025. Her enrolled actuary, David Reinhardt of Reinhardt Actuarial Services, informed her on February 18, 2025, that SECURE 2.0 Section 343 had modified the asset valuation, liability measurement, and funded percentage methodologies required in the annual funding notice under ERISA §101(f), effective for plan years beginning after December 31, 2023. He noted that the existing DOL regulations at 29 CFR 2520.101-5, last updated in 2015, had not yet been amended to reflect these SECURE 2.0 changes, creating apparent conflicts between the statute as amended and the pre-existing regulatory text.

Janet consulted with plan counsel, Rachel Edmonds of Edmonds & Hartley LLP, who reviewed DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-02, issued on April 3, 2025. Rachel advised Janet that the FAB provided model language and guidance that, if followed with accurate data, would be treated by EBSA enforcement offices as compliant with the annual funding notice requirements. The FAB explicitly stated that compliance with the bulletin constituted a 'reasonable, good faith interpretation' of ERISA §101(f) as amended by SECURE 2.0 pending further rulemaking or formal regulatory updates.

Janet directed David to recalculate the funded status using the SECURE 2.0 methodology as described in the FAB, incorporating the revised asset valuation approach. The recalculated funding percentage was 91.3%, compared to 88.7% under the prior regulatory methodology. Janet used the model appendices provided in FAB 2025-02 to draft the annual funding notice, populated the models with accurate data as verified by David, and furnished the notice to all participants, beneficiaries, and the PBGC by April 28, 2025 — two days before the April 30, 2025 deadline for calendar-year plans.

In May 2025, a participant named Gregory Stanton filed a complaint with the EBSA regional office, alleging that the plan's annual funding notice was deficient because it did not follow the format and calculations prescribed in the 2015 regulations at 29 CFR 2520.101-5. Stanton argued that the regulations remained the binding compliance standard and that the plan administrator improperly relied on non-binding sub-regulatory guidance.
question: Did the Greenfield Manufacturing plan administrator comply with the annual funding notice requirements under ERISA §101(f) as amended by SECURE 2.0, notwithstanding the fact that the notice deviated from the pre-existing 2015 regulations at 29 CFR 2520.101-5?
answer:
Janet Kowalski's actions constitute compliant conduct under ERISA §101(f) as amended by SECURE 2.0 Section 343. The analysis proceeds as follows.

First, ERISA §101(f) imposes the statutory obligation, and Section 343 of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-328) directly amended §101(f), modifying the asset valuation, liability measurement, and funding level disclosure methodologies effective for plan years beginning after December 31, 2023. For the Greenfield plan's 2024 calendar plan year, the amended statute governs. When a statute is amended by Congress, the amended statutory text supersedes conflicting pre-existing regulatory provisions. The 2015 regulations at 29 CFR 2520.101-5, which the DOL has acknowledged were not updated to reflect SECURE 2.0, cannot override the later-enacted statutory requirements.

Second, DOL FAB 2025-02, issued April 3, 2025, directly addresses the conflict between the amended statute and the outdated regulations. The FAB explicitly states that 'the Department will treat compliance with the guidance in this Bulletin as a reasonable, good faith interpretation of the annual funding notice disclosure requirements of section 101(f) of ERISA with respect to the issues discussed in this Bulletin.' The FAB further provides model appendices and instructs EBSA Offices of Enforcement that plan administrators who use the models and adhere to the bulletin's principles — provided that inputted information is accurate and notices are timely furnished — should be treated as compliant.

Janet satisfied every element of the FAB's safe harbor framework: (1) she used the SECURE 2.0 methodology as outlined in the FAB for asset and liability valuations; (2) she utilized the model appendices provided in the FAB; (3) her enrolled actuary verified the accuracy of the underlying data; and (4) the notice was furnished to all required recipients — participants, beneficiaries, and the PBGC — by April 28, 2025, within the 120-day statutory deadline (April 30, 2025 for calendar-year plans).

Regarding Gregory Stanton's complaint, his argument that the 2015 regulations remain the exclusive binding standard fails. The FAB directly contemplates this scenario, acknowledging 'apparent confusion, and even certain outright conflicts' between the amended statute and the pre-existing regulations. The statutory amendment controls, and the DOL has provided express enforcement guidance sanctioning reliance on the FAB pending formal rulemaking. While FABs are sub-regulatory guidance, they reflect the enforcement agency's authoritative interpretation and, critically, the FAB here aligns plan administrators with the statute itself rather than with outdated regulations. Janet's reliance was both legally sound and practically reasonable.
applicable_standard: ERISA §101(f) as amended by SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 §343 (Pub. L. 117-328); 29 CFR 2520.101-5; DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-02 (April 3, 2025); ERISA §104(a)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The plan administrator used the DOL FAB 2025-02 model appendices with accurate data and timely furnished the SECURE 2.0-compliant annual funding notice, which the DOL expressly treats as a reasonable, good faith interpretation of the amended statute pending regulatory updates.

fact_pattern:
The Heartland Small Business Alliance ('HSBA') is a trade association of 347 small employers across Kansas, Missouri, and Nebraska, primarily in the agricultural supply and equipment sector. In March 2022, the HSBA Board of Directors — chaired by Gerald Whitmore, who also serves as CEO of Whitmore Agricultural Supply, Inc. — voted to establish an Association Health Plan ('AHP') under ERISA to provide group health coverage to employees of its member employers. The AHP, branded as 'Heartland Health Choice,' enrolled approximately 4,200 participants by January 2023. The Board retained Pinnacle Benefits Consulting, LLC, led by adviser Diana Stokes, to design the plan and select insurance carriers.

In structuring the AHP, Diana Stokes recommended that the plan cover nine of the ten ACA essential health benefits but exclude pediatric dental and vision coverage entirely — not through a stand-alone product, but simply by omitting it from the benefit package altogether. Stokes argued to the Board that eliminating pediatric dental and vision would save the plan approximately $1.8 million annually, reducing per-participant costs by roughly $430 per year. The Board accepted this recommendation without conducting any independent analysis of whether stand-alone pediatric dental and vision products were available at competitive rates, and without soliciting bids from carriers offering such coverage. Board meeting minutes from the April 2022 session reflect that Gerald Whitmore stated, 'If it saves us money, that's acting in the best interest of the employers.'

In September 2023, three member employers with a combined workforce of 210 employees — including 87 children enrolled as dependents — filed complaints with the DOL alleging that the AHP Board breached its fiduciary duty under ERISA by failing to evaluate whether comprehensive pediatric dental and vision coverage could have been offered at a reasonable cost through stand-alone products. The complainants cited instances where families incurred out-of-pocket pediatric dental expenses averaging $2,100 per child annually, with one family paying $6,400 for orthodontic and vision care for two children. A DOL investigation revealed that at least four stand-alone pediatric dental and vision carriers had offered to provide coverage to Heartland Health Choice at a combined annual cost of approximately $780,000 — less than half of the $1.8 million Stokes had projected the plan would save by eliminating the benefits entirely.
question: Did the HSBA Board and its consultant Diana Stokes breach their ERISA fiduciary duties in the design and governance of the Heartland Health Choice AHP by eliminating pediatric dental and vision coverage without evaluating stand-alone product alternatives?
answer:
Yes, the HSBA Board and Diana Stokes likely breached their fiduciary duties under ERISA in the governance of the Heartland Health Choice AHP. The analysis proceeds on several grounds.

First, under ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) and (B), fiduciaries of an employee benefit plan must discharge their duties 'solely in the interest of the participants and beneficiaries' and 'with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a prudent man acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use.' The AHP Board, as the governing body of an ERISA-covered plan, owes these fiduciary duties to the 4,200 participants, including dependent children. The 'control test' applicable to associations sponsoring AHPs — as referenced in pre-rule DOL guidance and reaffirmed in the document's discussion — imposes a fiduciary duty on the Board to 'act in the best interest' of participants while keeping costs reasonable.

The Board's failure is procedural and substantive. Procedurally, the prudent man standard under §404(a)(1)(B) requires a deliberative process. The Board accepted Stokes's recommendation to eliminate pediatric dental and vision coverage without soliciting competitive bids from stand-alone carriers, without conducting any independent cost-benefit analysis, and without evaluating the impact on participants. The DOL investigation's finding that stand-alone coverage was available at approximately $780,000 — less than half of the projected savings from elimination — demonstrates that a prudent fiduciary would have at least explored this option. Board Chair Whitmore's statement equating cost savings to employer interest — rather than participant interest — further evidences a fundamental misunderstanding of the fiduciary obligation.

Substantively, under ERISA §404(a)(1)(A), the duty of loyalty requires that decisions be made solely in the interest of participants and beneficiaries. Eliminating an entire category of health benefits affecting 87 enrolled dependent children, without evaluating readily available and affordable alternatives, fails this standard. The document itself highlights that compliant AHPs cover all ten EHBs, often through stand-alone products specifically because Boards determine that such products provide equal or better coverage at lower cost — the precise analysis the HSBA Board failed to undertake.

Diana Stokes, as a consultant exercising discretionary authority over plan design, may also qualify as a functional fiduciary under ERISA §3(21)(A)(ii) by rendering investment advice or exercising authority over plan management. Her recommendation to eliminate benefits without market analysis would constitute a breach of the prudence standard.

The Board cannot defend on the grounds that AHPs are not legally required to cover EHBs. The fiduciary duty is independent of the ACA coverage mandate and requires prudent process regardless of minimum legal requirements. The failure to investigate available alternatives is the pivotal deficiency.
applicable_standard: ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) (duty of loyalty); ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) (duty of prudence); ERISA §3(21)(A) (definition of fiduciary); DOL pre-rule guidance on AHP 'control test' and fiduciary obligations of AHP governing boards; 29 CFR 2550.404a-1 (investment duties and prudent process requirements)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The AHP Board eliminated pediatric dental and vision coverage without conducting any analysis of available stand-alone product alternatives, failing the procedural prudence requirement under ERISA §404(a)(1)(B).

fact_pattern:
Meridian Benefits Consulting, LLC is a benefits brokerage firm based in Columbus, Ohio, that provides brokerage and consulting services to employer-sponsored group health plans. On January 15, 2022—shortly after the December 27, 2021 effective date of the CAA amendments to ERISA §408(b)(2)—Meridian entered into a new three-year service agreement with Lakewood Manufacturing, Inc., a mid-sized manufacturer with 340 employees and an ERISA-covered group health plan. Lakewood's VP of Human Resources, Sandra Whitfield, serves as the plan's responsible fiduciary.

Under the arrangement, Meridian receives direct compensation of $48,000 per year ($4,000/month) from Lakewood for plan consulting, carrier negotiations, and ongoing plan administration support. In addition, Meridian reasonably expects to receive indirect compensation of approximately $18,500 annually in the form of override commissions from Anthem Blue Cross, the health plan carrier Meridian has recommended, as well as $6,200 annually in referral fees from PharmaRx Solutions, a pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) to which Meridian routes Lakewood's prescription drug benefit. Meridian also expects to earn $3,800 from a wellness platform vendor, HealthFirst Technologies, for referring Lakewood to its services.

Prior to executing the agreement on January 15, 2022, Meridian's principal, Derek Layton, provided Sandra Whitfield with a written disclosure package on January 3, 2022. The disclosure described Meridian's direct compensation in exact dollar terms. For indirect compensation, however, Derek disclosed the override commissions from Anthem as a reasonable estimate expressed as a range ($16,000–$21,000), the PharmaRx referral fee as a flat dollar estimate ($6,200), and the HealthFirst referral fee as a percentage of the wellness platform contract value (approximately 4%). The disclosure also described the services Meridian would perform and identified the sources of all indirect compensation by name. Derek included a narrative explanation that exact indirect amounts could not be determined in advance because they depended on enrollment figures and claims experience. He also noted in the disclosure that Meridian would update the estimates if material changes occurred.

In March 2022, the DOL's regional office opened an inquiry into Meridian's compliance with the new §408(b)(2)(B) disclosure requirements as part of a broader health plan service provider audit initiative. The investigator reviewed Meridian's disclosure package and questioned whether Meridian's use of ranges and percentage-based estimates for indirect compensation satisfied the statutory requirements, given that the statute requires disclosure of 'direct and indirect compensation that the service provider expects to receive.'
question: Did Meridian Benefits Consulting's pre-contract disclosure to Lakewood Manufacturing's responsible plan fiduciary satisfy the requirements of ERISA §408(b)(2)(B) as interpreted under the DOL's temporary enforcement policy in FAB 2021-03?
answer:
Meridian Benefits Consulting's disclosure likely satisfies the requirements under the DOL's temporary enforcement policy articulated in Field Assistance Bulletin 2021-03. The analysis proceeds as follows.

ERISA §408(b)(2)(B), as amended by Section 202 of Title II of Division BB of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021, requires covered service providers—those providing brokerage services or consulting to ERISA-covered group health plans and reasonably expecting $1,000 or more in direct or indirect compensation—to disclose specified compensation information to the responsible plan fiduciary reasonably in advance of entering into the service arrangement. Meridian clearly qualifies as a covered service provider: it provides both brokerage and consulting services to an ERISA group health plan and expects total compensation well in excess of $1,000 (approximately $76,500 annually).

FAB 2021-03 explicitly acknowledges that the DOL had not issued implementing regulations as of December 30, 2021, and recognizes that 'group health plan service provider arrangements and compensation structures are not uniform, often complicated, and frequently structured to reflect state law.' Critically, the FAB establishes a temporary enforcement policy under which the DOL 'will not treat [a covered service provider] as having failed to make required disclosures... as long as the person made disclosures in accordance with a good faith, reasonable interpretation of ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B).' The standard is therefore good faith and reasonableness, not perfection.

Meridian's conduct maps favorably to every element of this standard. First, the disclosure was timely—provided January 3, 2022, twelve days before the January 15, 2022 contract execution, satisfying the 'reasonably in advance' requirement. Second, direct compensation was disclosed in exact dollar terms ($48,000/year). Third, indirect compensation was disclosed through reasonable methods: a dollar range for Anthem override commissions ($16,000–$21,000), a flat estimate for PharmaRx ($6,200), and a percentage for HealthFirst (4%), all accompanied by an explanation that exact amounts were contingent on enrollment and claims data. Fourth, Meridian identified each source of indirect compensation by name, directly advancing the statute's goal—emphasized in FAB 2021-03—of 'enhanc[ing] fee transparency, especially for service arrangements that involve the payment of indirect compensation as defined in ERISA section 408(b)(2)(B)(ii)(I)(dd)(CC).' Fifth, Meridian committed to updating estimates upon material changes.

The DOL investigator's concern about ranges and percentages is understandable but should not result in an enforcement action. FAB 2021-03 states the Department will consider 'whether the provider's disclosure of information is reasonably designed and implemented to provide the required information and transparency.' Using reasonable estimates where exact figures are unknowable at the time of disclosure is a hallmark of good faith compliance, consistent with longstanding DOL guidance under the parallel §408(b)(2)(A) regulations for retirement plan service providers (29 CFR §2550.408b-2(c)), which explicitly permit reasonable estimates. Meridian's disclosure was reasonably designed, substantively transparent, and provided Sandra Whitfield with sufficient information to assess compensation reasonableness and potential conflicts. Verdict: compliant under the FAB 2021-03 temporary enforcement policy.
applicable_standard: ERISA §408(b)(2)(B) as amended by CAA §202; ERISA §408(b)(2)(B)(ii)(I)(dd)(CC) (indirect compensation definition); ERISA §408(b)(2)(B)(viii) (fiduciary relief for disclosure failures); DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2021-03 (temporary enforcement policy—good faith, reasonable interpretation standard); 29 CFR §2550.408b-2(c) (analogous retirement plan service provider disclosure regulation)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Meridian disclosed all sources and reasonable estimates of both direct and indirect compensation in advance of the contract, consistent with a good faith, reasonable interpretation of the statute as required by FAB 2021-03's temporary enforcement policy.

fact_pattern:
Gerald Whitmore is a 63-year-old machinist at Trident Manufacturing, Inc., preparing for retirement in two years. He has accumulated $412,000 in the Trident Manufacturing 401(k) Plan, which is an ERISA-covered defined contribution plan. In February 2025, Gerald attends a retirement planning seminar hosted by Pinnacle Financial Advisors, LLC, a firm that holds itself out as providing personalized retirement guidance. At the seminar, Kevin Dasher, a licensed insurance agent affiliated with Pinnacle and appointed with National Heritage Life Insurance Company, presents himself as a 'trusted retirement advisor' and offers free one-on-one consultations.

During a private meeting on March 4, 2025, Kevin reviews Gerald's 401(k) statement and recommends that Gerald roll over his entire $412,000 balance into an individual retirement account (IRA) at Pinnacle, and then immediately purchase a National Heritage Heritage Plus Fixed Indexed Annuity with a 10-year surrender period. The annuity carries a 6.5% first-year commission paid to Kevin, totaling $26,780, along with a 1.15% annual trailing fee. Kevin does not disclose the commission structure to Gerald, nor does he discuss lower-cost alternatives such as keeping the funds in the 401(k) plan, which offers a suite of low-cost index funds with expense ratios averaging 0.04%. Kevin's internal notes indicate that he considered the Heritage Plus product 'a fine fit because Gerald wants guaranteed income,' but contain no documentation comparing the costs, features, or investment alternatives, and no analysis of whether the rollover itself was in Gerald's best interest.

Kevin relies on PTE 84-24 for exemptive relief from the prohibited transaction provisions of ERISA and the Code. However, Kevin does not implement any of the impartial conduct standards or disclosure requirements that the 2024 amendments to PTE 84-24 impose, nor does he acknowledge his fiduciary status under the Department of Labor's updated investment advice fiduciary definition. Pinnacle Financial Advisors has no written policies or procedures addressing conflicts of interest in annuity recommendations or rollover advice.
question: Did Kevin Dasher's recommendation of the annuity rollover comply with the requirements of amended PTE 84-24 and the DOL's fiduciary framework, and can Pinnacle Financial Advisors rely on PTE 84-24 for exemptive relief from ERISA's prohibited transaction provisions?
answer:
No. Kevin Dasher's conduct fails to satisfy the conditions of amended PTE 84-24, and neither he nor Pinnacle Financial Advisors can rely on the exemption. The analysis proceeds on multiple grounds.

First, under the Department of Labor's Retirement Security Rule (29 CFR Part 2550, ZRIN 1210-ZA33), Kevin is an investment advice fiduciary. He held himself out as a trusted retirement advisor, provided individualized advice regarding the disposition of Gerald's 401(k) assets (a rollover recommendation) and the investment of those assets (the annuity purchase), and received compensation in connection with that advice. This squarely satisfies ERISA §3(21)(A)(ii) and Code §4975(e)(3)(B). The rollover recommendation itself constitutes investment advice because it concerns 'moneys or other property' of a plan.

Second, Kevin's receipt of a $26,780 first-year commission and ongoing 1.15% trailing fee from National Heritage constitutes receiving 'consideration for his own personal account from any party dealing with such plan in connection with a transaction involving the assets of the plan,' which is a prohibited transaction under ERISA §406(b)(1) and (b)(3). Without a valid exemption, this self-dealing is categorically barred.

Third, the 2024 amendment to PTE 84-24 imposes conditions that must be met for exemptive relief. These include adherence to Impartial Conduct Standards—requiring advice in the Retirement Investor's best interest, charging no more than reasonable compensation, and making no materially misleading statements. Kevin failed all three prongs: (a) he conducted no comparative analysis of the rollover versus keeping funds in the low-cost 401(k), meaning he cannot demonstrate the advice was in Gerald's best interest; (b) a 6.5% commission on a fixed indexed annuity with a 10-year surrender period, when a 0.04% index fund alternative existed, raises serious reasonable compensation concerns; and (c) his failure to disclose the commission structure is itself a material omission.

Fourth, the amended PTE 84-24 requires disclosure of material conflicts of interest, compensation arrangements, and the fiduciary's status. Kevin made none of these disclosures. Additionally, Pinnacle has no written policies or procedures to manage conflicts, which the amended exemption framework contemplates as part of a financial institution's supervisory obligations.

Finally, ERISA §§404(a)(1)(A) and (B) impose duties of loyalty and prudence on fiduciaries. Kevin's failure to document any analysis, consider alternatives, or disclose conflicts violates both duties independently of the prohibited transaction analysis. Pinnacle, as the supervising entity, bears co-fiduciary liability under ERISA §405(a) for its failure to establish compliance infrastructure. The exemption is unavailable, and the transaction constitutes a prohibited transaction under ERISA §406(b) and Code §4975(c)(1)(E) and (F).
applicable_standard: ERISA §3(21)(A)(ii); ERISA §§404(a)(1)(A)-(B); ERISA §§406(b)(1), (b)(3); ERISA §405(a); ERISA §408; Code §4975(e)(3)(B); Code §4975(c)(1)(E)-(F); PTE 84-24 as amended (Application No. D-12060, ZRIN 1210-ZA33); DOL Retirement Security Rule (29 CFR Part 2550); PTE 2020-02 Impartial Conduct Standards
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Kevin failed to satisfy the Impartial Conduct Standards required under amended PTE 84-24 by conducting no comparative cost or suitability analysis, failing to disclose his $26,780 commission, and ignoring the lower-cost 401(k) alternative, thereby rendering the exemption unavailable and the annuity rollover a prohibited transaction.

fact_pattern: Marcus Reilly is a registered representative of Granite Peak Financial Services, a broker-dealer, and also holds the CFP® designation. On March 15, 2018, he met with Patricia Okonkwo, a 58-year-old public school teacher nearing retirement, who had accumulated $412,000 in her employer-sponsored 403(b) plan invested in a diversified portfolio of low-cost index funds with a blended expense ratio of 0.08%. Patricia contacted Marcus after attending a free 'Retirement Readiness' seminar organized by Granite Peak at a local hotel. During their meeting, Marcus recommended that Patricia roll her entire 403(b) balance into a new IRA at Granite Peak, where he proposed investing the proceeds into a suite of proprietary actively managed mutual funds offered by Granite Peak's affiliate, Granite Peak Asset Management. The recommended funds carried an average expense ratio of 1.35%, plus a 5.25% front-end sales load, which would generate approximately $21,630 in upfront commissions for Marcus personally. Marcus told Patricia that the rollover would give her 'more investment choices and personalized attention,' but he did not perform or document any comparative analysis of the costs, investment performance, or features of her existing 403(b) plan versus the proposed IRA. He did not disclose that Granite Peak paid enhanced compensation grids for sales of its proprietary funds, nor did he mention that Patricia's existing 403(b) plan offered institutional share classes unavailable in a retail IRA. Marcus prepared only a brief suitability questionnaire noting Patricia's moderate risk tolerance and retirement timeline of seven years, but conducted no analysis of the total cost differential over Patricia's expected retirement horizon. Patricia signed the rollover paperwork on March 22, 2018, and the rollover was completed on April 5, 2018. Over the next three years, Patricia's IRA underperformed what her 403(b) portfolio would have returned by approximately $38,000, largely attributable to the higher fee structure and the initial sales load drag.
question: Under the DOL's fiduciary rule framework, ERISA prohibited transaction provisions, and applicable exemption conditions, did Marcus Reilly's rollover recommendation to Patricia Okonkwo comply with his fiduciary obligations, and could Granite Peak rely on a prohibited transaction exemption for the compensation it received?
answer:
Marcus Reilly's conduct constitutes a clear violation of ERISA fiduciary standards and would not qualify for relief under the applicable Prohibited Transaction Exemptions. Under the DOL's fiduciary rule (29 CFR §2510.3-21), Marcus's individualized rollover recommendation to Patricia constituted 'investment advice' for compensation, rendering him a fiduciary under ERISA §3(21)(A)(ii). As an ERISA fiduciary, he was subject to ERISA §404(a)(1)'s duty of loyalty and prudence, requiring him to act solely in the interest of the participant and with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence that a prudent person would exercise.

Marcus's recommendation triggered ERISA §406(b) prohibited transaction rules because the compensation he and Granite Peak received from the rollover—$21,630 in front-end loads plus ongoing revenue from proprietary fund expense ratios—constituted self-dealing and transactions involving conflicts of interest. Specifically, §406(b)(1) prohibits a fiduciary from dealing with plan assets in his own interest, and §406(b)(3) prohibits receiving consideration from a party dealing with the plan in connection with a transaction involving plan assets.

To receive such conflicted compensation, Granite Peak would need to satisfy the conditions of a Prohibited Transaction Exemption, such as PTE 2016-01 (Best Interest Contract Exemption) or its successors. The BIC Exemption required, among other conditions, that the adviser provide advice in the 'best interest' of the retirement investor, meaning advice that reflects the care, skill, prudence, and diligence that a prudent person would exercise based on the investment objectives, risk tolerance, financial circumstances, and needs of the investor, without regard to the financial or other interests of the adviser. Marcus fundamentally failed this standard. He performed no documented cost-benefit analysis comparing Patricia's low-cost 403(b) plan (0.08% expense ratio, no loads, institutional share classes) against the proposed IRA (1.35% expense ratio plus 5.25% front-end load). The cost differential alone—approximately $5,238 annually in excess fees plus the initial load—was material and quantifiable. The BIC Exemption also required specific written disclosures of conflicts, including enhanced compensation arrangements for proprietary products, which Marcus failed to provide.

Marcus cannot rely on a defense that he completed a suitability questionnaire; suitability is a lower standard than the fiduciary best-interest obligation required under ERISA and the PTEs. The Financial Planning Coalition's comment letter in this very docket emphasized that advisers operating under fiduciary standards across business models—including CFP® professionals like Marcus—can and should perform this analysis. Marcus's CFP® designation independently obligated him to act as a fiduciary, making his failure doubly egregious. The rollover recommendation was non-compliant, the exemption conditions were unsatisfied, and Granite Peak faces prohibited transaction liability under ERISA §§406(a) and 406(b).
applicable_standard: ERISA §§3(21)(A)(ii), 404(a)(1)(A)-(B), 406(a), 406(b)(1), 406(b)(3); 29 CFR §2510.3-21 (DOL Fiduciary Rule); PTE 2016-01 (Best Interest Contract Exemption); IRC §4975(c)(1); CFP Board Standards of Professional Conduct
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Marcus failed to perform or document any comparative cost-benefit analysis between Patricia's low-cost 403(b) plan and the significantly more expensive proprietary IRA products, defeating any claim to the best-interest standard required under the BIC Exemption.

fact_pattern:
Margaret Hollister is the chair of the Investment Committee for the Greenfield Manufacturing Company 401(k) Plan, a defined contribution plan with approximately $340 million in assets covering 2,800 participants. In January 2019, Margaret attended a conference on sustainable investing and became enthusiastic about integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria into the plan's investment lineup. She subsequently directed the plan's investment consultant, Ridgeline Advisory Group, to replace four of the plan's twelve core investment options with ESG-themed alternatives.

Specifically, Margaret instructed Ridgeline to replace the plan's S&P 500 index fund (expense ratio: 0.03%, 10-year annualized return: 13.2%) with the Verdant Global ESG Leaders Fund (expense ratio: 0.72%, 10-year annualized return: 11.4%); the plan's mid-cap value fund (expense ratio: 0.18%, 10-year annualized return: 10.8%) with the SustainEquity Mid-Cap Impact Fund (expense ratio: 0.85%, 10-year annualized return: 9.1%); and two fixed-income options with ESG-screened bond funds that carried higher expense ratios and slightly lower yields. The total incremental annual cost to plan participants from these substitutions was estimated at approximately $1.9 million.

Ridgeline Advisory Group prepared an investment analysis for the committee that flagged the performance differential and higher fees of the ESG replacement funds. The analysis noted that while certain ESG factors could be material to long-term risk assessment, the specific funds selected were primarily marketed based on their alignment with social and environmental objectives, not superior risk-adjusted returns. Margaret nonetheless persuaded three of the five committee members to approve the changes, stating in the recorded committee meeting minutes from March 15, 2019: 'Our company has a responsibility to invest in a way that reflects our corporate sustainability values, and this plan should be no different. These funds align with who we are as a company.'

Two committee members, David Park and Susan Lehman, dissented, noting that the committee's duty was to plan participants, not to corporate branding. No participant survey was conducted, and no documentation was created analyzing whether the ESG factors embedded in the replacement funds presented material economic risks or opportunities that would justify their selection on a purely financial basis. The committee did not evaluate whether the ESG funds were economically equivalent or superior to the existing options.
question: Did Margaret Hollister and the Greenfield Manufacturing 401(k) Plan Investment Committee breach their ERISA fiduciary duties by replacing existing plan investment options with higher-cost, lower-performing ESG-themed funds based on the company's corporate sustainability values?
answer:
Yes. Margaret Hollister and the concurring committee members breached their fiduciary duties under ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) and (B). The analysis follows.

Under ERISA §404(a)(1)(A), fiduciaries must discharge their duties solely in the interest of plan participants and beneficiaries and for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits and defraying reasonable plan expenses. Under §404(a)(1)(B), fiduciaries must act with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence of a prudent person acting in a like capacity — the so-called 'prudent expert' standard.

As DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2018-01 makes clear, the Department's longstanding position — reiterated in Interpretive Bulletin 2015-01 (29 CFR §2509.2015-01) — is that ERISA fiduciaries are not permitted to sacrifice investment return or take on additional investment risk as a means of promoting collateral social policy goals. FAB 2018-01 clarified that ESG factors may be considered when they present material business risks or opportunities that qualified investment professionals would treat as economic considerations under generally accepted investment theories. In such cases, ESG factors are appropriate economic considerations — not mere tie-breakers. However, the bulletin explicitly cautioned against treating ESG considerations as standalone justifications for investment selection absent a documented economic rationale.

Here, the facts demonstrate multiple violations. First, the committee's stated rationale — aligning investments with corporate sustainability values — is a textbook example of promoting collateral social policy goals in violation of ERISA's exclusive purpose and sole interest requirements. Margaret's recorded statement that 'this plan should reflect who we are as a company' evidences loyalty to corporate identity rather than to participants. Second, the replacement funds carried demonstrably higher expense ratios (0.72% vs. 0.03% for the large-cap option; 0.85% vs. 0.18% for mid-cap) and lower historical returns, resulting in an estimated $1.9 million annual cost increase to participants. Third, the committee failed to document any analysis showing that ESG-specific factors in the selected funds presented material economic risks or opportunities justifying their selection on purely financial grounds. Ridgeline's own analysis flagged that the funds were marketed primarily on social and environmental alignment, not risk-adjusted economic merit. Fourth, the ESG funds were not shown to be economically equivalent to existing options — which would be the minimum threshold for the tie-breaker analysis permitted under IB 2015-01.

The dissent of Park and Lehman does not insulate the committee; fiduciary liability under ERISA §405(a) can attach to co-fiduciaries who participate in a known breach. However, their documented dissent would likely mitigate their individual exposure. Margaret and the three concurring members face potential personal liability for plan losses under ERISA §409(a). The absence of any documented economic analysis is particularly damaging, as it defeats any procedural prudence defense under the framework established in Tibble v. Edison International, 575 U.S. 523 (2015).
applicable_standard: ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) (duty of loyalty/exclusive purpose); ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) (duty of prudence); 29 CFR §2509.2015-01 (IB 2015-01 on ETIs/ESG); DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2018-01; ERISA §405(a) (co-fiduciary liability); ERISA §409(a) (liability for breach)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The committee selected higher-cost, lower-performing ESG funds based on corporate sustainability values rather than documented economic analysis demonstrating material financial benefits to plan participants, directly violating ERISA's sole interest and exclusive purpose requirements.

fact_pattern:
Pinnacle HR Solutions, Inc. is a professional employer organization (PEO) based in Columbus, Ohio, that sponsors the Pinnacle HR Solutions Multiple Employer 401(k) Plan (EIN 31-1234567, PN 002). The plan has been in operation since 2012 and, as of the 2016 plan year, covered approximately 3,200 participants across 47 small-business client employers. Total plan assets as of December 31, 2016 were approximately $84.3 million, and total contributions for the 2016 plan year were $11.7 million.

Margaret Hollis, the plan administrator and Pinnacle's Vice President of Benefits, was responsible for the annual Form 5500 filings. For the 2014 plan year — the first year ERISA §103(g) took effect — Margaret checked the multiple employer plan box on Part I, Line A of the Form 5500 but did not attach the required list of participating employers with their EINs and good faith estimates of each employer's percentage of total contributions. She followed the same deficient filing practice for the 2015 and 2016 plan years. Margaret was aware of the check-box language added by the November 2014 interim final rule referencing the participating employer attachment, but believed that because Pinnacle was the sole 'sponsor' and the individual client employers were merely co-employers under the PEO arrangement, the attachment requirement did not apply to Pinnacle's plan structure.

In early 2019, EBSA's enforcement division sent Pinnacle a correspondence identifying the deficiencies in the plan's 2014, 2015, and 2016 Form 5500 filings. Margaret contacted outside ERISA counsel, who advised her that the plan was clearly a MEP subject to §103(g) and that the omission of participating employer information for three consecutive plan years exposed Pinnacle to potential civil penalties under ERISA §502(c)(2) of up to $250 per day for each day of non-compliance. Counsel estimated potential aggregate penalty exposure exceeding $273,750 per filing year. Margaret immediately prepared corrected attachments for 2014–2016, listing all 47 participating employers by name, EIN, and contribution percentages, and filed amended Forms 5500 on March 15, 2019.

Pinnacle now seeks to invoke the transitional penalty relief described in FAB 2019-01 for its deficient filings for the 2016 plan year and prior years, arguing that its prompt corrective action and amended filings satisfy the conditions for relief.
question: Did Pinnacle HR Solutions' failure to include participating employer information on its Form 5500 filings for the 2014–2016 plan years violate ERISA §103(g), and is the plan eligible for the transitional penalty relief outlined in DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2019-01?
answer:
Pinnacle HR Solutions was clearly in violation of ERISA §103(g) for each of the three plan years at issue. Section 103(g), added by the CSEC Act (Pub. L. No. 113-97, §104(c)) and effective for plan years beginning after December 31, 2013, requires that the annual report for any multiple employer plan include (1) a list of participating employers and (2) a good faith estimate of the percentage of total contributions made by each participating employer during the plan year. The DOL's November 2014 interim final rule (79 Fed. Reg. 66617) implemented these requirements by adding specific instructions to the Form 5500, requiring an attachment labeled 'Multiple-Employer Plan Participating Employer Information' listing each participating employer by name and EIN with estimated contribution percentages.

Margaret Hollis's belief that the PEO-sponsored plan was exempt because Pinnacle was the sole 'sponsor' is legally incorrect. The Form 5500 instructions define a 'participating employer' as any employer who was obligated to make contributions, actually made contributions, or whose employees were covered under the plan. All 47 client employers clearly met this definition. PEO-sponsored MEPs are specifically identified in FAB 2019-01 as among those found to be non-compliant, confirming the DOL's position that PEO arrangements do not exempt plans from §103(g).

The penalty exposure is significant. Under ERISA §502(c)(2), the administrator of a plan who fails to file a complete and accurate annual report may be subject to a penalty of up to $250 per day. For three years of deficient filings, this could yield substantial aggregate penalties.

However, FAB 2019-01 provides transitional penalty relief for MEPs that failed to file complete and accurate participating employer lists for the 2017 plan year and before. Pinnacle's deficient filings cover 2014–2016, which fall squarely within the covered period. The bulletin was designed to address precisely the widespread non-compliance EBSA identified among MEP filers, including PEO-sponsored plans. By filing corrected amended Forms 5500 with complete participating employer information on March 15, 2019 — prior to any formal penalty assessment — Pinnacle has taken the type of corrective action contemplated by the transitional relief.

In conclusion, while Pinnacle violated ERISA §103(g) for three consecutive plan years, it is likely eligible for the transitional penalty relief under FAB 2019-01, provided it achieves full prospective compliance beginning with the 2018 plan year filing. EBSA expects full compliance going forward, and any future deficiency would not receive similar relief.
applicable_standard: ERISA §103(g); CSEC Act (Pub. L. No. 113-97, §104(c)); DOL Interim Final Rule, 79 Fed. Reg. 66617 (Nov. 10, 2014); ERISA §502(c)(2); DOL Field Assistance Bulletin No. 2019-01; 29 CFR 2520.104-44; Form 5500 Instructions Part I, Line A
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Pinnacle failed to attach the required list of participating employers with EINs and contribution percentages to its Form 5500 filings for three consecutive plan years, but the deficiencies fall within the pre-2018 transitional relief period established by FAB 2019-01.

fact_pattern:
Heritage Financial Partners, LLC is a mid-sized broker-dealer and registered investment adviser headquartered in Dallas, Texas. In March 2017, the firm's Chief Compliance Officer, Rachel Dominguez, spearheaded a $2.4 million compliance overhaul to prepare for the DOL Fiduciary Rule's applicability date of June 9, 2017. The firm built out a comprehensive compliance infrastructure including: (1) a proprietary conflict-of-interest disclosure platform that generated individualized BIC Exemption-compliant disclosures for each client transaction; (2) revised compensation grids that eliminated sales contests, quotas, and differential compensation incentives that could bias product recommendations; (3) a centralized product review committee that screened available investment products against impartial conduct standards, specifically evaluating whether recommendations were in the 'best interest' of retirement investors, whether compensation was reasonable, and whether communications were not misleading; and (4) mandatory annual training for all 87 registered representatives on fiduciary obligations under the expanded definition.

On May 7, 2018, following the Fifth Circuit's vacatur of the DOL Fiduciary Rule in Chamber of Commerce v. DOL, Heritage's senior management convened an emergency meeting. Dominguez presented two options: immediately revert to pre-rule practices and rely solely on pre-existing PTEs (such as PTE 84-24 in its unamended form), or continue operating under the compliance structures built for the BIC Exemption and impartial conduct standards. After reviewing FAB 2018-02, the firm elected to maintain all BIC Exemption compliance structures and continued to apply the impartial conduct standards to all retirement account recommendations.

Between June 2018 and February 2019, Heritage representative Mark Ellison recommended that 62-year-old client Patricia Langford, a retired school administrator with a $485,000 traditional IRA, roll over her funds from a low-cost 403(b) plan into a managed IRA account invested primarily in a diversified portfolio of mutual funds and a variable annuity rider providing guaranteed lifetime income. The variable annuity carried a 1.35% M&E charge and a 6-year surrender schedule. Ellison documented the recommendation rationale, disclosed all compensation (including the 4.5% front-end load he received, totaling approximately $8,700), provided Langford with a written best interest disclosure, and memorialized that the guaranteed income feature addressed her expressed concern about outliving her savings given her family history of longevity. Heritage's product review committee had previously approved the variable annuity for suitability within retirement portfolios for investors within five years of retirement with documented income protection needs.

In October 2019, during a routine DOL audit of Heritage's IRA rollover practices, an EBSA investigator flagged Ellison's recommendation to Langford as a potential prohibited transaction under ERISA §406(b) and IRC §4975(c)(1)(D)-(F), given the conflicted compensation Ellison received. The investigator questioned whether adequate exemptive relief covered the transaction following the Fifth Circuit's vacatur of the BIC Exemption.
question: Was Heritage Financial Partners protected from DOL prohibited transaction enforcement with respect to Ellison's recommendation to Langford, given that the firm continued applying BIC Exemption impartial conduct standards after the Fifth Circuit vacated the DOL Fiduciary Rule?
answer:
Yes, Heritage Financial Partners was protected under the temporary enforcement policy announced in FAB 2018-02. The analysis turns on whether Heritage satisfies the conditions articulated in that bulletin for the post-vacatur period.

FAB 2018-02 established that, for the period from June 9, 2017, until after the DOL issues new regulations, exemptions, or other administrative guidance, the Department will not pursue prohibited transaction claims against investment advice fiduciaries who are 'working diligently and in good faith to comply with the impartial conduct standards for transactions that would have been exempted in the BIC Exemption and Principal Transactions Exemption.' The bulletin explicitly recognized that some financial institutions had 'devoted significant resources to comply with the BIC Exemption' and 'may prefer to continue to rely upon the new compliance structures,' and that disrupting these arrangements could harm retirement investors.

Heritage demonstrably meets every element of this enforcement safe harbor. First, the firm invested $2.4 million in building compliance infrastructure specifically designed to satisfy the BIC Exemption requirements, including conflict-of-interest disclosures, reformed compensation structures, a product review committee, and representative training — all hallmarks of diligent, good-faith compliance. Second, after the Fifth Circuit vacatur, Heritage affirmatively elected to maintain these structures rather than reverting to less protective pre-rule practices, which is precisely the conduct FAB 2018-02 sought to encourage. Third, the specific transaction at issue — Ellison's recommendation involving conflicted compensation on the variable annuity — is the type of transaction that would have been covered by the BIC Exemption under Section IX(d)(1) of PTE 2016-01 (81 FR 44773), which required that recommendations be in the retirement investor's best interest, compensation be reasonable, and statements not be misleading.

Ellison's conduct satisfies the impartial conduct standards: the recommendation was documented with a client-specific rationale tied to Langford's longevity concern and income needs; all compensation was disclosed in writing; the product had been vetted by the firm's review committee for suitability in retirement portfolios for near-retirees; and the 4.5% load and 1.35% M&E charge, while not the lowest-cost option available, were within reasonable ranges for a product delivering a guaranteed lifetime income benefit that addressed an articulated client need.

The DOL investigator's concern under ERISA §406(b) and IRC §4975(c)(1)(D)-(F) regarding conflicted compensation is precisely the type of prohibited transaction that the BIC Exemption was designed to exempt, and FAB 2018-02 extends enforcement relief to such transactions during the interim period. Heritage need not prove that a formal exemption technically applies post-vacatur; rather, the enforcement policy itself provides the protective umbrella so long as good-faith compliance with impartial conduct standards is demonstrated. Heritage clearly meets this threshold, and the DOL should not pursue an enforcement action.
applicable_standard: DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2018-02; ERISA §406(b); IRC §4975(c)(1)(D)-(F); BIC Exemption (PTE 2016-01) Section IX(d)(1), 81 FR 44773 (impartial conduct standards); Principal Transactions Exemption Section VII(d)(1), 81 FR 44784; 29 CFR 2510.3-21 (pre- and post-vacatur fiduciary definition)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Heritage's affirmative decision to maintain its BIC Exemption compliance infrastructure and continue applying the impartial conduct standards in good faith after the Fifth Circuit vacatur placed the firm squarely within the protective scope of FAB 2018-02's temporary enforcement policy.

fact_pattern:
In March 2017, Robert Calloway, a registered representative with Pinnacle Financial Partners, LLC, a broker-dealer and insurance agency based in Dallas, Texas, was contacted by Margaret Dunleavy, a 62-year-old recently retired schoolteacher from Irving, Texas. Margaret had accumulated $485,000 in a 403(b) plan through the Irving Independent School District and wanted guidance on her options. Robert met with Margaret at his office on March 22, 2017, and during the meeting recommended she roll her entire 403(b) balance into a new IRA at Pinnacle, and then invest the proceeds into a fixed indexed annuity issued by Southwest Heritage Life Insurance Company, the 'Heritage Growth Plus 10' product. The annuity carried a 10-year surrender period with a declining surrender charge starting at 9%, a 1.25% annual spread charge, and a 2.5% participation rate cap on the S&P 500 index. Pinnacle would receive a 7% upfront commission ($33,950) on the annuity sale, paid by Southwest Heritage Life. Margaret's existing 403(b) plan offered a menu of low-cost target-date funds with expense ratios averaging 0.12%, and she was eligible to leave her money in the plan post-retirement with continued access to those institutional share classes.

Robert did not perform a written comparison of Margaret's existing 403(b) investment options versus the proposed IRA rollover. He did not document why the rollover was in Margaret's best interest, nor did he disclose that his compensation on the fixed indexed annuity was approximately six times what he would earn if Margaret remained in the 403(b) or chose a fee-based IRA advisory account. Robert's internal notes stated only: 'Client wants guaranteed income and protection from market downside. Recommended Heritage Growth Plus 10 FIA.' Margaret signed the annuity application and rollover paperwork on April 5, 2017.

Pinnacle's compliance department had adopted a policy in early 2017, in anticipation of the DOL Fiduciary Rule's phased implementation beginning June 9, 2017, requiring advisers to document a reasonable basis for rollover recommendations and to provide a cost comparison. However, Robert completed the transaction before the June 9 applicability date. The DOL Fiduciary Rule was ultimately vacated by the Fifth Circuit in Chamber of Commerce v. DOL in March 2018, but Pinnacle's internal policy remained nominally in effect. Margaret later discovered the high surrender charges when she needed funds for an unexpected medical procedure in 2019 and faced a $29,175 surrender penalty.
question: Did Robert Calloway's recommendation that Margaret Dunleavy roll her 403(b) into an IRA to purchase a fixed indexed annuity violate applicable fiduciary or suitability obligations, and what is the regulatory significance of the Fifth Circuit's vacatur of the 2016 DOL Fiduciary Rule to this analysis?
answer:
Robert Calloway's conduct raises serious compliance concerns under multiple overlapping frameworks, though the precise legal exposure depends on the applicable regulatory regime at the time of the transaction and the survival of certain internal firm policies.

First, regarding the 2016 DOL Fiduciary Rule: The transaction occurred on April 5, 2017, before the Rule's initial applicability date of June 9, 2017. Even under the phased implementation schedule, the full Best Interest Contract Exemption (BIC Exemption) conditions—including the requirement to act in the client's best interest, provide cost disclosures, and avoid misleading statements in connection with IRA rollover recommendations—had not yet taken legal effect. Moreover, the Fifth Circuit in Chamber of Commerce of the United States v. DOL, No. 17-10238 (5th Cir. Mar. 15, 2018), vacated the entire Fiduciary Rule package, finding that DOL had overreached its statutory authority under ERISA and the Internal Revenue Code by redefining 'investment advice fiduciary' in a manner inconsistent with the five-part test under 29 C.F.R. § 2510.3-21 and by imposing legally unauthorized contract terms. The vacatur means the 2016 Rule cannot serve as an independent basis for liability.

However, Robert's conduct is not absolved. Under the pre-2016 regulatory framework, the rollover recommendation to an IRA was not treated as fiduciary advice under ERISA because IRAs are not Title I plans (they fall under IRC § 4975). But FINRA suitability obligations under Rule 2111 (and now Reg BI under SEC Rule 15l-1, effective June 30, 2020, though not yet applicable here) still governed. Under FINRA Rule 2111, the recommendation had to be suitable considering Margaret's investment profile, including her age, liquidity needs, risk tolerance, time horizon, and existing holdings. A 10-year surrender period with a 9% initial surrender charge for a 62-year-old retiree who might need liquidity presents a significant suitability red flag. The failure to document any comparison of the 403(b) plan's low-cost institutional funds versus the high-commission FIA, and the failure to consider the cost differential, would likely constitute a violation of FINRA Rule 2111's reasonable-basis and customer-specific suitability components.

Additionally, Pinnacle's own internal compliance policy—adopted in anticipation of the DOL Rule—required rollover documentation and cost comparisons. Even after the Rule's vacatur, FINRA and state regulators routinely hold firms accountable for following their own written supervisory procedures. Robert's failure to comply with the firm's internal policy could support a FINRA Rule 3110 supervisory violation against the firm and a separate violation by Robert for disregarding established procedures.

The pivotal compliance failure is Robert's complete lack of documentation showing the rollover and annuity were in Margaret's interest relative to her existing low-cost 403(b) options, compounded by the undisclosed compensation differential that created an acute conflict of interest.
applicable_standard: ERISA §§ 3(21), 404(a)(1)(A)-(B), 406(b)(3); 29 C.F.R. § 2510.3-21 (pre-2016 five-part test); IRC § 4975(e)(3); FINRA Rules 2111 (Suitability), 2232 (Customer Account Statements), 3110 (Supervision); Chamber of Commerce v. DOL, No. 17-10238 (5th Cir. 2018); Pinnacle Financial Partners internal WSPs regarding rollover documentation
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Robert failed to document any reasonable basis or cost comparison for recommending the rollover from a low-cost 403(b) into a high-commission, illiquid fixed indexed annuity, creating an undisclosed compensation-driven conflict in violation of FINRA suitability requirements and the firm's own written supervisory procedures.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Whitfield is a registered representative of Clearpoint Financial Services, a dual-registered broker-dealer and RIA based in Charlotte, North Carolina. In March 2016, shortly before the DOL's final fiduciary rule was published in April 2016, Marcus contacted Linda Okafor, a 58-year-old middle school teacher who was preparing to retire from the Wake County Public School System after 30 years of service. Linda had accumulated $410,000 in her employer-sponsored 403(b) plan, which was invested in a diversified mix of low-cost Vanguard target-date funds with an all-in expense ratio of 0.12%. Linda also had a modest traditional IRA with $35,000 at Fidelity, invested in index funds.

Marcus, who had obtained Linda's contact information through a retirement seminar he hosted at a local hotel, met with her and recommended she roll her entire $410,000 403(b) balance into a new IRA at Clearpoint. He told Linda that consolidating her retirement assets would 'simplify her financial life' and give her access to 'institutional-quality investment management.' He recommended allocating the rollover IRA into a combination of Class A mutual funds with 5.25% front-end loads and two variable annuities — a Jackson National Perspective II ($150,000) and an Allianz Benefit Control ($100,000) — each carrying surrender periods of seven and nine years respectively, mortality and expense charges of 1.35%, and optional living benefit riders adding another 1.10% annually. Marcus's total first-year compensation from the rollover would be approximately $18,700 in commissions and trail fees.

Marcus did not perform or document any comparative analysis of the costs, investment options, or services available in Linda's existing 403(b) plan versus the proposed IRA. He did not disclose the specific dollar amount of his compensation, nor did he explain that Linda's existing plan investments had substantially lower fees.
