This scenario presents a likely ERISA fiduciary breach, though the outcome depends on the evolving and currently divergent case law on forfeiture allocation.

First, regarding the prohibited transaction claim under ERISA §406(a)(1)(D), plaintiffs allege that using plan assets (forfeitures) to reduce the employer's own contribution obligation constitutes a transfer of plan assets for the benefit of a party in interest (the employer). Several district courts have rejected this theory, reasoning that forfeitures used to offset employer contributions are expressly contemplated by IRS regulations (Treas. Reg. §1.401-7(a)) and standard plan design, and thus do not constitute a prohibited transaction. However, the claim gains traction where, as here, the fiduciary exercises discretion exclusively to benefit the employer without any documented consideration of participant welfare.

Second, and more critically, the exclusive purpose rule under ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) requires that fiduciaries discharge their duties solely in the interest of participants and beneficiaries and for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits and defraying reasonable plan expenses. The key vulnerability for Hargrove is the complete absence of a prudent process. Where a plan document grants discretion among multiple permissible uses of forfeitures, courts have increasingly held that the exercise of that discretion is itself a fiduciary act subject to ERISA's fiduciary standards. Hargrove's email stating that the company needed to "keep our contribution costs down" due to "margin pressure" is powerful evidence that the decision was motivated by employer interests rather than participant welfare — directly implicating the exclusive purpose rule.

The anti-inurement provision under §403(c)(1) provides that plan assets shall never inure to the benefit of any employer except under narrow exceptions. While an argument exists that forfeiture reversion via contribution offsets is not technically "inurement" because contributions were still made, the systematic and unanalyzed diversion of $9.2 million over three years strengthens plaintiffs' position.

Hargrove's primary defense — that the plan document authorized this use — is insufficient. ERISA fiduciary obligations are imposed by statute and cannot be waived by plan documents. The fact that the Plan document listed three permissible uses imposed a fiduciary obligation to evaluate which use best served participants. The 18% increase in recordkeeping fees flagged by Mark Tyson in 2023 makes the failure to even consider using forfeitures to defray plan expenses particularly damaging. Under Hughes v. Northwestern University's framework, courts must give "due regard to the range of reasonable judgments a fiduciary may make," but that deference presupposes an actual deliberative process — which is entirely absent here.

The fiduciaries are likely to be found in violation of ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) and potentially §406(a)(1)(D), with the lack of any documented process being the decisive factor.
applicable_standard: ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) (exclusive purpose/prudent process); ERISA §406(a)(1)(D) (prohibited transactions with parties in interest); ERISA §403(c)(1) (anti-inurement); Hughes v. Northwestern University, 595 U.S. 170 (2022); Treas. Reg. §1.401-7(a)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The Plan fiduciary exercised discretion to allocate 100% of $9.2 million in forfeitures to offset employer contributions without any documented analysis of alternative uses or consideration of participant interests, motivated by corporate cost pressures rather than participant welfare.

fact_pattern: Meridian Capital Advisors LLC is an SEC-registered investment adviser headquartered in Miami, Florida, with approximately $4.2 billion in assets under management. The firm specializes in serving high-net-worth Latin American clients and family offices, primarily from Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, and Argentina. In March 2023, Meridian's managing director, Ricardo Fuentes, traveled to São Paulo, Brazil, to attend a private wealth conference. During the trip, Fuentes met with 14 prospective Brazilian investors, including the Oliveira Family Office (with approximately $85 million in investable assets) and three institutional investors affiliated with Brazilian pension funds. At these meetings, Fuentes distributed detailed marketing materials describing Meridian's model portfolios, fee structures (a 1.25% annual advisory fee on assets under management), and performance track records. The materials were printed in Portuguese and included specific references to three U.S.-domiciled mutual funds that Meridian frequently recommends—Vanguard Total Stock Market Index Fund, PIMCO Income Fund, and a Dechert-advised offshore Cayman-domiciled feeder fund structured under Regulation S. Fuentes collected signed advisory agreements from six of the prospective clients during his São Paulo meetings, including the Oliveira Family Office, without conducting any suitability analysis or obtaining information about their investment objectives, risk tolerance, or financial circumstances prior to execution. The agreements contained no disclosures regarding the applicability of U.S. fiduciary obligations, no Form ADV Part 2A brochure was delivered, and no mention was made of potential conflicts of interest arising from Meridian's receipt of revenue-sharing payments from two of the three recommended funds. Additionally, Meridian did not evaluate whether its solicitation activities in Brazil required registration with the Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (CVM), Brazil's securities regulator, or whether the in-person meetings and distribution of Portuguese-language marketing materials in São Paulo constituted 'directed selling efforts' under Regulation S. Meridian's chief compliance officer, Angela Torres, was not informed of Fuentes's client solicitation activities in Brazil until after the agreements were signed and assets were being transferred to Meridian's custodian at Pershing LLC.
question: Did Meridian Capital Advisors and Ricardo Fuentes comply with applicable U.S. investment adviser regulations and cross-border regulatory requirements in soliciting and onboarding Brazilian clients during the São Paulo trip?
answer:
Meridian Capital Advisors and Ricardo Fuentes committed multiple serious compliance violations spanning U.S. federal investment adviser regulation, securities offering rules, and cross-border regulatory obligations.

First, under Section 206 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, a registered investment adviser owes a fiduciary duty to all clients—including non-U.S. clients—once a client relationship is established. The SEC has consistently taken the position that once registered, a U.S.-based adviser must comply with the full panoply of U.S. investment adviser regulations with respect to both U.S. and non-U.S. clients. By executing advisory agreements with six Brazilian clients without first conducting any suitability or know-your-customer analysis, Meridian breached its fiduciary duty. The suitability obligation requires that an adviser obtain sufficient information about a client's investment objectives, financial situation, and risk tolerance before making recommendations, as outlined in SEC guidance and the duty of care component of the fiduciary standard under Sections 206(1) and 206(2).

Second, Meridian violated Rule 204-3 under the Advisers Act by failing to deliver Form ADV Part 2A brochures to the prospective clients before or at the time of entering into advisory agreements. This rule requires delivery no later than the time of entering into the advisory contract, and this obligation applies regardless of the client's domicile.

Third, the failure to disclose revenue-sharing arrangements with two of the three recommended funds constitutes a material omission under Section 206(2), which prohibits any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit upon any client. Revenue-sharing creates a direct conflict of interest that must be disclosed prominently.

Fourth, Fuentes's in-person solicitation in São Paulo, distribution of Portuguese-language marketing materials targeting Brazilian investors, and execution of advisory agreements on Brazilian soil raise significant concerns under Regulation S of the Securities Act. The distribution of fund-specific marketing materials in-country likely constitutes 'directed selling efforts' under Rule 902(c), potentially jeopardizing any Regulation S safe harbor for the Cayman feeder fund offering.

Fifth, Meridian failed to assess whether its activities triggered registration or licensing requirements with the CVM, Brazil's securities regulator, which generally requires that entities providing advisory services to Brazilian residents be locally registered or operate under an applicable exemption.

Finally, the CCO's lack of awareness of Fuentes's activities reflects a failure of supervisory procedures under Rule 206(4)-7 of the Advisers Act, which requires advisers to adopt and implement written compliance policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations. The firm's compliance infrastructure failed to capture or pre-approve cross-border solicitation activity, a critical control for firms serving Latin American clients.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Sections 206(1), 206(2), 206(4); Rule 204-3 (brochure delivery); Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance procedures); Securities Act Regulation S, Rules 901-905 (offshore transactions and directed selling efforts); FINRA Rules 2111 (suitability), 3110 (supervision); CVM regulations governing cross-border advisory services to Brazilian residents
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Meridian executed advisory agreements with Brazilian clients during in-person meetings in São Paulo without conducting suitability analysis, delivering required disclosures, or disclosing material conflicts of interest, while failing to evaluate local regulatory requirements—all in violation of the firm's fiduciary obligations under the Advisers Act.

fact_pattern:
Greenleaf Wealth Partners LLC is a dually registered firm — registered as both an investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and as a broker-dealer with FINRA. Marcus Holloway, a 58-year-old representative of Greenleaf, holds both Series 7 and Series 66 licenses. In March 2023, Holloway onboarded a new client, Dorothy Kessler, a 72-year-old retired schoolteacher with a $1.2 million IRA rollover from her former employer's 403(b) plan and approximately $340,000 in a taxable brokerage account. Kessler's stated investment objectives were capital preservation and income generation, with a moderate risk tolerance. She told Holloway during their initial meeting that she relied on this money to fund her retirement living expenses of approximately $5,800 per month.

Holloway opened a discretionary advisory account for Kessler's IRA assets under Greenleaf's wrap-fee advisory program, charging an annual fee of 1.45% on assets under management. For the taxable brokerage account, however, Holloway recommended a commission-based arrangement and characterized the relationship as a standard brokerage account subject to Reg BI rather than a fiduciary standard. During the first six months, Holloway made 47 trades in the brokerage account, generating $28,400 in commissions — an annualized cost-to-equity ratio of approximately 16.7%. The trades consisted primarily of Class A mutual fund shares in aggressive growth funds and speculative small-cap equities, none of which aligned with Kessler's stated conservative objectives. Holloway did not document any change in Kessler's investment profile or risk tolerance, nor did he provide updated Form CRS or Reg BI disclosure at the point of any recommendation.

When Kessler's brokerage account declined by $67,000 (approximately 19.7%) over eight months, she complained to Greenleaf's chief compliance officer, Linda Matsuda. Matsuda reviewed the account but concluded that because the brokerage account was subject only to Reg BI — not the Advisers Act fiduciary standard — and the trades were individually suitable at the time of recommendation, no violation had occurred. Matsuda took no further action, did not escalate the complaint, and did not review whether the totality of Holloway's conduct might give rise to a de facto advisory relationship or fiduciary obligation under common law or the Advisers Act.
question: Did Holloway and Greenleaf violate their regulatory obligations — under both Reg BI and potential fiduciary duty standards — in their handling of Kessler's taxable brokerage account, and was Matsuda's compliance determination adequate?
answer:
Holloway and Greenleaf violated multiple regulatory obligations, and Matsuda's compliance determination was materially deficient.

First, under Regulation Best Interest (Exchange Act Rule 15l-1), a broker-dealer must act in the best interest of a retail customer at the time a recommendation is made, without placing the financial or other interest of the broker-dealer ahead of the customer's interest. Reg BI has four component obligations: Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance. Holloway failed the Care Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii)) because the aggressive growth funds and speculative small-cap equities were plainly inconsistent with Kessler's stated objectives of capital preservation and income generation and her moderate risk tolerance. While Reg BI evaluates recommendations at the point of each transaction, FINRA and SEC guidance make clear that a pattern of recommendations — here, 47 trades in six months with an annualized cost-to-equity ratio of 16.7% — can evidence excessive trading that is not in the customer's best interest. An annualized cost-to-equity ratio above 6% has historically been treated by FINRA arbitration panels and courts as presumptive evidence of churning or excessive trading, even under the old suitability standard of FINRA Rule 2111.

Second, Holloway failed the Disclosure Obligation (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i)) by not providing updated Form CRS or point-of-sale Reg BI disclosures with each new recommendation, particularly given the shift toward increasingly aggressive and speculative positions that conflicted with the documented investor profile.

Third, and critically, as Brodsky's chapter emphasizes, courts may look beyond the formal label of a relationship. Where a registered representative of a dually registered firm exercises de facto discretion, provides ongoing advice, and the customer reposes trust and confidence — as a 72-year-old retiree relying on these assets for living expenses clearly does — courts have found a fiduciary relationship exists under common law and potentially under Section 206 of the Investment Advisers Act. Holloway's pattern of continuous, unsolicited trading in Kessler's account without meaningful client direction is functionally indistinguishable from discretionary management, potentially elevating his duty to that of a fiduciary regardless of account documentation.

Finally, Matsuda's compliance review was inadequate under FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision), which requires member firms to establish and maintain a system to supervise the activities of each associated person that is reasonably designed to achieve compliance. Dismissing the complaint solely because the account was labeled as brokerage — without examining the totality of the trading pattern, the cost-to-equity ratio, or whether a de facto advisory relationship had formed — constitutes a supervision failure. The firm's Compliance Obligation under Reg BI (Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iv)) independently required written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with the Care and Disclosure Obligations, which plainly were not followed here.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest (Exchange Act Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i)-(iv)); Investment Advisers Act §206; FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); SEC Form CRS (Rule 17a-14)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Holloway executed 47 commission-generating trades with a 16.7% annualized cost-to-equity ratio in speculative securities directly contrary to a 72-year-old retiree's documented conservative objectives, while the firm's compliance officer failed to evaluate the trading pattern or the potential existence of a de facto fiduciary relationship.

fact_pattern:
Pinnacle Fund Advisors, LLC is a registered investment adviser that serves as the investment adviser to the Pinnacle Growth Equity Fund and the Pinnacle Balanced Income Fund, both open-end mutual funds registered on Form N-1A. The funds collectively have approximately $4.2 billion in assets under management and roughly 85,000 retail shareholders. Sarah Whitfield, Pinnacle's Chief Compliance Officer, was aware of the SEC's October 2022 adoption of rule and form amendments requiring tailored shareholder reports and the July 24, 2024 compliance date.

For the fiscal year ending September 30, 2024, Pinnacle transmitted annual shareholder reports to all fund shareholders in November 2024. However, rather than adopting the new concise and visually engaging format required by the Final Rules, Pinnacle continued to use its legacy shareholder report format — a 42-page document dense with technical financial tables, lengthy management discussion sections, and no graphical representations of key performance data. The reports did not include the required new broad-based securities market index comparison, instead continuing to benchmark solely against the Russell 1000 Growth Index for the Growth Equity Fund and a custom blended index for the Balanced Income Fund, neither of which qualified as a broad-based securities market index under the amended requirements. Additionally, Pinnacle did not make the information removed from the concise reports (such as detailed financial statements and fund holdings) available online as required by the layered disclosure framework.

When questioned by a FINRA examiner during a routine sweep examination in January 2025, Whitfield explained that Pinnacle's fund accounting vendor had experienced system migration delays and that the firm had made a business judgment to prioritize accuracy over format compliance. She noted that shareholders received all the same substantive information they had always received — indeed more information than the new tailored format would require — and argued that no investor was harmed. Pinnacle had not filed any request for exemptive relief or no-action guidance, nor had it disclosed the non-compliance to the funds' boards of trustees.
question: Did Pinnacle Fund Advisors violate the SEC's tailored shareholder report requirements by transmitting legacy-format annual reports for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2024, and does the firm's argument that shareholders received more information than required constitute a valid defense?
answer:
Pinnacle Fund Advisors is non-compliant with the SEC's Final Rules adopted in Release No. IC-34731 (October 26, 2022), which amended Form N-1A, Rule 30e-1, and related provisions under the Investment Company Act of 1940 to require tailored shareholder reports. The compliance date was July 24, 2024, meaning any shareholder reports transmitted after that date must conform to the new requirements regardless of when the fiscal period began.

First, the Final Rules require funds registered on Form N-1A to transmit concise and visually engaging annual and semi-annual shareholder reports highlighting key information the SEC determined best helps investors assess and monitor their investments. Pinnacle's continued use of the 42-page legacy format directly contravenes the amended Form N-1A requirements for report content and presentation. The SEC explicitly designed the new framework to replace lengthy, complex, and technical disclosure with streamlined graphical presentations — Pinnacle's approach is the antithesis of what the amendments require.

Second, the Final Rules require many funds to adopt a new broad-based securities market index for performance comparison purposes. Pinnacle's continued exclusive use of the Russell 1000 Growth Index (a style-specific index) and a custom blended index fails to satisfy this requirement. The amendments were designed to improve comparability across funds by requiring a broad-based benchmark.

Third, the layered disclosure framework requires funds to make available online certain detailed information (financial statements, complete portfolio holdings) that was removed from the concise report format. Pinnacle failed to establish this online availability, breaking the layered disclosure chain that the SEC considers integral to the new regime.

Pinnacle's defense — that shareholders received more information, not less — is unavailing. The SEC's rulemaking was explicitly premised on investor feedback that overly dense, technical reports obscure rather than illuminate key fund information. The Final Rules reflect a regulatory judgment that more information is not necessarily better disclosure. Providing excessive technical detail without the mandated concise format and visual presentation frustrates the regulatory purpose and violates the specific form and content requirements.

The vendor delay explanation, while potentially relevant as a mitigating factor in an enforcement context, does not excuse non-compliance. Pinnacle had 18 months to prepare and failed to seek exemptive relief under Section 6(c) of the Investment Company Act or SEC staff no-action guidance. The failure to disclose the non-compliance to the funds' boards of trustees further compounds the issue, as fund directors have oversight responsibilities regarding regulatory compliance. This represents a clear violation of the amended rules under the Investment Company Act of 1940 and Form N-1A.
applicable_standard: Investment Company Act of 1940 §30(e); Rule 30e-1 thereunder; Form N-1A (as amended); Release No. IC-34731 (Oct. 26, 2022); Securities Act of 1933 Rule 482 (fee presentation in advertisements); Investment Company Act §6(c) (exemptive relief)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Pinnacle transmitted legacy-format shareholder reports after the July 24, 2024 compliance date without adopting the required concise, visually engaging tailored format, the new broad-based securities market index, or the online layered disclosure framework.

fact_pattern:
Wefea Capital LLC is a state-registered investment adviser based in New York with approximately $85 million in regulatory assets under management. Hariharan Iyer serves as the firm's principal, sole portfolio manager, and Chief Compliance Officer. The firm adopted its Investment Advisor Compliance Policy Manual on January 25, 2021, which contains policies on rendering suitable investment advice, conflicts of interest, trading, and supervision. Under Section 9 of the manual, the firm committed to assessing client investment objectives, risk tolerance, financial situation, and time horizon before making recommendations.

In March 2023, Wefea Capital onboarded Margaret Donnelly, a 72-year-old retired schoolteacher from Westchester County, New York, with a $1.2 million IRA rollover from TIAA. Mrs. Donnelly's signed client profile indicated conservative risk tolerance, an income-oriented investment objective, a 7-10 year time horizon, and limited investment experience beyond target-date retirement funds. Her annual income from Social Security and a small pension was approximately $48,000, and the IRA represented roughly 85% of her liquid net worth. The advisory agreement specified a 1.25% annual management fee and granted Wefea Capital discretionary authority over the account.

Between April and September 2023, Iyer allocated approximately 62% of Mrs. Donnelly's portfolio ($744,000) to a concentrated position in three micro-cap technology stocks—NovaTech Solutions (NVTS), Qubit Dynamics Inc. (QBDI), and FusionGrid Corp. (FSGC)—none of which paid dividends and all of which had market capitalizations below $200 million and beta values exceeding 1.8. An additional 18% ($216,000) was placed in a leveraged ETF tracking the NASDAQ-100 (ProShares UltraPro QQQ, ticker TQQQ). Only the remaining 20% was allocated to investment-grade bonds and a money market fund. By December 2023, the portfolio had declined approximately 38%, losing roughly $456,000 in value. Mrs. Donnelly's daughter, a CPA, reviewed the account statements and filed a written complaint with the firm in January 2024. Iyer, acting in his dual capacity as CCO and portfolio manager, reviewed and responded to the complaint himself, concluding that the allocations were appropriate given 'long-term growth potential.' No independent review of the complaint was conducted, and the complaint was not logged in a formal complaint register as contemplated by Section 8 of the compliance manual.
question: Did Wefea Capital LLC and Hariharan Iyer breach their fiduciary duty and internal compliance obligations under the Investment Advisers Act and the firm's own compliance manual with respect to the management of Margaret Donnelly's account?
answer:
Yes, Wefea Capital LLC and Hariharan Iyer committed multiple violations of both federal fiduciary standards and the firm's own compliance policies. The analysis proceeds on several grounds.

First, under Section 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, an investment adviser owes a fiduciary duty to its clients, which encompasses duties of care and loyalty. The duty of care requires that investment advice and portfolio management be suitable and in the client's best interest, considering the client's stated objectives, risk tolerance, financial circumstances, and time horizon. Allocating 62% of a 72-year-old conservative retiree's IRA—representing 85% of her liquid net worth—to speculative micro-cap equities with no income component, plus an additional 18% to a triple-leveraged ETF (TQQQ), is fundamentally incompatible with a conservative, income-oriented mandate. Leveraged ETFs like TQQQ are designed for short-term tactical trading and are widely recognized by regulators, including in FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 and SEC staff guidance, as unsuitable for long-term holding in retail retirement accounts due to compounding risk and volatility decay. This allocation pattern constitutes a breach of the duty of care under Section 206(2) and potentially a fraudulent or deceptive act under Section 206(1) given the magnitude of the departure from the client's documented profile.

Second, the firm's own compliance manual, Section 9 (Rendering Suitable Investment Advice), requires assessment of suitability factors prior to making investment decisions. The facts demonstrate that Iyer disregarded every documented suitability parameter. Under SEC and state regulatory expectations, an adviser's written policies and procedures adopted under Rule 206(4)-7 of the Advisers Act create an enforceable compliance framework; systematic deviation from those policies constitutes a violation of Rule 206(4)-7.

Third, the supervision structure is fatally compromised. Under Section 5.1 of the manual and Rule 206(4)-7, the CCO must provide independent oversight. Iyer's dual role as sole portfolio manager and CCO—without any independent compliance review mechanism—meant there was no meaningful supervisory check on his investment decisions. This structural deficiency is precisely the kind of inadequacy the SEC has cited in enforcement actions such as In re Sands Brothers Asset Management, LLC.

Fourth, Iyer's self-review and dismissal of Mrs. Donnelly's complaint, without independent escalation or formal logging as required by Section 8 of the manual, violates the firm's own complaint-handling procedures and further evidences a breakdown in compliance infrastructure. The absence of a complaint register undermines recordkeeping obligations under Rule 204-2(a)(7) of the Advisers Act.

No credible defense exists that 'long-term growth potential' justified the allocation for this client. The suitability determination is client-specific, not product-specific, and the documented profile unambiguously precluded speculative, high-volatility, non-income-producing positions of this magnitude.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§206(1), 206(2); Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Policies and Procedures); Rule 204-2(a)(7) (Recordkeeping); FINRA Regulatory Notice 09-31 (Non-Traditional ETFs); SEC guidance on fiduciary duty of care and loyalty for registered investment advisers
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Iyer allocated over 80% of a conservative 72-year-old retiree's IRA to speculative micro-cap stocks and a triple-leveraged ETF in direct contradiction of her documented conservative, income-oriented investment objectives and risk tolerance.

fact_pattern:
Triton Capital Advisors, LLC is an SEC-registered investment adviser based in Greenwich, Connecticut, with approximately $3.2 billion in regulatory assets under management as of December 31, 2022. Triton serves as the investment adviser to three qualifying hedge funds: Triton Global Macro Fund ($1.8 billion AUM), Triton Relative Value Fund ($900 million AUM), and Triton Credit Opportunities Fund ($500 million AUM). Because Triton advises qualifying hedge funds and manages at least $1.5 billion in hedge fund assets, it qualifies as a 'large hedge fund adviser' under Form PF.

On January 8, 2024, following a sudden spike in Treasury yields and a rapid unwinding of basis trades, Triton Global Macro Fund experienced extraordinary investment losses of approximately $540 million over a 48-hour period, representing a 30% decline in the fund's net asset value. The losses triggered a cascade of margin calls from the fund's prime brokers—Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley—totaling $320 million. Triton's Chief Compliance Officer, Rebecca Langford, was immediately notified and convened an emergency meeting with the fund's portfolio managers and legal counsel on January 9, 2024. During the meeting, the team discussed the potential obligation to file a current report on Form PF under the new Section 5 event reporting requirements that became effective on December 11, 2023.

Langford determined that the reporting could wait because the firm's quarterly Form PF filing for Q4 2023 was due in mid-February, and she believed the losses could be disclosed in that filing as part of the fund's regular quarterly update. She also reasoned that since the fund had not formally defaulted on any margin call—Triton managed to meet the calls by liquidating other positions and drawing on a $150 million credit facility—there was no immediate 'triggering event.' Additionally, the CCO was concerned about the reputational damage that could result from a current report filing with the SEC and FSOC, even though such filings are confidential. As a result, Triton did not file a current report on Form PF. The SEC's Division of Investment Management later opened an inquiry into Triton's activities during the January market volatility after reviewing prime brokerage data and noticing the absence of any Form PF current report filing from the adviser.

Triton's outside counsel at a prominent New York law firm subsequently advised the firm on February 5, 2024, that the failure to file was likely a violation. By that point, the 72-hour window had long passed. Triton then filed the current report on February 7, 2024, approximately 30 days late.
question: Did Triton Capital Advisors violate its obligation to file a current report on Form PF within 72 hours of the qualifying hedge fund's extraordinary investment losses, and was the CCO's rationale for delaying the filing legally sufficient?
answer:
Triton Capital Advisors violated its current reporting obligations under the amended Form PF rules. The analysis is as follows:

Under the amendments to Form PF adopted by the SEC on May 3, 2023 (SEC Release No. IA-6297), effective December 11, 2023, large hedge fund advisers are required to file a current report on new Section 5 of Form PF within 72 hours of the occurrence of certain specified triggering events with respect to their qualifying hedge funds. Among these triggering events are extraordinary investment losses, which the SEC defined as losses equal to or exceeding 20% of a qualifying hedge fund's most recent reported net asset value over a rolling 10-business-day period.

Triton Global Macro Fund's losses of approximately $540 million—representing a 30% decline in NAV over a 48-hour period—clearly exceeded the 20% threshold. The triggering event occurred on or about January 8, 2024, meaning Triton was required to file a current report no later than January 11, 2024 (72 hours after the event). The firm did not file until February 7, 2024.

CCO Langford's rationale was legally insufficient on multiple grounds. First, the current reporting requirement under Section 5 of Form PF is a standalone, event-driven obligation that is independent of the quarterly filing schedule. The SEC specifically designed the current reporting framework to provide timely information to the Commission and FSOC during periods of market stress, precisely the scenario Triton faced. Waiting for a quarterly filing defeats the regulatory purpose. Second, Langford's determination that no 'triggering event' occurred because the fund met its margin calls is incorrect. Extraordinary investment losses are independently reportable regardless of whether the fund also defaulted on margin calls or other obligations. The triggering events are disjunctive, not conjunctive—each stands alone. Third, concerns about reputational harm are irrelevant to the legal obligation; moreover, Form PF filings are confidential and are not publicly disclosed, undermining even the practical basis for Langford's concern.

Triton's late filing does not cure the initial violation, though it may mitigate potential sanctions. The SEC staff, as noted in the Dechert memo, was expected to closely monitor current report filings (analogous to monitoring of Form N-RN and Form N-MFP) and to target outreach during market stress. The absence of a filing from a $3.2 billion large hedge fund adviser during a period of known market volatility would be precisely the type of gap the SEC would identify. Triton faces potential enforcement action under Section 204 of the Investment Advisers Act for failure to file required reports, and Langford personally faces scrutiny for a compliance program failure under Rule 206(4)-7.
applicable_standard: Amendments to Form PF, Section 5 (Event Reporting for Large Hedge Fund Advisers), SEC Release No. IA-6297 (May 3, 2023); Investment Advisers Act §204 (Reports by Investment Advisers); Investment Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Procedures and Practices); Form PF General Instructions, Instruction 1 (definitions of large hedge fund adviser and qualifying hedge fund)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Triton failed to file a current report on Form PF within 72 hours of extraordinary investment losses exceeding the 20% NAV threshold in its qualifying hedge fund, based on the CCO's legally erroneous conclusion that meeting margin calls negated the independent reporting trigger for extraordinary losses.

fact_pattern:
Crestview Capital Advisors, LLC ('Crestview') is a registered investment adviser based in Boston, Massachusetts, managing approximately $4.2 billion in assets across a family of seven private funds and several separately managed accounts. As of December 31, 2024, Crestview held discretionary authority over a portfolio of U.S. equity securities that included positions in 342 Section 13(f) securities with an aggregate fair market value of approximately $1.87 billion. The firm's Chief Compliance Officer, Diana Morales, was aware that the firm exceeded the $100 million threshold triggering the Form 13F filing obligation under Section 13(f) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and had historically filed the form on a timely basis.

In early January 2025, Crestview underwent a significant internal restructuring. Ms. Morales resigned effective January 10, 2025, and her deputy, Ryan Chen, assumed interim CCO responsibilities. During the transition, several year-end compliance tasks were deprioritized. Specifically, Mr. Chen focused his attention on completing the annual Form ADV amendment (due March 31, 2025) and the firm's Form PF filing, believing those to be the most urgent regulatory deadlines. He was generally aware of the Form 13F requirement but mistakenly believed the filing was due annually on March 15, rather than within 45 days of the end of each calendar quarter.

As a result, Crestview failed to file its Form 13F for the quarter ending December 31, 2024, by the February 14, 2025 deadline. The omission was not discovered until March 22, 2025, when an outside compliance consultant, Tara Whitfield of Beacon Compliance Solutions, conducted a routine review. She also discovered that two of Crestview's positions—a 6.1% stake in NovaTech Industries, Inc. (valued at $188 million) and a 5.4% stake in Meridian Health Systems, Inc. (valued at $142 million)—had not been reported on any Schedule 13D or Schedule 13G filings, despite both positions having crossed the 5% beneficial ownership threshold in November 2024. The NovaTech stake was acquired with the express purpose of influencing the company's board composition, while the Meridian stake was acquired passively as part of a quantitative strategy with no activist intent.

Upon discovery, Mr. Chen immediately retained outside counsel and filed the delinquent Form 13F on March 24, 2025. However, no Schedule 13D for NovaTech or Schedule 13G for Meridian had yet been filed as of that date.
question: What reporting violations has Crestview committed with respect to its Form 13F, Schedule 13D, and Schedule 13G obligations, and what are the potential regulatory consequences?
answer:
Crestview has committed multiple reporting violations under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and related SEC rules.

First, regarding Form 13F: Under Section 13(f)(1) of the Exchange Act and Rule 13f-1 thereunder, an institutional investment manager exercising investment discretion over $100 million or more in Section 13(f) securities must file Form 13F with the SEC within 45 days of the end of each calendar quarter. Crestview's $1.87 billion in qualifying equity securities clearly exceeds the threshold. The filing for Q4 2024 was due by February 14, 2025. Crestview's failure to file until March 24, 2025—38 days late—constitutes a clear violation. While the late filing was remediated, the SEC has historically pursued enforcement actions or issued deficiency letters for delinquent 13F filings, particularly where the manager is large and sophisticated. Mr. Chen's mistaken belief about the filing deadline does not constitute a defense; ignorance of filing deadlines is not a recognized excuse under the securities laws.

Second, regarding the NovaTech position: Under Section 13(d) of the Exchange Act and Rules 13d-1 through 13d-7, any person who acquires beneficial ownership of more than 5% of a class of equity securities registered under Section 12 and who has the purpose or effect of changing or influencing control of the issuer must file Schedule 13D within 10 business days of crossing the 5% threshold. Crestview's 6.1% stake in NovaTech, acquired with the express purpose of influencing board composition, unambiguously triggers Schedule 13D. Given that the threshold was crossed in November 2024, the Schedule 13D was due no later than approximately mid-November 2024. As of March 24, 2025, the filing remains outstanding—a violation of over four months' duration. This is a serious violation that could subject Crestview to SEC enforcement action, including injunctive relief, civil penalties, and potential Section 21(a) reports.

Third, regarding the Meridian position: Under revised Rule 13d-1(c), a passive investor that acquires more than 5% of a class of equity securities and has not acquired the securities with a control purpose may file the shorter Schedule 13G rather than Schedule 13D. Under the amended Schedule 13G rules effective September 30, 2024, Qualified Institutional Investors filing under Rule 13d-1(b) must file Schedule 13G within 45 calendar days of the end of the calendar quarter in which the 5% threshold was crossed (i.e., by February 14, 2025 for a November 2024 crossing). Crestview's failure to file Schedule 13G for Meridian by this deadline also constitutes a violation.

The combination of these failures—spanning three separate filing obligations—suggests a systemic compliance infrastructure breakdown. The SEC could view this as evidence of inadequate compliance policies and procedures under Rule 206(4)-7 of the Investment Advisers Act, compounding Crestview's regulatory exposure.
applicable_standard: Section 13(f) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 13f-1; Section 13(d) of the Exchange Act and Rules 13d-1 through 13d-7 (Schedule 13D); Rule 13d-1(b) and (c) (Schedule 13G); Rule 206(4)-7 under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The interim CCO's mistaken understanding of the Form 13F filing deadline and the firm's failure to have adequate compliance procedures to track beneficial ownership reporting thresholds resulted in three separate delinquent or missing SEC filings.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Reinhold is the founder and sole portfolio manager of Reinhold Capital Advisors LLC, a registered investment adviser based in Austin, Texas, with approximately $185 million in assets under management across 74 client accounts. Reinhold Capital's Form ADV Part 2A brochure states that the firm manages client portfolios on a discretionary basis using a 'core equity growth strategy' and that 'all clients are treated fairly and equitably with respect to trade allocation.' Reinhold personally maintains two accounts at the firm: a proprietary account holding approximately $2.3 million and a separate account for his spouse, Helen Reinhold, holding approximately $1.1 million.

From January 2023 through September 2024, Reinhold executed a recurring pattern involving block trades in volatile small-cap equities. On each occasion, Reinhold would place a single block order through the firm's omnibus account at Interactive Brokers without pre-designating the allocation among specific client accounts. He would then wait until the end of the trading day to observe the performance of the purchased securities. On days when the block trade generated a gain — which occurred on 47 separate occasions totaling approximately $612,000 in profits — Reinhold disproportionately allocated the profitable trades to his personal account and his spouse's account, which together received 68% of all profitable allocations despite representing only 1.8% of the firm's total AUM. On the 31 occasions when the block trade resulted in a loss — totaling approximately $289,000 — Reinhold allocated 91% of those losing positions to client accounts, particularly to three elderly retired clients: Dorothy Gaines (age 78, account value $420,000, moderate risk tolerance), Samuel Okafor (age 81, account value $310,000, conservative risk tolerance), and Patricia Yuen (age 74, account value $275,000, moderate risk tolerance).

Reinhold Capital's compliance manual requires that trade allocations be determined prior to order execution and documented in writing. However, the firm's Chief Compliance Officer, Brenda Tallmadge, who is Reinhold's sister-in-law, conducted only one cursory annual review and did not examine trade allocation records or compare performance across accounts. When the SEC's Office of Compliance Inspections and Examinations (OCIE) conducted a routine examination in October 2024, examiners identified the allocation disparities through a statistical analysis showing that Reinhold's personal accounts outperformed the composite client average by 14.3 percentage points annualized — a deviation that OCIE flagged as statistically inconsistent with fair allocation absent cherry-picking.
question: Did Marcus Reinhold and Reinhold Capital Advisors violate their fiduciary duties under the Investment Advisers Act by engaging in the trade allocation pattern described, and what are the specific legal bases for any such violation?
answer:
Marcus Reinhold and Reinhold Capital Advisors committed clear and serious violations of their fiduciary duties under Section 206 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The conduct constitutes classic 'cherry-picking,' which the SEC has consistently treated as a fraud upon advisory clients.

First, Section 206(1) of the Advisers Act prohibits an investment adviser from employing any device, scheme, or artifice to defraud any client or prospective client. Reinhold's systematic practice of placing block trades without pre-designating allocations, waiting to observe end-of-day performance, and then disproportionately directing profitable trades to his own accounts while burdening client accounts with losses constitutes precisely such a scheme. The statistical evidence — a 14.3 percentage point annualized performance disparity between Reinhold's accounts and client composites, combined with the fact that accounts representing 1.8% of AUM received 68% of profitable allocations — establishes the pattern with compelling force. The SEC has successfully prosecuted nearly identical conduct, as referenced in In the Matter of James C. Dawson (Advisers Act Release No. 3057, July 23, 2010), where an adviser was barred for cherry-picking trades in a manner that 'undercuts the trust that is the foundation of the investment advisory relationship.'

Second, Section 206(2) prohibits any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit upon any client. Unlike Section 206(1), Section 206(2) does not require scienter — negligence is sufficient. Here, however, the deliberate and repeated nature of the allocation decisions over 21 months across 78 block trades clearly satisfies even the higher scienter standard. The allocation of losses disproportionately to vulnerable elderly clients with moderate-to-conservative risk tolerances (Gaines, Okafor, and Yuen) further aggravates the misconduct.

Third, the fiduciary duty articulated by the Supreme Court in SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, 375 U.S. 180 (1963), imposes on advisers an affirmative obligation to act with utmost good faith, to make full and fair disclosure of all material facts, and to employ reasonable care to avoid misleading clients. Reinhold's Form ADV affirmatively represented that 'all clients are treated fairly and equitably with respect to trade allocation,' a statement rendered materially false and misleading by his actual conduct. This constitutes a breach of the duty of loyalty and the duty of care simultaneously.

Reinhold Capital's compliance failures compound the violations. The firm's own written procedures required pre-trade allocation documentation — a standard industry control designed to prevent cherry-picking — yet the CCO performed no meaningful review of allocation records. This constitutes a failure of the firm's supervisory obligations and potentially a violation of Rule 206(4)-7 under the Advisers Act, which requires advisers to adopt and implement written compliance policies reasonably designed to prevent violations. A CCO who is a family member performing only perfunctory reviews does not satisfy this obligation.

No credible defense is available. Reinhold cannot argue that post-trade allocation is inherently impermissible — rather, it is the systematic pattern of self-favoring allocation that constitutes fraud. The statistical evidence effectively rebuts any claim that the disparities were coincidental.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206(1), §206(2), §206(4); Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Rule); SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, 375 U.S. 180 (1963); In the Matter of James C. Dawson, Advisers Act Release No. 3057 (July 23, 2010)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Reinhold systematically allocated profitable block trades to his personal and spousal accounts while directing losing trades to client accounts, constituting cherry-picking in breach of his fiduciary duty of loyalty under Section 206 of the Advisers Act.

The board's annual review of the compliance program in March 2018 lasted approximately 25 minutes and consisted solely of Ellison reading her summary report aloud. No independent directors asked questions about gaps in the program. The board unanimously voted to approve the compliance programs of the Fund and its service providers, including RCA, without requesting supplemental documentation or engaging independent compliance consultants. An SEC examination in June 2018 uncovered these deficiencies.
question: Did the Fund's board of directors and its CCO satisfy their obligations under Rule 38a-1 with respect to the adoption, implementation, and annual review of the Fund's compliance program?
answer:
No. The Fund's board and CCO failed to satisfy multiple requirements under Rule 38a-1 under the Investment Company Act of 1940, and the facts reveal both substantive and procedural deficiencies.

First, regarding the CCO's annual report obligation under Rule 38a-1(a)(4)(iii), the CCO must prepare an annual written report to the board that addresses, at a minimum, the operation of the compliance policies and procedures and any material compliance matters that occurred since the last report. Ellison's 3-page summary omitted three categories of material compliance matters: (1) significant style drift involving $87 million in off-mandate high-yield fixed income investments, which implicates portfolio management compliance (a specific area identified in the Rule 38a-1 adopting release); (2) apparent misuse of Rule 17a-7 cross-transactions to dump underperforming securities from an affiliate into the Fund, which raises concerns under Section 17(a) of the 1940 Act; and (3) a complete failure to review execution quality, directly contravening the trading practices compliance area identified in the adopting release. The omission of these matters from the annual report constitutes a failure to fulfill the CCO's reporting obligations.

Second, the board failed in its annual review obligation under Rule 38a-1(a)(3). The Rule requires the board, including a majority of independent directors, to annually review the adequacy and effectiveness of the compliance programs of both the Fund and its service providers. A 25-minute session with no questions, no supplemental documentation, and no independent assessment does not constitute a meaningful review of adequacy and effectiveness. The board's approval was not based on a finding — as required by Rule 38a-1(a)(1) — that the programs were reasonably designed to prevent violations.

Third, Ellison's dual role as CCO and Deputy General Counsel of RCA raises structural concerns. While Rule 38a-1 permits a CCO to be an employee of an adviser, the adopting release emphasizes that conflicts of interest must be addressed. The board's failure to independently evaluate whether Ellison's reporting relationship to RCA's CEO compromised her independence undermines the integrity of the compliance framework.

The Fund cannot rely on the Independent Directors Council No-Action Letter to excuse the board's failures. That letter permits boards to rely on the CCO's quarterly written representations regarding specific exemptive rule compliance but expressly states this "would not change the board's oversight role with respect to a fund's overall compliance program." The board's superficial annual review demonstrates an abdication of that oversight role rather than legitimate reliance on the CCO's administrative functions.
applicable_standard: Rule 38a-1 under the Investment Company Act of 1940; Sections 10(f), 17(a), and 17(e) of the 1940 Act; Independent Directors Council SEC No-Action Letter (October 12, 2018); Rule 38a-1 Adopting Release (Compliance Programs of Investment Companies and Investment Advisers, IC-26299, December 17, 2003)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The CCO's annual report omitted material compliance matters — including style drift, misuse of affiliated cross-transactions, and failure to review execution quality — and the board conducted no meaningful review of program adequacy, rendering its approval of the compliance program unsupported by the requisite finding under Rule 38a-1(a)(1).

Marcus Dalton is a registered representative at Meridian Securities LLC, a FINRA-member broker-dealer based in Washington, DC. Dalton has 18 years of experience in the securities industry, including six years as an enforcement attorney at the SEC's Division of Enforcement before transitioning to the private sector. He is dually registered as an investment adviser representative with Meridian's affiliated RIA, Meridian Wealth Advisors.

In March 2019, Dalton was approached by GlobalTech Components Inc., a mid-cap technology manufacturer with significant supply chain operations in China, to serve as outside counsel and compliance consultant on an internal investigation into potential Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) violations at its Shenzhen subsidiary. GlobalTech offered Dalton $275,000 for approximately six months of consulting work. Dalton, drawing on his SEC enforcement background and his relationships with former DOJ colleagues, accepted the engagement without notifying Meridian Securities' compliance department or seeking written approval. He signed the consulting agreement in his personal capacity on April 1, 2019.

Simultaneously, Dalton continued to serve as the primary financial adviser and broker for GlobalTech's CEO, Jennifer Hargrove, managing approximately $4.2 million in her brokerage and advisory accounts at Meridian. Between April and August 2019, Dalton recommended that Hargrove increase her concentrated position in GlobalTech stock by an additional $380,000, citing the company's 'strong fundamentals,' while he was privately aware—through his undisclosed consulting role—that the FCPA investigation had uncovered evidence of systematic bribery payments totaling approximately $1.8 million to Chinese government officials, which could expose GlobalTech to significant fines, debarment, and reputational harm.

In September 2019, when GlobalTech publicly disclosed the FCPA investigation, the company's stock dropped 34% in a single trading day. Hargrove's portfolio lost approximately $1.56 million. Meridian's compliance department only learned of Dalton's consulting engagement when Hargrove filed a complaint alleging that Dalton had a material undisclosed conflict of interest.
question: Did Marcus Dalton violate applicable regulatory obligations by failing to disclose his outside consulting engagement with GlobalTech and by recommending increased concentration in GlobalTech stock to the CEO while possessing material nonpublic information obtained through that engagement?
answer:
Marcus Dalton committed multiple serious regulatory violations spanning FINRA rules, the Investment Advisers Act, and federal securities law.

First, Dalton violated FINRA Rule 3270 (Outside Business Activities of Registered Persons), which requires that a registered representative provide prior written notice to their member firm before engaging in any outside business activity. The rule is broadly construed—Dalton's $275,000 consulting engagement with GlobalTech clearly constitutes a business activity outside the scope of his relationship with Meridian Securities. His failure to provide prior written notice deprived Meridian's compliance department of the opportunity to evaluate the engagement for conflicts of interest, impose conditions, or prohibit it entirely. This also implicates FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision), as Meridian may face secondary liability for supervisory failures if it lacked adequate systems to detect such undisclosed activities, though the primary violation rests with Dalton.

Second, Dalton violated his fiduciary duty under Section 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, which prohibit investment advisers from employing any device, scheme, or artifice to defraud clients, and from engaging in any transaction, practice, or course of business that operates as a fraud or deceit upon any client. As a dually registered adviser managing Hargrove's advisory accounts, Dalton owed her an affirmative duty of full and fair disclosure of all material conflicts of interest. His simultaneous role as GlobalTech's FCPA investigation consultant while advising the CEO on her personal investments—including recommending increased concentration in GlobalTech stock—represents a textbook material conflict that was never disclosed.

Third, and most gravely, Dalton's recommendation to increase Hargrove's GlobalTech position while aware of the undisclosed FCPA investigation implicates Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The FCPA investigation findings—including $1.8 million in bribery payments—constituted material nonpublic information. By recommending purchases while in possession of this information, Dalton potentially engaged in securities fraud. Under Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI), specifically the Conflict of Interest Obligation under Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iv), broker-dealers must establish policies to identify and disclose or eliminate material conflicts. Dalton's conduct violated both the Disclosure Obligation and Care Obligation components of Reg BI, as no reasonable basis existed for recommending concentration in a security about which he possessed undisclosed adverse material information.

No viable defense exists. Dalton cannot claim ignorance of disclosure requirements given his 6 years at SEC Enforcement. The consulting engagement was not de minimis, and the conflict was not theoretical but actively harmful.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 3270 (Outside Business Activities); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); Investment Advisers Act §206(1)-(2); Securities Exchange Act §10(b); Rule 10b-5; Regulation Best Interest Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i)-(iv)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Dalton's undisclosed $275,000 outside consulting engagement with GlobalTech created a direct, material conflict of interest that he exploited by recommending the CEO increase her concentration in company stock while possessing material nonpublic information about the FCPA investigation.

In March 2023, Ridgeline Capital Partners LLC ('Ridgeline'), a mid-tier investment bank headquartered in New York, was retained by Velora Technologies, Inc. ('Velora'), a privately held SaaS company with approximately $180 million in annual revenue, to serve as its exclusive financial adviser in connection with a potential sale of the company. Velora's board of directors, chaired by CEO and founder Priya Chandrasekaran, had no prior experience with M&A transactions. The engagement letter, governed by New York law, described Ridgeline's role as providing 'financial advisory services in connection with the Transaction' and contained a standard limitation-of-liability clause stating that Ridgeline's obligations were 'solely as set forth herein' and that 'nothing in this agreement shall be construed to create a fiduciary relationship.' The letter did not contain a specific disclaimer of fiduciary duties using the word 'fiduciary.'

Over the ensuing four months, Ridgeline's Managing Director, Thomas Hargrove, developed an unusually close advisory relationship with Chandrasekaran. Hargrove participated in weekly board calls, advised the board on governance matters unrelated to the sale process, recommended that the company restructure its equity compensation plans, and personally assured Chandrasekaran on multiple occasions that he was 'looking out for Velora's best interests at every turn.' Hargrove told Chandrasekaran that she should 'trust us completely — this is what we do.' Internal Ridgeline emails show Hargrove instructing his team to 'make sure we keep Velora feeling like we're their partners, not just hired guns.'

In July 2023, Ridgeline presented Velora's board with a single acquisition offer from Orion Enterprises at $425 million. Ridgeline's fairness opinion concluded the price was fair from a financial point of view. However, Ridgeline had not disclosed that Orion was simultaneously a buy-side advisory client of Ridgeline's leveraged finance group, which stood to earn $6.2 million in financing fees if the acquisition closed. Ridgeline also failed to solicit competing bids from three other potential acquirers who had expressed preliminary interest at valuations ranging from $460 million to $510 million. Velora's board approved the sale to Orion at $425 million in reliance on Ridgeline's recommendation. After the deal closed in September 2023, Chandrasekaran learned of the conflict and the unsolicited indications of higher interest, and Velora's former shareholders filed suit alleging breach of fiduciary duty under New York law.
question: Under New York law, as articulated in EBC I, Inc. v. Goldman, Sachs & Co. and related precedent, did Ridgeline Capital Partners owe an extra-contractual fiduciary duty to Velora Technologies despite the contractual limitation in the engagement letter, and if so, did Ridgeline's conduct constitute a breach of that duty?
answer:
Under the framework established by New York's highest court in EBC I, Inc. v. Goldman, Sachs & Co. (the 'eToys' decision), a trier of fact could conclude that Ridgeline owed and breached an extra-contractual fiduciary duty to Velora, notwithstanding the engagement letter's limitation-of-liability language.

First, regarding the existence of a fiduciary duty: The EBC I court held that under New York law, investment banks may owe fiduciary duties to their clients where the client reposes trust and confidence in the bank due to the bank's superior knowledge and expertise, and the bank accepts that trust. Here, Velora's board had no M&A experience and was wholly dependent on Ridgeline's guidance. Critically, Hargrove's conduct went far beyond the contractual scope of 'financial advisory services' — he participated in governance decisions, restructured equity compensation, and made repeated affirmative representations that he was 'looking out for Velora's best interests.' Internal communications confirm Ridgeline deliberately cultivated a relationship of trust exceeding an arm's-length advisory engagement. Under EBC I, these facts would permit a jury to find that Ridgeline assumed fiduciary obligations.

The contractual disclaimer is not dispositive under New York law. The engagement letter stated that nothing 'shall be construed to create a fiduciary relationship,' but it did not use the specific term 'fiduciary duty' as a waiver, and more importantly, New York courts have held that boilerplate contractual limitations cannot override fiduciary obligations that arise from the actual conduct and relationship of the parties. Ridgeline's affirmative representations of loyalty and its expansion of the advisory relationship beyond the engagement letter's scope undercut any attempt to rely on the contractual limitation.

Second, regarding breach: Even if the duty's existence must be determined by a jury, the undisclosed conflict of interest is a textbook fiduciary breach. Ridgeline failed to disclose that its leveraged finance group stood to earn $6.2 million from Orion's financing of the acquisition — a material conflict that directly incentivized Ridgeline to favor Orion's bid. Under the duty of loyalty, a fiduciary must disclose all material conflicts. Additionally, Ridgeline's failure to solicit or present competing bids from acquirers offering $460–$510 million — a potential $85 million premium — while presenting only the conflicted Orion offer, constitutes a breach of the duty of care. The fairness opinion, rendered without a market check, cannot insulate Ridgeline when it deliberately suppressed superior alternatives.

Ridgeline's likely defense — that the engagement letter's limitation clause governs — fails under the Joyce v. Morgan Stanley framework as applied in New York. Unlike Joyce (decided under Illinois law, which confined duties to the contract), New York's EBC I standard explicitly permits extra-contractual fiduciary findings where conduct creates a relationship of trust and confidence. Ridgeline's conduct overwhelmingly satisfies this standard.
applicable_standard: EBC I, Inc. v. Goldman, Sachs & Co., 5 N.Y.3d 11 (2005); Joyce v. Morgan Stanley & Co., 2008 U.S. App. LEXIS 17588 (7th Cir. 2008); Bear Stearns & Co. v. Daisy Sys. Corp., 97 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 1996); New York common law fiduciary duty (duty of loyalty and duty of care); Restatement (Second) of Torts §874 (fiduciary duty breach)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Ridgeline's managing director affirmatively cultivated a relationship of trust and confidence with an inexperienced client board while concealing a $6.2 million conflict of interest with the sole bidder and suppressing materially higher competing indications of interest.

Granite Peak Capital Management LLC ('Granite Peak') is a registered investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 with its principal office in Boston, Massachusetts. As of December 31, 2024, the firm managed approximately $3.8 billion in discretionary assets across seven private funds organized as Delaware limited partnerships and three separately managed accounts for institutional clients, including a state pension fund and two university endowments. The firm's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Whitfield, has held the role since 2019. Granite Peak's investment strategy focuses heavily on U.S. mid-cap equities, and the firm routinely holds concentrated positions across approximately 85 issuers listed on NASDAQ and the NYSE.

On February 14, 2025, the firm's operations team, led by portfolio operations director Michael Tanaka, ran a routine report and discovered that Granite Peak had accumulated a beneficial ownership position in MedVantage Inc. (NASDAQ: MVTG) totaling 6.3% of the outstanding shares, crossing the 5% threshold on January 22, 2025. The position was built gradually over a four-week period through purchases across multiple fund accounts. Tanaka flagged the issue to Whitfield, who instructed the trading desk to halt further purchases but did not file a Schedule 13G until March 7, 2025 — 44 calendar days after the threshold was crossed. Under the SEC's amended Schedule 13G rules effective September 30, 2024, passive investors (those qualifying under Rule 13d-1(c)) must file a Schedule 13G within five business days of crossing the 5% threshold.

Separately, Granite Peak's Form 13F for Q4 2024 was filed on February 18, 2025, which was timely. However, an internal audit conducted in March 2025 revealed that the Form 13F omitted three equity positions, collectively valued at approximately $47 million, due to a coding error in the firm's portfolio management system that excluded holdings acquired through a specific prime brokerage account at Jefferies LLC. The firm's prior Form 13F filings for Q2 and Q3 2024 contained the same omission. Whitfield acknowledged the error but noted that the firm's written supervisory procedures had not been updated since 2021 and did not include a reconciliation step for cross-checking holdings across all prime brokerage relationships before filing Form 13F.

Additionally, Granite Peak's Form ADV annual updating amendment was due within 90 days of its fiscal year end (December 31, 2024), i.e., by March 31, 2025. The firm filed its amendment on April 8, 2025, nine days late, after Whitfield realized the deadline had been missed while addressing the 13F and 13G issues.
question: What reporting and compliance violations has Granite Peak Capital Management committed with respect to its Schedule 13G, Form 13F, and Form ADV obligations, and what are the regulatory implications?
answer:
Granite Peak has committed multiple reporting violations that collectively indicate a systemic compliance failure.

**Schedule 13G Late Filing.** Under the SEC's amended beneficial ownership reporting rules (effective September 30, 2024), a qualified institutional investor or passive investor filing under Rule 13d-1(c) under the Exchange Act must file a Schedule 13G within five business days of the date on which the investor's beneficial ownership exceeds 5% of a class of equity securities registered under Section 13 of the Exchange Act. Granite Peak crossed the 5% threshold in MedVantage on January 22, 2025, which required a Schedule 13G filing by approximately January 29, 2025 (five business days). The firm did not file until March 7, 2025 — approximately 37 business days late. This constitutes a violation of Section 13(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 13d-1 thereunder. The SEC has brought enforcement actions and imposed penalties for late Schedule 13D/13G filings, and the amended rules specifically shortened the filing deadlines to enhance market transparency. The fact that Granite Peak's monitoring systems failed to detect the threshold crossing until February 14 — over three weeks later — demonstrates inadequate surveillance procedures.

**Form 13F Inaccuracies.** Section 13(f) of the Exchange Act and Rule 13f-1 require institutional investment managers exercising investment discretion over $100 million or more in Section 13(f) securities to file Form 13F within 45 days after the end of each calendar quarter. While Granite Peak's Q4 2024 Form 13F was filed timely, the omission of $47 million in holdings due to a coding error across three consecutive quarters (Q2–Q4 2024) renders those filings materially inaccurate. The SEC's instructions for Form 13F require disclosure of all Section 13(f) securities over which the manager exercises investment discretion. Repeated inaccuracies suggest a failure in the firm's internal controls and supervisory procedures, potentially violating Section 206(4) of the Investment Advisers Act and Rule 206(4)-7 (the Compliance Rule), which requires registered advisers to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of the Advisers Act and the rules thereunder. The failure to reconcile holdings across all prime brokerage accounts is a clear procedural gap.

**Form ADV Late Filing.** Rule 204-1 under the Investment Advisers Act requires registered advisers to file an annual updating amendment to Form ADV within 90 days of fiscal year end. Granite Peak's nine-day delay (filed April 8 instead of March 31, 2025) violates this requirement. While a brief delay may attract less severe sanctions, it compounds the pattern of compliance failures.

**Systemic Compliance Failure.** The root cause across all three violations traces to Whitfield's failure to maintain current written supervisory procedures and to implement adequate pre-filing reconciliation and beneficial ownership monitoring controls, constituting a violation of the Compliance Rule under Rule 206(4)-7. The SEC could pursue enforcement on multiple grounds, including potential cease-and-desist proceedings and civil penalties.
applicable_standard: Securities Exchange Act §13(d), §13(f); Rule 13d-1(c) (amended Schedule 13G 5-business-day filing deadline); Rule 13f-1 (Form 13F quarterly reporting); Investment Advisers Act §206(4); Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Rule); Rule 204-1 (Form ADV annual updating amendment)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Granite Peak's failure to maintain adequate monitoring systems and updated written supervisory procedures resulted in a 37-business-day-late Schedule 13G filing, three quarters of materially inaccurate Form 13F filings, and a late Form ADV annual amendment, demonstrating a systemic compliance program breakdown under Rule 206(4)-7.

Enduring Wealth Advisors LLC ('EWA') is a registered investment adviser that sponsors a wrap fee program custodied at LPL Financial, LLC. In September 2023, shortly after the firm's SEC registration, investment adviser representative David Parrish onboarded a new client, Margaret Stillwell, age 58, a recently widowed schoolteacher who rolled over her late husband's 401(k) plan, totaling $612,000, into an individual IRA. Parrish recommended the wrap fee program, explaining that Margaret would pay a single annual advisory fee of 1.45% on assets under management, which would cover both advisory services and all custodial transaction costs. Based on Margaret's moderate risk tolerance and 7-year time horizon to retirement, Parrish constructed a portfolio of 60% equities and 40% fixed income, allocated across a mix of individual stocks, bond ETFs, and two actively managed mutual funds.

Over the next twelve months (October 2023 through September 2024), Margaret's account experienced only three trades: the initial purchase allocation in October 2023, a single rebalancing trade in March 2024 adjusting the equity/fixed-income split by 2%, and a dividend reinvestment. During the same period, EWA's non-wrap advisory accounts with similar asset levels and risk profiles averaged 18 trades per year due to tax-loss harvesting, sector rotation, and periodic rebalancing. An internal compliance review in November 2024 flagged that Margaret's account, along with 14 other wrap fee accounts managed by Parrish, had trading activity significantly below the firm's non-wrap accounts. The review also revealed that Parrish had not documented any rationale for why the wrap fee structure was more suitable for Margaret than EWA's non-wrap advisory service, which charged a 1.25% advisory fee plus per-trade transaction costs averaging $4.95 per trade.

When questioned, Parrish acknowledged that he placed most of his newer clients into the wrap program because it simplified billing and he did not need to explain individual transaction charges. He conceded that for a low-trading account like Margaret's, the non-wrap service would have cost her approximately $1,275 less per year. EWA's Wrap Fee Brochure disclosed the general incentive to limit trading in wrap accounts but did not specifically describe any procedures the firm used to monitor whether wrap accounts were being actively managed in a manner consistent with the higher bundled fee.
question: Did EWA and its representative David Parrish violate their fiduciary obligations and applicable disclosure requirements by placing Margaret Stillwell in the wrap fee program without documenting suitability, failing to adequately manage trading activity, and benefiting from the fee differential?
answer:
Yes, EWA and Parrish violated their fiduciary duties under Section 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and failed to meet the disclosure and conduct requirements applicable to wrap fee programs under Form ADV Part 2A, Appendix 1.

First, as a fiduciary, EWA owes a duty of care and loyalty to Margaret under the Advisers Act. The SEC's 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation (IA-5248) makes clear that the duty of care requires an adviser to provide advice that is in the client's best interest, including the duty to seek best execution and to provide advice and monitoring over the course of the relationship at a frequency that is in the client's best interest. When a wrap fee program is recommended, the adviser must have a reasonable basis for believing the wrap program is suitable for that particular client given their anticipated trading needs. Here, Parrish's own admission that he selected the wrap program for administrative convenience—not based on Margaret's investment needs or expected trading frequency—is a direct breach of the duty of care.

Second, the wrap fee brochure itself acknowledges that 'an incentive exists to limit trading activities in client accounts' because the firm absorbs transaction costs. This disclosure, while required by Form ADV Part 2A, Appendix 1, Item 4, does not immunize the firm from the obligation to actually manage the conflict. The SEC has emphasized in multiple enforcement actions (e.g., In re Robare Group, Ltd., 2016) that disclosure alone is insufficient—an adviser must adopt and implement policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations, per Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-7. EWA's brochure disclosed the conflict but the firm failed to implement monitoring procedures to ensure wrap accounts received trading activity commensurate with the fees charged, and Parrish failed to document why the wrap fee was appropriate for a low-turnover client.

Third, the fee differential is material. Margaret paid approximately $8,874 annually (1.45% of $612,000) versus an estimated $7,599 (1.25% plus roughly ~$89 in transaction costs for three trades at $4.95 each under the non-wrap program), resulting in roughly $1,275 in excess annual cost with no corresponding benefit. This implicates the duty of loyalty, as Parrish's economic incentive—higher fee revenue with minimal trading effort—was not adequately disclosed or mitigated.

Parrish's conduct across 14 similarly situated accounts suggests a pattern rather than an isolated oversight, which elevates this from a single suitability lapse to a systemic compliance failure under Rule 206(4)-7. EWA's defense that the brochure disclosed the general conflict would likely fail, as the SEC consistently holds that boilerplate conflict disclosure does not substitute for individualized suitability analysis and active conflict management.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §206(1), §206(2); Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-7; SEC Fiduciary Interpretation (IA-5248, June 2019); Form ADV Part 2A, Appendix 1 (Wrap Fee Program Brochure), Item 4; FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) as applicable to dual registrants
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Parrish placed Margaret in the higher-cost wrap fee program for his own administrative convenience without documenting a reasonable basis to believe the wrap structure was in her best interest given her low anticipated trading activity.

Helen, a non-professional with no securities licenses or financial services background, sought guidance on what to do with the estate's brokerage account.

Marcus recommended that Helen, in her capacity as executor of the estate, liquidate Robert's existing portfolio—which consisted primarily of investment-grade municipal bonds and a diversified equity index fund—and reinvest the $620,000 proceeds into a proprietary structured note issued by Pinnacle's affiliate, Pinnacle Capital Markets. The structured note, the 'Pinnacle Enhanced Yield Note Series 2024-A,' carried a 7-year maturity, a 5.25% initial coupon that stepped down to 2.75% after year three, principal exposure linked to the S&P 500 with a 25% downside barrier, and a 2.85% upfront placement fee paid to Pinnacle Securities. Marcus did not discuss any alternative products, did not inquire about the estate's liquidity needs or the timeline for distributions to beneficiaries, and did not disclose the placement fee or the affiliated nature of the issuer. Pinnacle Securities' compliance department had recently updated its written supervisory procedures for Reg BI but had not implemented any specific training module addressing recommendations made to non-professional legal representatives of deceased customers' estates.

Pinnacle's branch manager, Sandra Liu, approved the transaction the same day after a cursory review of the account paperwork.
