Third, to the extent Montrose acted in a broker-dealer capacity, Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1) required him to satisfy four component obligations: Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance. He failed the Care Obligation by recommending products inconsistent with the trust's investment profile and risk tolerance. He failed the Disclosure Obligation by not disclosing the magnitude of commissions and proprietary product conflicts. He failed the Conflict of Interest Obligation because Pinnacle's compensation structure created incentives to recommend proprietary products without adequate mitigation.

Fourth, FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) and its successor obligations under Reg BI required Montrose to have a reasonable basis for his recommendations and to ensure customer-specific suitability. Illiquid, high-commission alternative investments are facially unsuitable for a trust with explicit liquidity requirements and a conservative IPS benefiting a 78-year-old lifetime income beneficiary.

Montrose's email defense that 'modern wealth management requires flexibility' is legally unavailing. A trustee cannot unilaterally override the terms of a governing instrument without proper amendment procedures, and the IPS constitutes an integral part of the trust's investment mandate. His failure to consult the co-trustee further compounds the breach. Montrose's conduct represents a severe fiduciary failure across all applicable standards.
applicable_standard: Uniform Prudent Investor Act §§ 2, 5; Conn. Gen. Stat. § 45a-541b; Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§ 206(1), 206(2); SEC Release IA-5248 (2019); Regulation Best Interest 17 CFR § 240.15l-1; FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); Restatement (Third) of Trusts §§ 78, 90
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Montrose's wholesale reallocation of trust assets into proprietary illiquid products generating substantial personal commissions — without disclosure, consent, co-trustee consultation, or IPS amendment — constitutes self-dealing and a breach of both the duty of loyalty and the duty of prudence.

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners LLC is an SEC-registered investment adviser based in Hartford, Connecticut, managing approximately $620 million in assets for roughly 1,400 retail clients, primarily pre-retirees and retirees with moderate risk tolerance. The firm's principal, David Kowalski, CFA, also serves as a registered representative of a dually registered broker-dealer, NorthStar Financial Services, Inc. Between January 2019 and March 2023, Meridian systematically placed new client assets into Class A shares of the Pinnacle Growth & Income Fund, which carried a 5.25% front-end sales load and ongoing 12b-1 fees of 0.25%, rather than the institutional share class of the same fund (Pinnacle Growth & Income Fund – Institutional Class), which had no sales load and an expense ratio 42 basis points lower. Meridian's advisory agreements permitted the firm to select mutual fund share classes on behalf of clients, and Meridian charged a 1.00% wrap fee on top of the underlying fund expenses. The 12b-1 fees from the Class A shares were paid to NorthStar Financial Services, which in turn paid a portion to Meridian's representatives, including Kowalski himself, as additional compensation.

Meridian's Form ADV Part 2A, last amended in March 2020, contained a general disclosure stating: 'Our firm and its representatives may receive compensation from third parties in connection with the purchase of certain investment products. This creates a potential conflict of interest, as our firm has a financial incentive to recommend products that pay such compensation.' The disclosure did not specifically identify the 12b-1 fee arrangement, did not quantify the additional compensation received, did not explain that lower-cost share classes of the same funds were available, and did not describe any steps Meridian took to mitigate this conflict.

During a routine SEC examination in June 2023, examiners identified that over 870 client accounts had been placed in the higher-cost Class A shares when the institutional share class was available at the same custodian, Fidelity Institutional. The cumulative excess costs borne by clients over the four-year period were estimated at approximately $1.87 million. When questioned, Kowalski stated that his firm believed the general disclosure in the ADV was sufficient and that clients had the opportunity to review the ADV before signing advisory agreements. He also noted that the Class A shares had the same portfolio management team and investment strategy as the institutional shares.

Meridian did not participate in the SEC's Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative, which had wrapped up in April 2020, despite being aware of the initiative through industry communications. The firm's compliance manual contained no written policies or procedures specifically addressing share class selection or the evaluation of available share classes when lower-cost alternatives existed.
question: Did Meridian Wealth Partners LLC violate its fiduciary duty of loyalty under the Investment Advisers Act by placing clients in higher-cost mutual fund share classes while receiving undisclosed 12b-1 fee compensation, and was its Form ADV disclosure sufficient to address this conflict?
answer:
Meridian Wealth Partners LLC violated its fiduciary duty of loyalty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and related SEC guidance on multiple grounds. The analysis proceeds as follows.

First, under SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963), an investment adviser owes an affirmative duty of utmost good faith, full and fair disclosure of all material facts, and an obligation to employ reasonable care to avoid misleading clients. The Commission's 2019 Interpretation (IA Release No. 5248, 84 FR 33669, July 12, 2019) reaffirmed that the duty of loyalty requires an adviser to not place its own interests ahead of its client's interests, and specifically mandates that an adviser must either eliminate material conflicts of interest or provide full and fair disclosure sufficient for the client to provide informed consent.

Meridian's conduct fails this standard in several critical respects. The firm's general ADV disclosure—referencing only 'potential' conflicts and unspecified 'compensation from third parties'—falls far short of the specificity required. The 2019 SEC Staff Guidance on Disclosure of Certain Financial Conflicts Related to Investment Adviser Compensation (October 18, 2019) explicitly addresses this scenario, stating that advisers must disclose the specific conflict created by 12b-1 fee arrangements, identify the availability of lower-cost share classes, and explain the financial incentive the adviser or its representatives have in selecting higher-cost shares. Boilerplate or generic conflict language does not constitute 'full and fair disclosure' as required by the fiduciary standard.

Second, the firm's failure to adopt and implement written compliance policies and procedures addressing share class selection constitutes an independent violation of Rule 206(4)-7 under the Advisers Act, which requires every registered adviser to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of the Advisers Act.

Third, Meridian's decision not to participate in the SCSD Initiative, while not itself a violation, eliminated an opportunity to self-report and remediate. The SEC's enforcement actions following the SCSD Initiative—over 100 actions resulting in more than $139 million in disgorgement—demonstrate that this exact fact pattern (selecting higher-cost share classes that pay 12b-1 fees without adequate disclosure and when lower-cost alternatives are available) has been treated as a serious breach of fiduciary duty under Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Advisers Act.

Kowalski's defense that clients received the ADV and could review it is unavailing. The Interpretation makes clear that the obligation rests on the adviser to ensure the disclosure is sufficiently specific to enable informed consent; merely providing a document containing vague language does not discharge the duty. The fact that the Class A and institutional shares had the same portfolio manager is irrelevant—the material fact is the cost differential and the adviser's financial incentive in selecting the more expensive class.

The $1.87 million in excess costs over four years across 870 accounts represents concrete, quantifiable harm. Meridian would likely face disgorgement of the 12b-1 fees received, prejudgment interest, civil penalties, and a mandate to convert all affected accounts to the lowest-cost available share class, consistent with prior SCSD-related enforcement outcomes.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Sections 206(1) and 206(2); SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963); Commission Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers, IA Release No. 5248 (July 12, 2019); SEC Staff FAQ on Disclosure of Certain Financial Conflicts Related to Investment Adviser Compensation (October 18, 2019); Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-7 (Compliance Policies and Procedures); SEC Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Meridian systematically selected higher-cost mutual fund share classes generating 12b-1 fee compensation to its affiliated representatives while providing only generic, non-specific conflict disclosure in its Form ADV that failed to identify the availability of lower-cost share classes or quantify the financial incentive.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Delgado, a registered investment adviser representative operating through Pinnacle Wealth Strategies, LLC (an SEC-registered investment advisory firm based in Newport Beach, California), managed approximately $14.2 million in assets for 38 retail clients between 2016 and 2021. Delgado held himself out as a specialist in retirement income planning, primarily targeting clients aged 55-72 who were rolling over employer-sponsored retirement plans into individual retirement accounts.

Beginning in March 2018, Delgado began directing client funds into two private placement offerings — Pacific Coast Bridge Fund I, LP and Pacific Coast Bridge Fund II, LP — which purported to invest in short-term bridge loans for commercial real estate projects in Southern California. Delgado told clients these funds offered 8-10% annual returns with 'bank CD-level safety' and that principal was 'fully secured by first-lien real estate collateral.' Between March 2018 and September 2020, Delgado moved approximately $6.8 million of client assets into these funds across 22 client accounts, representing between 35% and 70% of individual client portfolios.

In reality, Pacific Coast Bridge Fund I and II were controlled by Delgado's college roommate, Gregory Nolan, and the funds were not making legitimate bridge loans. Instead, approximately $2.1 million was used to pay earlier investors (creating the appearance of promised returns), $1.4 million was diverted to Nolan's personal accounts, and $850,000 was kicked back to Delgado through a shell consulting company, Coastal Advisory Partners, LLC. The remaining funds were placed in speculative, illiquid investments that bore no resemblance to the described strategy. Delgado never disclosed his financial relationship with Nolan or his receipt of undisclosed compensation through Coastal Advisory Partners. Client account statements generated by Pinnacle Wealth Strategies continued to show the Pacific Coast Bridge Fund investments at their original cost basis plus accrued returns, even after the underlying assets had become substantially worthless.

When several clients requested redemptions in late 2020, Delgado fabricated excuses about 'COVID-related liquidity constraints' and 'temporary NAV calculation delays.' He also began alternating between cooperating with SEC examination staff and then refusing to produce documents, at one point claiming he needed psychiatric evaluation before he could respond to subpoenas — a pattern the SEC staff characterized as dilatory. By January 2021, the scheme collapsed when Nolan fled the country, and clients discovered that approximately $5.3 million of the $6.8 million invested was unrecoverable.
question: Did Marcus Delgado violate his fiduciary duties under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, and what are the specific legal bases for potential civil enforcement and criminal liability arising from his conduct?
answer:
Delgado's conduct constitutes flagrant violations of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, specifically Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4), and would also support criminal charges under federal securities fraud statutes, wire fraud, and potentially mail fraud — closely paralleling the type of investment adviser fraud scheme at issue in United States v. Turner.

First, under Section 206(1) of the Advisers Act (15 U.S.C. § 80b-6(1)), Delgado employed a device, scheme, or artifice to defraud clients by recommending investments in the Pacific Coast Bridge Funds while concealing his undisclosed financial interest (the $850,000 in kickbacks through Coastal Advisory Partners). As a fiduciary, Delgado owed his clients an affirmative duty of utmost good faith and full disclosure of all material conflicts of interest. See SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963). The undisclosed compensation arrangement is a per se material conflict.

Second, under Section 206(2) (15 U.S.C. § 80b-6(2)), Delgado engaged in transactions, practices, and courses of business that operated as a fraud upon clients. This includes misrepresenting the nature and risk profile of the investments (claiming 'bank CD-level safety' for what were effectively Ponzi-like vehicles), fabricating account valuations, and providing false explanations for redemption delays. Unlike Section 206(1), Section 206(2) does not require scienter — negligence suffices — though Delgado's conduct clearly demonstrates intentional fraud.

Third, under Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-8 (17 C.F.R. § 275.206(4)-8), Delgado made untrue statements of material fact to investors in pooled investment vehicles regarding the use of proceeds, the security of investments, and the nature of returns.

For criminal liability, the scheme supports charges under 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (wire fraud) and 15 U.S.C. § 80b-17 (willful violations of the Advisers Act). The Ponzi-like payment structure — using $2.1 million from new investors to pay earlier investors — and the diversion of funds to personal use establish the requisite intent to defraud. Delgado's dilatory tactics with regulators, while not independently criminal, mirror the manipulative procedural behavior seen in Turner and would likely be presented as consciousness of guilt.

No viable defense exists. Delgado cannot claim reliance on Nolan's representations given his direct financial stake and control over client allocations. The concentration of 35-70% of retirement portfolios in a single illiquid, related-party investment would independently violate his fiduciary duty of care even absent fraud.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940, §§ 206(1), 206(2), 206(4) (15 U.S.C. §§ 80b-6(1), 80b-6(2), 80b-6(4)); SEC Rule 206(4)-8 (17 C.F.R. § 275.206(4)-8); 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (wire fraud); 18 U.S.C. § 1341 (mail fraud); SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Delgado's receipt of $850,000 in undisclosed kickback compensation from the fund manager while recommending those same funds to advisory clients constitutes the core fiduciary breach and transforms negligent mismanagement into intentional securities fraud.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Devereux, a registered investment adviser and principal of Devereux Capital Advisors LLC based in Washington, D.C., managed approximately $180 million in assets for high-net-worth clients, several of whom were politically connected. Between March 2017 and November 2019, Devereux was approached by Hamid Al-Rashidi, a wealthy foreign national and citizen of Qatar, who sought to channel $2.4 million in political contributions to various U.S. federal candidates through Devereux's network of domestic clients and business associates. Al-Rashidi wired $2.4 million in three tranches ($800,000 each in April 2017, September 2017, and February 2018) to a shell entity Devereux controlled called 'Patriot Advisory Holdings LLC,' which had no legitimate advisory business. Devereux then disbursed the funds to six U.S. persons—including three of his own advisory clients—who made contributions in their own names to federal campaigns and super PACs, totaling $1.95 million, with the remaining $450,000 retained by Devereux as a commission.

To conceal the scheme, Devereux created fabricated consulting invoices between Patriot Advisory Holdings and the six conduit contributors, making it appear the disbursements were legitimate consulting fees. He also directed two of the contributors—both advisory clients—to provide false information to FEC investigators in early 2019 when the unusual contribution pattern attracted scrutiny. Specifically, Devereux told client Sarah Lindhurst via encrypted messaging on January 14, 2019, 'If anyone asks, say the money was a bonus for advisory work you did for Patriot. Do not mention Hamid or Qatar under any circumstances.' He sent a similar message to client Brian Torrence on January 22, 2019.

When the DOJ opened a criminal investigation, a federal grand jury issued subpoenas to Devereux Capital Advisors for records related to Patriot Advisory Holdings. Devereux directed his office manager to alter QuickBooks records for Patriot Advisory Holdings, changing the description of three incoming wire transfers from 'H. Al-Rashidi – Doha' to 'Client Retainer – Domestic.' The altered records were produced to the grand jury in April 2019. Devereux was subsequently indicted on charges including conspiracy to defraud the United States and make illegal foreign and conduit contributions (52 U.S.C. § 30121, 52 U.S.C. § 30122), concealment of material facts (18 U.S.C. § 1001), making false entries in records (18 U.S.C. § 1519), witness tampering (18 U.S.C. § 1512), and obstruction of justice.
question: Did Devereux's conduct in facilitating foreign national contributions through conduit donors, directing witnesses to provide false statements, and altering business records produced to a grand jury violate federal criminal statutes, and what are the implications for his status as a registered investment adviser?
answer:
Devereux's conduct constitutes multiple serious federal criminal violations and independently triggers severe consequences under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940.

First, regarding the conduit contribution scheme: 52 U.S.C. § 30121 prohibits foreign nationals from directly or indirectly making contributions to federal elections, and prohibits any person from knowingly soliciting, accepting, or receiving such contributions. 52 U.S.C. § 30122 prohibits making contributions in the name of another person. Devereux orchestrated a scheme where Al-Rashidi's foreign funds were laundered through domestic conduits who contributed in their own names—precisely the conduct these statutes target. The conspiracy charge under 18 U.S.C. § 371 is well-supported: there was an agreement between Devereux and Al-Rashidi, an unlawful objective (circumventing FECA's foreign contribution ban), and overt acts (the wire transfers, disbursements, and actual contributions). As demonstrated in United States v. Michel, the government need not show that the foreign principal directly handed cash to candidates; indirect facilitation through conduits satisfies the statutory elements.

Second, the concealment and false records charges are independently devastating. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1001, Devereux's fabricated consulting invoices constitute material false statements designed to conceal the true source of funds from federal authorities. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, his direction to alter QuickBooks records before production to the grand jury constitutes making false entries in records with intent to obstruct a federal investigation—a standalone felony carrying up to 20 years imprisonment.

Third, the witness tampering charges under 18 U.S.C. § 1512(b) are supported by Devereux's encrypted messages to Lindhurst and Torrence, which constitute corrupt persuasion of witnesses to provide false testimony to federal investigators. The specificity of his instructions—fabricating the 'advisory bonus' cover story and directing concealment of Al-Rashidi's identity—demonstrates corrupt intent.

From a regulatory perspective, these convictions would constitute grounds for revocation of Devereux's investment adviser registration under Section 203(e) of the Investment Advisers Act (15 U.S.C. § 80b-3(e)), which authorizes the SEC to censure, limit, or revoke registration upon conviction of any felony involving misappropriation of funds, dishonesty, or breach of fiduciary duty. Moreover, Devereux's use of his advisory client relationships to recruit conduit contributors represents a profound breach of fiduciary duty under Section 206 of the Advisers Act, as he exploited positions of trust for an illegal purpose entirely adverse to his clients' interests, exposing them to criminal liability. The conduct here is unambiguously non-compliant across every applicable standard.
applicable_standard: 52 U.S.C. § 30121 (foreign national contribution ban); 52 U.S.C. § 30122 (conduit contribution prohibition); 18 U.S.C. § 371 (conspiracy to defraud the United States); 18 U.S.C. § 1001 (concealment of material facts); 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (false entries in records); 18 U.S.C. § 1512(b) (witness tampering); Investment Advisers Act §§ 203(e), 206 (15 U.S.C. §§ 80b-3(e), 80b-6)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Devereux exploited his position as a registered investment adviser and his fiduciary relationships with clients to recruit them as conduit contributors for illegal foreign national campaign contributions, then obstructed the federal investigation by tampering with witnesses and falsifying records.

fact_pattern:
In March 2022, Greenfield Capital Advisors, a registered investment adviser based in San Jose, California, recommended that its client Marjorie Tran, a 58-year-old retired school administrator with a $1.4 million portfolio and moderate risk tolerance, invest $210,000 in shares of NovaStar Biometrics, Inc. (NASDAQ: NVBM), a publicly traded company specializing in fingerprint and iris recognition sensors for consumer electronics. Greenfield's research analyst, Derek Fujimoto, had conducted thorough due diligence on NovaStar's financials, competitive position, and management team, and believed the company's Q4 2021 revenue growth of 23% year-over-year was sustainable. The recommendation was consistent with Marjorie's investment policy statement, which allocated up to 15% of her portfolio to individual growth equities in the technology sector.

On August 14, 2022, NovaStar issued a press release stating that its audit committee had initiated an internal investigation into 'certain revenue recognition practices related to channel partner agreements during fiscal years 2021 and 2022.' The press release contained no admission of wrongdoing, no restatement of financials, and no specific details about the nature or scope of the potential irregularities. NovaStar's stock dropped 31% the following trading day, from $38.50 to $26.57 per share, reducing Marjorie's position from approximately $210,000 to $144,800—a paper loss of roughly $65,200.

Marjorie, alarmed by the sudden decline, contacted Greenfield and demanded answers. Derek Fujimoto promptly reviewed the situation, consulted with Greenfield's compliance officer, and called Marjorie on August 15, 2022 to discuss the development. He advised her that while the investigation announcement was concerning, no actual wrongdoing had been confirmed, and that selling immediately could lock in losses that might prove unnecessary if the investigation cleared the company. He also noted the position still represented roughly 10% of her total portfolio. Marjorie chose to hold. By November 2022, NovaStar completed its investigation, announced that no material restatement was required, and the stock recovered to $35.20 per share.

Marjorie later filed a complaint with FINRA alleging that Greenfield was negligent in recommending NovaStar and that the firm should have anticipated the accounting irregularities. She also filed a putative class action in the Northern District of California against NovaStar and its officers under Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5, alleging loss causation based solely on the August 14, 2022 stock decline following the investigation announcement.
question: Under the loss causation standard articulated in Loos v. Immersion Corp. and the Ninth Circuit's framework, can Marjorie establish loss causation for her Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 claims against NovaStar based solely on the stock price decline following the announcement of the internal investigation, absent any subsequent disclosure of actual wrongdoing?
answer:
No, Marjorie cannot establish loss causation based solely on the stock price decline following the announcement of the internal investigation. Under the Ninth Circuit's holding in Loos v. Immersion Corp., No. 12-15100 (9th Cir. 2014), the announcement of an investigation, standing alone and without any disclosure of actual wrongdoing, is insufficient to establish loss causation for a Section 10(b) or Rule 10b-5 claim.

To prevail on a Section 10(b) claim, a plaintiff must establish loss causation—that is, a causal connection between the defendant's material misrepresentation and the plaintiff's economic loss. See Dura Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Broudo, 544 U.S. 336, 342 (2005). Loss causation typically requires a 'corrective disclosure' that reveals the truth behind the alleged fraud to the market, causing the stock price to decline. The Ninth Circuit in Loos, agreeing with the Eleventh Circuit's reasoning in Meyer v. Greene, 710 F.3d 1189 (11th Cir. 2013), held that the mere announcement of an internal investigation does not constitute such a corrective disclosure because it does not 'reveal to the market the pertinent truth of anything.'

Critically, the Ninth Circuit's amended opinion added a nuanced footnote clarifying that an investigation announcement is not categorically excluded from forming the basis of a loss causation theory. If the announcement itself contains 'an express disclosure of actual wrongdoing,' it might suffice. However, here, NovaStar's August 14, 2022 press release contained no admission of wrongdoing, no financial restatement, and no specific details about the nature of any irregularity—it merely announced the existence of an investigation into 'certain revenue recognition practices.' This is factually analogous to the Immersion Corporation announcement at issue in Loos.

Moreover, the subsequent completion of NovaStar's investigation in November 2022, which concluded that no material restatement was required, further undermines any theory that the investigation announcement revealed a 'pertinent truth' about fraud. The stock's recovery to $35.20 demonstrates that the market's initial reaction was based on uncertainty and fear rather than the unveiling of actual misconduct.

With respect to Greenfield Capital Advisors, the firm's conduct was compliant. The initial recommendation was supported by documented due diligence, was consistent with Marjorie's IPS and risk profile, and the position sizing was within stated allocation parameters. The firm's prompt response to the investigation announcement—reviewing the situation, consulting compliance, and providing balanced counsel—reflects the standard of care expected under both the Investment Advisers Act § 206 fiduciary duty and Regulation Best Interest (17 C.F.R. § 240.15l-1). Greenfield had no obligation to anticipate undisclosed internal accounting issues at NovaStar that the company itself had not yet identified.
applicable_standard: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §§ 10(b), 20(a), 20A; SEC Rule 10b-5 (17 C.F.R. § 240.10b-5); Dura Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Broudo, 544 U.S. 336 (2005); Loos v. Immersion Corp., No. 12-15100 (9th Cir. 2014); Meyer v. Greene, 710 F.3d 1189 (11th Cir. 2013); Investment Advisers Act § 206
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The plaintiff's loss causation theory fails because it relies exclusively on the stock price decline following the announcement of an internal investigation that contained no express disclosure of actual wrongdoing, which the Ninth Circuit in Loos held is insufficient as a matter of law.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Devereaux is a registered investment adviser who has managed the Ridgeline Capital Partners Fund, LP since 2016, with approximately $45 million in assets under management. In March 2020, the SEC initiated a civil enforcement action against Devereaux in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleging that between 2017 and 2019 he engaged in a scheme to manipulate the price of shares of Terravolt Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (ticker: TVLT) by publishing misleading short-selling research reports while holding significant short positions in the stock through Ridgeline Capital. The SEC alleged violations of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.

After a three-week jury trial in September 2023, the jury returned a mixed verdict. It found Devereaux liable on one count of making materially misleading statements in connection with the purchase or sale of securities but acquitted him on two counts of market manipulation and one count of fraud related to his fund's disclosures. The district court entered a final judgment on January 15, 2024, imposing a civil penalty of $200,000 (far less than the $2.8 million the SEC had sought), ordering no disgorgement, and enjoining Devereaux from violating Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 for a period of four years.

On June 3, 2024, the SEC's Division of Enforcement initiated a follow-on administrative proceeding under Section 203(f) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. § 80b-3(f)), seeking to permanently bar Devereaux from association with any investment adviser, broker-dealer, or other regulated entity. The SEC cited the district court's four-year injunction as the statutory predicate. On July 10, 2024, Devereaux filed suit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, seeking (1) a preliminary injunction halting the administrative proceeding, (2) a declaratory judgment that the follow-on proceeding violates res judicata because the SEC already litigated its claims and largely lost, and (3) a claim that the SEC's in-house adjudication violates the Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial and Article III of the Constitution. Devereaux argues that because the jury acquitted him of the most serious charges and the district court imposed a modest penalty, the SEC should not be permitted to seek the far more severe sanction of a permanent industry bar through an administrative tribunal where he would have no jury right.
question: Does Devereaux have viable grounds to enjoin the SEC's follow-on administrative proceeding under Section 203(f) of the Investment Advisers Act in federal district court, or must he exhaust administrative remedies and challenge any final order through the statutory appellate review process?
answer:
Devereaux's challenge is almost certainly going to fail at the district court level, and the SEC's follow-on proceeding is lawfully initiated. Here is why:

First, Section 203(f) of the Investment Advisers Act, codified at 15 U.S.C. § 80b-3(f), expressly authorizes the SEC to initiate a follow-on administrative proceeding to suspend or bar a person from the securities industry when the person has been 'enjoined from any action, conduct, or practice' specified under 15 U.S.C. § 80b-3(e)(4), which includes being enjoined from 'engaging in or continuing any conduct or practice in connection with the purchase or sale of any security.' Devereaux was enjoined from violating Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 for four years — this injunction is a qualifying statutory predicate regardless of the scope of the jury's verdict on other counts. The SEC need only demonstrate that (1) the proceeding is 'in the public interest' and (2) the predicate condition (here, an injunction) exists. Both are satisfied on their face.

Second, Devereaux's res judicata argument fails because a follow-on proceeding under Section 203(f) is not a relitigation of the underlying fraud charges. As the D.C. Circuit held in Bartko v. SEC, 845 F.3d 1217, 1219 (D.C. Cir. 2017), follow-on proceedings address a distinct question — whether the public interest requires suspension or barring — and involve different elements than the underlying enforcement action. The SEC is not re-proving fraud; it is using the established injunction as a predicate to assess prospective fitness to participate in the industry.

Third, the Seventh Amendment and Article III challenges, while animated by concerns raised in SEC v. Jarkesy, 603 U.S. 1 (2024), are inapplicable here because follow-on proceedings do not impose penalties for fraud — they impose prophylactic, forward-looking sanctions (suspension or bar) based on previously adjudicated judicial findings. Courts have consistently distinguished this remedial posture from the imposition of civil penalties that triggered Jarkesy concerns.

Finally, and critically, the Advisers Act provides an exclusive statutory review mechanism: 15 U.S.C. § 80b-13(a) allows any 'person aggrieved' by a final SEC order to obtain review in the appropriate United States Court of Appeals. Under the doctrine of Thunder Basin Coal Co. v. Reich, 510 U.S. 200 (1994), district courts generally lack jurisdiction to entertain pre-emptive challenges to agency proceedings when Congress has provided a comprehensive review scheme. Devereaux must exhaust his administrative remedies and, if barred, seek review in the D.C. Circuit or his home circuit. The district court should dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) for lack of subject matter jurisdiction over the claims seeking to halt the proceeding and under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim on the merits.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act § 203(f), 15 U.S.C. § 80b-3(f); 15 U.S.C. § 80b-3(e)(4); 15 U.S.C. § 80b-13(a) (statutory review of SEC orders); Securities Exchange Act § 10(b), 15 U.S.C. § 78j(b); SEC Rule 10b-5, 17 C.F.R. § 240.10b-5; Bartko v. SEC, 845 F.3d 1217 (D.C. Cir. 2017); Thunder Basin Coal Co. v. Reich, 510 U.S. 200 (1994)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The SEC's follow-on administrative proceeding is lawfully predicated on an existing federal court injunction under Section 203(f), and the district court lacks jurisdiction to enjoin the proceeding because Congress provided an exclusive appellate review mechanism for final SEC orders.

fact_pattern:
Ridgeway Capital Advisors, LLC is an SEC-registered investment adviser based in Chicago, Illinois, managing approximately $2.8 billion in assets under management as of December 2022. Ridgeway serves as the investment adviser to the Ridgeway Multi-Strategy Fund, LP (the 'Fund'), a private fund with 47 limited partners consisting primarily of pension funds, university endowments, and family offices. The Fund's limited partnership agreement and advisory agreement authorize Ridgeway to invest in a diversified portfolio of equity, fixed income, and alternative strategies, subject to certain concentration limits and liquidity parameters outlined in the Fund's offering memorandum.

In March 2023, Ridgeway's Chief Investment Officer, Marcus Delaney, directed the portfolio management team to allocate approximately $340 million—roughly 28% of the Fund's NAV—into a series of illiquid structured credit instruments issued by Harborview Structured Products, a newly formed special purpose vehicle. Harborview's principals included a college roommate of Delaney's, though this relationship was not disclosed to the Fund's limited partners or the Fund's advisory committee. The structured credit instruments carried no independent credit rating, had a weighted average maturity of 12 years, and featured a liquidity lock-up preventing redemption for 7 years. The Fund's offering memorandum stated that no more than 15% of net assets would be invested in any single illiquid strategy and that the adviser would maintain sufficient portfolio liquidity to honor quarterly redemption requests with 90 days' notice.

Ridgeway's investment committee met briefly on March 10, 2023, to discuss the Harborview allocation. Meeting minutes reflect a 20-minute discussion with no independent credit analysis, no stress testing of the instruments under adverse market scenarios, and no assessment of the impact on the Fund's ability to meet redemption obligations. No third-party valuation was obtained. When the Fund's compliance officer, Janet Kowalski, flagged the concentration limit breach and liquidity concerns in a written memo dated March 14, 2023, Delaney responded via email that the 'opportunity is time-sensitive and the returns justify the risk.' The allocation proceeded on March 17, 2023. By September 2023, two limited partners—a state teachers' pension fund and a university endowment—submitted redemption requests totaling $195 million. Ridgeway was forced to gate redemptions, citing insufficient portfolio liquidity, and the Harborview instruments were subsequently marked down by 40% following a deterioration in underlying collateral performance.
question: Did Ridgeway Capital Advisors breach its fiduciary duty of care under Section 206 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, as articulated in the SEC's 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation, in connection with the Harborview allocation?
answer:
Yes, Ridgeway Capital Advisors breached its fiduciary duty of care under Section 206 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (the 'Advisers Act') in multiple respects. The SEC's 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation ('Release No. IA-5248') reaffirmed and clarified that an investment adviser owes its clients—including institutional fund clients—a fiduciary duty comprising both a duty of care and a duty of loyalty, enforceable under the antifraud provisions of Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Advisers Act.

The duty of care, as articulated by the SEC, requires an adviser to provide advice that is in the client's best interest, which encompasses (1) the duty to provide advice that is suitable and in the best interest of the client based on the client's objectives, (2) the duty to seek best execution, and (3) the duty to provide advice and monitoring over the course of the relationship. Each of these sub-duties was violated here.

First, Ridgeway failed to conduct a reasonable investigation before recommending and executing the Harborview allocation. The investment committee's 20-minute discussion with no independent credit analysis, no stress testing, and no third-party valuation falls far short of the reasonable inquiry standard. The Fiduciary Interpretation makes clear that an adviser must have a 'reasonable understanding of the... risks and rewards associated with the recommendation.' Investing 28% of Fund NAV in unrated, illiquid structured credit instruments issued by a newly formed SPV without any independent diligence is a paradigmatic failure of reasonable care.

Second, the allocation directly contravened the Fund's own offering memorandum, which imposed a 15% concentration limit on illiquid strategies and required maintaining sufficient liquidity for quarterly redemptions. An adviser's duty of care requires adherence to the investment parameters agreed upon with the client. By breaching these contractual constraints—which defined the scope of the advisory mandate—Ridgeway acted outside the bounds of its fiduciary authority.

Third, Ridgeway's disregard of its own compliance officer's written warning compounds the violation. The SEC has emphasized in enforcement actions that an adviser's internal compliance infrastructure is integral to discharging the duty of care, and the deliberate override of a compliance flag—particularly one identifying a concentration limit breach—evidences a knowing or reckless disregard of fiduciary obligations, supporting liability under both Section 206(1) (fraud) and Section 206(2) (negligence-based antifraud).

Fourth, the undisclosed personal relationship between Delaney and the Harborview principals implicates both the duty of care (failure to evaluate conflicts that could impair investment judgment) and the duty of loyalty (failure to disclose material conflicts). While the duty of loyalty analysis is separate, the failure to account for conflicts in the investment process itself is a duty of care deficiency.

Ridgeway cannot defend on the basis that the Fund's investors are sophisticated institutional parties. The SEC's Fiduciary Interpretation and subsequent statements—including in the 2022 Private Fund Advisers proposal—expressly confirm that the duty of care applies to advisers serving private fund clients. Sophistication of investors does not relieve the adviser of its independent obligation to act with care. The gating of redemptions and 40% markdown are consequential harms, but liability attaches to the process failures irrespective of outcome.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Sections 206(1) and 206(2); SEC Release No. IA-5248 (June 5, 2019) (Commission Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers — the Fiduciary Interpretation); SEC proposed rule on Private Fund Advisers (Release No. IA-5955)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Ridgeway executed a $340 million allocation into illiquid, unrated structured credit instruments—nearly double the Fund's stated concentration limit—without conducting any independent credit analysis, stress testing, or third-party valuation, and over the express written objection of its compliance officer.

fact_pattern:
In March 2017, Sandra Nguyen, age 62, and her husband Paul Nguyen, age 65, held a joint brokerage account at Westfield Securities, LLC, a dual-registered broker-dealer and investment adviser, with approximately $485,000 in diversified equity and fixed-income holdings. Their registered representative, Marcus Holt, had managed their account on a commission basis since 2012, executing roughly 8-12 trades per year at their direction. The Nguyens had moderate investment knowledge, having previously managed a small self-directed IRA, and retained full decision-making authority over their brokerage account—approving each trade before execution.

In April 2017, Westfield Securities rolled out a new fee-based advisory platform charging 1.25% annually on assets under management. During a routine portfolio review meeting on April 22, 2017, Holt informed the Nguyens about the new advisory platform and suggested they consider switching their joint brokerage account to the fee-based advisory account, noting it would provide ongoing portfolio monitoring and quarterly rebalancing. He presented a comparison sheet showing that their historical commissions over the prior three years averaged $3,200 per year, while the advisory fee at 1.25% would be approximately $6,062 annually. The Nguyens asked Holt whether he thought the switch was a good idea, and Holt responded that 'it depends on your preferences—some clients prefer the predictability of an annual fee and the additional services, but the math shows you'd pay more given your current trading activity.' The Nguyens ultimately decided to switch.

By late 2018, the Nguyens realized they were paying nearly double in fees compared to their prior brokerage arrangement. They filed a class action in the Eastern District of California against Westfield Securities, alleging breach of fiduciary duty under FINRA Rules, the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, and California common law, claiming Holt had a duty to recommend only the account type that was in their best interest. Critically, the Nguyens structured their claims to avoid SLUSA preemption by framing the alleged misconduct as advice about account type rather than advice about the purchase or sale of securities. At the time of the recommendation (April 2017), Regulation Best Interest had not yet been adopted.
question: Did Westfield Securities breach a fiduciary duty owed to the Nguyens by recommending they switch from a commission-based brokerage account to a fee-based advisory account in April 2017, when the recommendation resulted in nearly double the annual fees?
answer:
Based on the legal framework analyzed in Anderson v. Edward D. Jones & Co. (9th Cir. 2025, No. 24-6164), Westfield Securities likely did not breach a fiduciary duty, and summary judgment in its favor would be appropriate.

First, FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) cannot serve as the source of fiduciary duty here. Under 15 U.S.C. § 78c(a)(4)(A) and § 78o(b)(8), FINRA suitability obligations apply to broker-dealers acting 'in connection with the purchase or sale of securities.' The Nguyens deliberately framed their claim as involving advice about account type—not the purchase or sale of specific securities—to avoid preemption under the Securities Litigation Uniform Standards Act (SLUSA). This strategic framing, while preserving their state-law class action vehicle, simultaneously removes the conduct from FINRA Rule 2111's regulatory scope. Moreover, Regulation Best Interest (17 C.F.R. pt. 240, effective June 30, 2020; adopted at 84 Fed. Reg. 33318 (July 12, 2019)) did not exist in April 2017 when the recommendation was made. Therefore, no federal broker-dealer best-interest standard applied to account-type recommendations at that time.

Second, the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 § 206 (15 U.S.C. § 80b-6) imposes on investment advisers a duty not to engage in fraud or deceit. At the time of the recommendation, Holt was acting in a brokerage capacity with respect to the joint account. Even if Westfield's dual registration triggered some IAA obligations, the Nguyens have disclaimed any fraud-based theory. Holt disclosed the fee comparison transparently, showing the Nguyens that they would pay more under the advisory arrangement. Absent evidence of fraudulent misrepresentation or material omission, § 206(2) is not violated.

Third, under California common law, a fiduciary duty arises when the financial professional exercises a high degree of control over the client's accounts. See Twomey v. Mitchum, Jones & Templeton, Inc., 69 Cal. Rptr. 222, 242 (Ct. App. 1968). Here, the Nguyens retained full decision-making authority, approved each trade individually, and independently decided to switch account types after receiving a transparent cost comparison. There is insufficient evidence that Holt was 'the controlling factor in the transactions.' Without such control, California law does not impose a fiduciary best-interest obligation on account-type advice.

Holt's transparent disclosure of the cost differential and the Nguyens' autonomous decision-making are dispositive. The higher fee alone does not establish breach absent a cognizable fiduciary duty.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); Investment Advisers Act of 1940 § 206 (15 U.S.C. § 80b-6); Regulation Best Interest (17 C.F.R. pt. 240); Securities Litigation Uniform Standards Act (SLUSA) 15 U.S.C. § 78bb(f); California fiduciary duty under Twomey v. Mitchum, Jones & Templeton, Inc., 69 Cal. Rptr. 222 (Ct. App. 1968)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: No cognizable fiduciary duty attached to account-type advice where FINRA suitability rules did not cover non-transactional recommendations, Reg BI had not yet been adopted, no fraud was alleged under the IAA, and the adviser did not exercise the degree of control over client accounts necessary to trigger California common-law fiduciary obligations.

fact_pattern:
Greenfield Capital Advisors, LLC ('Greenfield'), a registered investment adviser based in Houston, Texas, managed approximately $4.2 billion in assets under management as of December 2021. Greenfield specialized in energy-sector strategies and maintained model portfolios heavily weighted toward fossil fuel equities, including concentrated positions in large integrated oil and gas companies. In March 2022, the Massachusetts Securities Division, acting under the direction of the state Attorney General, opened an investigation into whether Greenfield had made materially misleading statements to its advisory clients about climate-related financial risks in its portfolio holdings. Specifically, the AG's office issued a Civil Investigative Demand ('CID') requesting all internal communications, research memoranda, and client presentation materials from January 2018 through March 2022 relating to Greenfield's assessment of stranded asset risk, carbon transition scenarios, and ESG-related disclosures made to clients.

Greenfield's chief compliance officer, Dana Harrington, immediately retained outside counsel and filed a motion to quash the CID in Massachusetts state court (Suffolk Superior Court), arguing that the CID was overbroad, unduly burdensome, and constituted viewpoint discrimination under the First Amendment because the investigation was allegedly motivated by the AG's publicly stated hostility toward the fossil fuel industry. The Suffolk Superior Court denied the motion to quash in August 2022, finding that the AG had articulated a sufficient basis for the investigation under Massachusetts General Laws ch. 93A. Greenfield did not appeal this ruling in the Massachusetts Appeals Court.

Instead, in November 2022, Greenfield filed a separate federal lawsuit in the Southern District of New York (where its primary custodian was located) under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging that the Massachusetts AG's investigation violated its First Amendment rights, its Fourteenth Amendment due process rights, and was preempted by the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Greenfield sought a preliminary injunction barring enforcement of the CID. Meanwhile, in January 2023, the Massachusetts AG concluded its investigation without filing any enforcement action, issuing a closing letter stating that it found insufficient evidence of violations. Despite the investigation's closure, Greenfield continued to press its federal claims, seeking declaratory relief and nominal damages, arguing that the investigation itself caused reputational harm and chilled its speech regarding climate and energy policy.
question: Can Greenfield Capital Advisors sustain its federal lawsuit against the Massachusetts Attorney General for alleged constitutional violations arising from the state investigation, given that the investigation has closed without enforcement and that Greenfield previously litigated the validity of the CID in Massachusetts state court?
answer:
Greenfield's federal lawsuit will almost certainly fail on two independent grounds: mootness and res judicata, closely tracking the Second Circuit's analysis in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Healey, No. 18-1170 (2d Cir. 2022).

First, regarding mootness: The Massachusetts AG closed the investigation in January 2023 without filing any enforcement action. Under Article III standing requirements, a plaintiff must demonstrate a concrete, ongoing injury that is capable of judicial redress. Once the investigation concluded with a closing letter and no adverse action, the threat of compelled disclosure under the CID ceased to exist. While Greenfield argues that reputational harm and chilling effects persist, federal courts have consistently held that speculative future injury from a concluded investigation does not satisfy the 'case or controversy' requirement. The Second Circuit in Exxon Mobil found that when the New York AG closed its investigation and the resulting enforcement action resolved in Exxon's favor, the federal claims were mooted. Greenfield's claims for declaratory relief similarly lack a live controversy. Its request for nominal damages may keep the case technically alive under Uzuegbunam v. Preczewski, 592 U.S. 279 (2021), but the merits barrier discussed next would still apply.

Second, and more dispositively, res judicata bars Greenfield's federal claims. Greenfield actively litigated the validity and enforceability of the CID in Suffolk Superior Court and lost when its motion to quash was denied in August 2022. Under Massachusetts claim preclusion principles—which federal courts must apply under 28 U.S.C. § 1738—a final judgment on the merits precludes relitigation of claims that were or could have been raised in the prior proceeding between the same parties. Greenfield's First Amendment and due process challenges to the AG's investigation could have been raised as defenses or counterclaims in the state court CID proceeding. Its failure to appeal the state court ruling forecloses a second bite at the apple in federal court. The Second Circuit applied precisely this reasoning to Exxon's claims against the Massachusetts AG, holding that the federal suit was barred because Exxon could have pursued the same constitutional challenges in the Massachusetts state court proceeding.

Greenfield's federal preemption argument under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 § 222 (savings clause preserving state authority) is also unavailing, as the IAA expressly preserves concurrent state regulatory authority over investment advisers. The federal complaint should be dismissed.
applicable_standard: U.S. Const. Art. III (case or controversy / mootness); 42 U.S.C. § 1983; 28 U.S.C. § 1738 (full faith and credit to state court judgments); Investment Advisers Act of 1940 § 222 (state regulatory authority savings clause); Massachusetts General Laws ch. 93A (consumer protection / CID authority); Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Healey, No. 18-1170 (2d Cir. 2022); Uzuegbunam v. Preczewski, 592 U.S. 279 (2021)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Greenfield's failure to raise its constitutional challenges in the Massachusetts state court CID proceeding, combined with the subsequent closure of the investigation, renders its federal lawsuit barred by res judicata and likely moot.

fact_pattern:
Greenfield Manufacturing, Inc. is a mid-size industrial equipment company headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, with approximately 4,200 employees. The company sponsors the Greenfield Manufacturing 401(k) Savings Plan (the 'Plan'), a defined contribution plan under ERISA with approximately $620 million in total assets as of December 31, 2022. The Plan's Investment Committee, consisting of CFO Margaret Dunham, VP of Human Resources Robert Kelsey, and General Counsel Patricia Nguyen, serves as the named fiduciary responsible for selecting and monitoring the Plan's investment options and service providers.

Since 2014, the Plan has used Apex Retirement Services as its recordkeeper. Apex charges the Plan through a combination of direct per-participant fees ($42 per participant per year) and revenue-sharing arrangements with 11 of the Plan's 22 investment options. The revenue-sharing payments range from 15 to 45 basis points on assets invested in those particular funds, resulting in total recordkeeping compensation to Apex of approximately $1.87 million in 2022. Comparable recordkeepers serving plans of similar size in the same industry were charging between $800,000 and $1.1 million in total annual compensation during the same period. The Investment Committee has not conducted a formal request for proposals (RFP) from competing recordkeepers since Apex was initially selected in 2014, and meeting minutes from 2018 through 2022 contain no substantive discussion of the reasonableness of Apex's fees relative to market benchmarks.

In addition, the Plan offers several actively managed equity funds with expense ratios between 0.72% and 1.15%, including the Ridgeway Large Cap Growth Fund (0.95% expense ratio) and the Cascade Mid-Cap Value Fund (1.15% expense ratio). Both funds have consistently underperformed their benchmark indices over trailing 3-, 5-, and 10-year periods. Lower-cost institutional share classes of both funds were available to the Plan given its asset size, which would have reduced expense ratios by 25 to 40 basis points. The Investment Committee's meeting minutes from 2019 to 2022 show that investment performance reviews were conducted annually but do not reflect any analysis of whether cheaper share classes were available or any evaluation of replacing underperforming funds with passively managed index fund alternatives. Plan participant Marcus Thompson, a production line supervisor who has been contributing 8% of his $67,000 annual salary to the Plan since 2016, filed suit in the Eastern District of Wisconsin in March 2023, alleging that the fiduciaries breached their duties of prudence and loyalty under ERISA §404.
question: Did the Greenfield Manufacturing Plan's Investment Committee breach its ERISA fiduciary duties of prudence and loyalty by failing to monitor and control recordkeeping fees and by retaining high-cost, underperforming investment options without adequate review?
answer:
The Investment Committee likely breached its fiduciary duties under ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) (duty of loyalty) and §404(a)(1)(B) (duty of prudence), and Thompson has stated viable claims that should survive a motion to dismiss under the framework articulated in Hughes v. Northwestern University, 142 S. Ct. 737 (2022), and applied in cases like Albert v. Oshkosh Corporation.

First, regarding recordkeeping fees: ERISA fiduciaries have a continuing duty to monitor plan expenses and ensure they are reasonable. See Tibble v. Edison Int'l, 575 U.S. 523, 529 (2015). The Plan paid Apex approximately $1.87 million in 2022 when comparable services were available for $800,000 to $1.1 million — an overpayment of roughly $770,000 to $1.07 million annually. The failure to conduct an RFP or any competitive benchmarking since 2014 — an eight-year gap — is particularly damaging. As the Seventh Circuit recognized in Albert, the duty of prudence requires fiduciaries to employ a deliberative process, and the total absence of recordkeeper fee benchmarking in committee minutes over four consecutive years strongly suggests a failure to engage in the kind of ongoing monitoring that a prudent fiduciary 'familiar with such matters' would undertake. 29 U.S.C. §1104(a)(1)(B). Revenue-sharing arrangements that obscure total recordkeeper compensation compound the problem, as fiduciaries must understand and evaluate the full cost of services, not merely direct fees.

Second, regarding investment options: The retention of the Ridgeway Large Cap Growth Fund and Cascade Mid-Cap Value Fund — both with high expense ratios and persistent benchmark underperformance over 3-, 5-, and 10-year periods — without any documented analysis of lower-cost share classes or index alternatives constitutes a plausible breach of prudence. Hughes made clear that the availability of cheaper alternatives within the plan's own menu does not excuse fiduciaries from ensuring each individual investment option is prudent. The fact that institutional share classes were available at 25-40 basis points less, and the committee never evaluated them, demonstrates a deficient monitoring process.

The Investment Committee might defend by arguing that offering a range of active and passive options satisfies its duties, but after Hughes, this defense is significantly weakened. The Supreme Court rejected the notion that merely providing adequate choices insulates fiduciaries from scrutiny of individual offerings. The Committee could also argue business judgment deference under the 'range of reasonable alternatives' standard, but the complete absence of documented deliberation on fee competitiveness and share class availability undermines any such defense. Under 29 U.S.C. §1109(a), the Committee members are personally liable to make the Plan whole for losses resulting from their breaches, including the excess fees paid to Apex and the drag on participant returns from unnecessarily expensive fund share classes.
applicable_standard: ERISA §404(a)(1)(A) (duty of loyalty), 29 U.S.C. §1104(a)(1)(A); ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) (duty of prudence), 29 U.S.C. §1104(a)(1)(B); ERISA §502(a)(2), 29 U.S.C. §1132(a)(2); ERISA §409(a), 29 U.S.C. §1109(a); Tibble v. Edison Int'l, 575 U.S. 523 (2015); Hughes v. Northwestern University, 142 S. Ct. 737 (2022)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: The Investment Committee's failure to conduct any competitive benchmarking of recordkeeping fees for eight years and its failure to evaluate the availability of lower-cost share classes for consistently underperforming funds demonstrate a deficient fiduciary monitoring process in violation of ERISA's duty of prudence.

fact_pattern:
Marcus Reinhardt co-founded Apex Capital Partners, LLC ('Apex') in 2016 with managing member David Calloway in Chicago, Illinois. Apex was a registered investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 that also operated a family of subsidiary LLCs focused on real estate investment management, including Apex Student Housing Manager, LLC, Apex Senior Living Fund, LLC, and Apex Industrial Holdings, LLC. Under the Operating Agreement of each subsidiary LLC, Reinhardt accumulated profits interests, Class B membership units, and carried interest allocations over his tenure, collectively valued at approximately $45 million by Q1 2020.

In March 2020, Calloway informed Reinhardt that his employment was being terminated 'for cause,' citing alleged misrepresentations on client performance reports and unauthorized personal trades in a competing fund. The Operating Agreements of the subsidiary LLCs contained forfeiture provisions stating that upon a 'for cause' termination, the departing member would forfeit all unvested and vested economic interests, whereas a 'without cause' termination entitled the departing member to repurchase of vested interests at fair market value within 90 days. The 'cause' definition in most of the agreements included 'material dishonesty,' 'gross negligence,' and 'willful misconduct,' but notably did not include a catch-all provision for breach of fiduciary duty standing alone.

Reinhardt maintains that the purported 'for cause' grounds were pretextual — that he never misrepresented performance data and that his personal investments were fully disclosed and did not compete with Apex. He alleges Calloway fabricated the cause determination in bad faith to avoid a $45 million repurchase obligation, and instead sought to redistribute Reinhardt's equity to a new partner, Anthony Ferraro, who joined Apex in January 2020. Reinhardt further alleges that Calloway, as managing member and controlling person, owed him fiduciary duties under both the LLC agreements and Delaware law, and that stripping his vested interests without a legitimate cause determination constituted a breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and conversion. Calloway and Apex counter that the Operating Agreements contain an express provision eliminating default fiduciary duties to the maximum extent permitted under Delaware's LLC Act (6 Del. C. § 18-1101(c)) and that the implied covenant claim is duplicative of the breach of contract claim.
question: Did Calloway and Apex breach their fiduciary duties and the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing by terminating Reinhardt 'for cause' under pretextual grounds to avoid paying fair market value for his $45 million in vested interests, and can the fiduciary duty and implied covenant claims survive a motion to dismiss given the contractual elimination of default fiduciary duties?
answer:
The analysis turns on several intersecting Delaware LLC Act provisions and common law principles. First, regarding the fiduciary duty claim: Under 6 Del. C. § 18-1101(c), an LLC agreement may restrict or eliminate fiduciary duties, but it may not eliminate the implied contractual covenant of good faith and fair dealing (§ 18-1101(e)). If the Operating Agreements contain an express fiduciary duty waiver, then Reinhardt's standalone fiduciary duty claim (analogous to Count IV in Smith v. Scott) is likely subject to dismissal. Delaware courts consistently enforce such waivers where the language is clear and unambiguous. See Feeley v. NHAOCG, LLC, 62 A.3d 649 (Del. Ch. 2012). Therefore, the fiduciary duty claim would likely fail at the motion to dismiss stage unless Reinhardt can demonstrate the waiver provision was ambiguous or did not cover the specific conduct alleged.

However, the implied covenant claim presents a closer question. Under Delaware law, the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing applies where the contract is silent on a particular issue and one party exercises discretion in a manner that deprives the other of the fruits of the bargain. See Nemec v. Shrader, 991 A.2d 1120 (Del. 2010). Here, the 'for cause' determination involves Calloway exercising discretion as managing member. If the Operating Agreements do not specify who determines 'cause' or what process must be followed, the implied covenant may fill that gap by requiring that the determination be made in good faith. Reinhardt's allegation that Calloway fabricated the basis to avoid a $45 million repurchase obligation — and redirected the equity to Ferraro — is precisely the type of bad faith exercise of contractual discretion that the implied covenant is designed to police.

That said, as illustrated in Smith v. Scott, defendants will argue the implied covenant claim is duplicative of the breach of contract claim where the same conduct (wrongful for-cause termination) underlies both. Delaware courts dismiss implied covenant claims where the contract directly addresses the disputed conduct. If the Operating Agreements explicitly define 'cause' and the dispute is merely whether the factual predicates were met, the implied covenant claim may be subsumed by the breach of contract claim. But if Calloway's discretion in making the determination itself is the issue — and the agreements are silent on the standard of review — the implied covenant claim should survive.

The conversion claim likely fails as duplicative where the remedy sought is the same monetary recovery available under contract. The breach of contract claim (wrongful forfeiture of vested interests) is the strongest vehicle for Reinhardt's recovery. Overall, Calloway and Apex likely violated their contractual obligations by stripping Reinhardt's vested interests under a pretextual cause determination, but the fiduciary duty claim is vulnerable to the contractual waiver defense.
applicable_standard: 6 Del. C. § 18-1101(c) (elimination of fiduciary duties in LLC agreements); 6 Del. C. § 18-1101(e) (implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing cannot be eliminated); Investment Advisers Act § 206 (anti-fraud provisions); Nemec v. Shrader, 991 A.2d 1120 (Del. 2010); Feeley v. NHAOCG, LLC, 62 A.3d 649 (Del. Ch. 2012)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Calloway's exercise of discretion to declare a pretextual 'for cause' termination to avoid a $45 million repurchase obligation, while redirecting Reinhardt's equity to a new partner, constitutes the pivotal bad faith conduct underlying both the breach of contract and implied covenant claims.

fact_pattern:
Greenfield Capital Advisors, LLC is a registered investment adviser based in New York managing approximately $3.2 billion in discretionary accounts across 47 institutional and high-net-worth clients. The firm's founder and CIO, Margaret Chen, CFA, has full discretionary investment authority under standardized investment management agreements (IMAs) signed by each client. The IMAs grant Greenfield broad authority to buy and sell securities on behalf of clients without prior approval, subject to each client's stated investment policy parameters.

In March 2023, Margaret Chen identified Precision Medical Holdings, Inc. (PMH), a publicly traded medical device company with a market capitalization of $680 million, as significantly undervalued. Over the period from March 15, 2023 through April 30, 2023, Greenfield accumulated 12.8% of PMH's outstanding common stock across 31 client accounts, triggering a Schedule 13D filing on May 3, 2023. The 13D identified Greenfield as the reporting person and disclosed that Margaret Chen had been appointed to PMH's board of directors effective April 28, 2023. The filing listed aggregated beneficial ownership but did not individually name the 31 client accounts.

One of those clients was the Harmon Family Trust, managed by trustee David Harmon, which held approximately 1.4% of PMH's outstanding shares purchased by Greenfield on its behalf between March 20 and April 10, 2023. The Harmon Family Trust's IMA was a standard, non-issuer-specific discretionary agreement—it did not reference PMH or any particular security. David Harmon had no communication with Margaret Chen or anyone at Greenfield about PMH specifically, never discussed the PMH investment, and was not consulted before or after the purchases. On July 15, 2023, Greenfield sold the Harmon Family Trust's entire PMH position at a profit of $1.85 million, completing a purchase-and-sale cycle within six months.

On September 10, 2023, PMH shareholder plaintiff Robert Adler filed a Section 16(b) action in the Southern District of New York against the Harmon Family Trust, Greenfield Capital Advisors, Margaret Chen, and David Harmon individually, seeking disgorgement of the $1.85 million in short-swing profits. Adler's theory was that the Harmon Family Trust was a member of a Section 13(d)(3) 'group' with Greenfield and its other clients because the Trust had delegated discretionary authority to Greenfield, and Greenfield had filed a Schedule 13D and placed a director on PMH's board, thereby imputing insider status to all clients whose shares were aggregated in the filing.
question: Is the Harmon Family Trust liable for disgorgement of short-swing profits under Section 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act solely because its investment adviser, Greenfield Capital Advisors, filed a Schedule 13D and placed a director on the issuer's board, where the Trust's only connection to the issuer was a standard, non-issuer-specific discretionary investment management agreement?
answer:
The Harmon Family Trust is NOT liable for disgorgement of short-swing profits under Section 16(b). This conclusion follows directly from the Second Circuit's holding in Rubenstein v. International Value Advisers, LLC, No. 19-560-cv (2d Cir. 2020).

Section 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act, 15 U.S.C. § 78p(b), imposes strict liability for disgorgement of profits from short-swing trading—any purchase and sale, or sale and purchase, of an issuer's equity securities within six months—on statutory insiders, including beneficial owners of more than 10% of any class of equity security. Section 13(d)(3), 15 U.S.C. § 78m(d)(3), extends this concept by providing that two or more persons acting as a 'group' for the purpose of acquiring, holding, or disposing of securities shall be deemed a single person for purposes of beneficial ownership calculations.

The pivotal legal question is whether the Harmon Family Trust became a member of a Section 13(d)(3) group with Greenfield and its other clients by virtue of the standard discretionary IMA. The Second Circuit in Rubenstein squarely held that an investment management agreement delegating discretionary investment authority to an investment adviser is NOT an agreement to trade in the securities of a particular issuer and therefore is not a standalone basis for group membership under Section 13(d)(3). The court reasoned that group membership requires an agreement among persons specifically directed at acquiring, holding, or disposing of a particular issuer's securities. A generic discretionary mandate—one that does not reference any specific issuer—does not satisfy this requirement.

Further, the Rubenstein court held that an investment adviser's filing of a Schedule 13D or deputization of a director on an issuer's board does not, without more, impute insider status to each individual client account. The adviser's insider activities are attributable to the adviser, not automatically to passive clients who had no involvement in or knowledge of issuer-specific decisions.

Applying these principles, David Harmon and the Harmon Family Trust: (1) signed only a standard, non-issuer-specific IMA; (2) had no communication with Greenfield about PMH; (3) were not consulted regarding the PMH purchases or sales; and (4) entered no agreement with other Greenfield clients to acquire PMH stock. The Trust's inclusion in Greenfield's aggregated 13D filing is a function of regulatory attribution rules for beneficial ownership reporting—not evidence of a group agreement to trade PMH securities. Plaintiff Adler's Section 16(b) claim against the Harmon Family Trust should therefore be dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim, as the Trust is not a statutory insider subject to the short-swing profit rule.
applicable_standard: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 § 16(b), 15 U.S.C. § 78p(b); Securities Exchange Act § 13(d)(3), 15 U.S.C. § 78m(d)(3); SEC Rule 13d-3 (beneficial ownership definition); Rubenstein v. Int'l Value Advisers, LLC, No. 19-560-cv (2d Cir. 2020); Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: A standard, non-issuer-specific discretionary investment management agreement does not constitute an agreement to trade in a particular issuer's securities and therefore cannot serve as the sole basis for imputing Section 13(d)(3) group membership—and consequent Section 16(b) short-swing profit liability—to an investment adviser's client.

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners, LLC is a dually registered investment adviser and broker-dealer headquartered in Bethesda, Maryland, with approximately $1.2 billion in assets under management across 4,300 client accounts. On March 12, 2023, Meridian's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Reeves, received an alert from the firm's IT vendor, CyberShield Solutions, indicating anomalous outbound data transfers from Meridian's client relationship management (CRM) system. The transfers had been occurring intermittently since January 8, 2023, following a spear phishing attack in which a senior financial adviser, Thomas Kline, clicked a malicious link embedded in an email disguised as a routine compliance update from FINRA. Kline had elevated system privileges because he also served as a branch manager with administrative access to the CRM platform containing client names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, account numbers, net worth data, and investment holdings.

Upon discovering the anomaly, Reeves engaged an outside forensic cybersecurity firm, TridentTech, which determined on April 3, 2023, that threat actors had exfiltrated personally identifying information (PII) and financial data for approximately 2,800 clients. TridentTech's investigation revealed several deficiencies: (1) Meridian had not implemented multi-factor authentication (MFA) on its CRM system despite a recommendation from CyberShield in August 2022; (2) Kline's administrative credentials were never revoked or reset after the January phishing incident because Kline told Reeves he had not been logged into the CRM at the time of the click, which turned out to be false; (3) Meridian's written information security policies, last updated in 2019, did not require periodic penetration testing or intrusion detection monitoring; and (4) Meridian waited until May 15, 2023—over five months after the initial intrusion and six weeks after TridentTech's confirmation—to notify affected clients.

Among those affected was Helen Davenport, age 72, a retired federal employee with a $3.4 million advisory account at Meridian. In the weeks following the breach, unauthorized parties used Davenport's exfiltrated data to open two fraudulent credit card accounts totaling $47,000 and attempted an ACH transfer of $82,000 from her brokerage account, which was flagged and blocked by the custodian. Davenport and approximately 350 other affected clients retained counsel and filed a class action in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, asserting claims for breach of fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206, breach of implied contract to safeguard PII, negligence, and violations of the Maryland Consumer Protection Act (MCPA) §13-301. Meridian moved for summary judgment on all claims, arguing that the breach was caused by a sophisticated third-party criminal act and that no client suffered actual financial loss because the attempted ACH transfer was blocked.
question: Did Meridian Wealth Partners breach its fiduciary duty and implied contractual obligations to safeguard client PII, and can it successfully defend on summary judgment by attributing the breach to a sophisticated third-party cyberattack?
answer:
Meridian Wealth Partners likely breached both its fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act §206 and its implied contractual obligation to safeguard client PII, and its motion for summary judgment should be denied on those claims—though the MCPA claim presents a closer question.

First, as to fiduciary duty under §206 of the Advisers Act, the SEC has made clear through its 2019 interpretive guidance and enforcement actions (e.g., In re Cetera Advisor Networks, IA Rel. No. 5765 (2021); In re Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, IA Rel. No. 4415 (2016)) that an investment adviser's fiduciary duty encompasses a duty to protect client information. Regulation S-P (17 C.F.R. §248.30(a)), the Safeguards Rule, requires registered investment advisers to adopt written policies and procedures reasonably designed to protect customer records and information. Meridian's failure to implement MFA despite a specific vendor recommendation, its failure to revoke Kline's elevated credentials after a known phishing incident, its outdated 2019 information security policies lacking penetration testing requirements, and its prolonged failure to detect the ongoing exfiltration collectively demonstrate that its safeguards were not 'reasonably designed.' The parallel to CareFirst in Attias is instructive: there, the court denied summary judgment on the breach of implied contract claim precisely because a reasonable jury could find that the defendant failed to take reasonable steps to protect PII, particularly where an IT employee's elevated credentials were exploited after inadequate remediation of a phishing incident.

Second, on the implied contract claim, following the reasoning in Attias v. CareFirst, Inc. (D.D.C. 2023), courts have recognized that when a company collects sensitive PII in the course of a business relationship, an implied promise to take reasonable steps to safeguard that information arises. Meridian's client agreements, while not containing explicit cybersecurity warranties, implicitly required reasonable data protection as a condition of the advisory relationship. The multiple documented failures create genuine issues of material fact precluding summary judgment.

Third, Meridian's defense that the breach was caused by a 'sophisticated' third-party attack fails because the attack vector—spear phishing—is a well-known and foreseeable threat that reasonable cybersecurity measures (MFA, credential rotation, intrusion detection) are specifically designed to mitigate. The sophistication defense is unavailing where the defendant's own negligence provided the access pathway.

However, the MCPA claim under §13-301 may fail, as in Attias, if plaintiffs cannot demonstrate reliance on specific misrepresentations by Meridian regarding its data security practices. Unless Meridian affirmatively marketed its cybersecurity capabilities to clients in ways that were misleading, the reliance element will be difficult to establish.

Regarding actual harm, Davenport's $47,000 in fraudulent credit card charges and the attempted $82,000 ACH transfer establish concrete injury-in-fact sufficient for Article III standing and damages, even where the ACH transfer was blocked, because mitigation costs and time spent remedying identity theft constitute compensable harm under applicable precedent.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §206 (fiduciary duty); SEC Regulation S-P, 17 C.F.R. §248.30(a) (Safeguards Rule); FINRA Rule 3110 (supervision); Maryland Consumer Protection Act §13-301; implied contract doctrine under Maryland common law; Attias v. CareFirst, Inc., No. 15-cv-882 (D.D.C. 2023)
key_violation_or_compliance_factor: Meridian's failure to revoke the administrative credentials of a branch manager after a known phishing incident, combined with the absence of multi-factor authentication and outdated information security policies, constituted an unreasonable failure to safeguard client PII in breach of both fiduciary and implied contractual duties.
